This Book is Cheerfully Dedicated To An Educator, Jurist and Humanitarian Former Chief Judge Henry D. Harlan In Recognition Of: 

His thirty-six years of continuous services as President of the Board of Trustees of Johns Hopkins Hospital, and of his forty-four years of continuous services as a member of the Board of Trustees of this world-famous educational and humanitarian institution.

His thirty-five years of continuous services as a member of the Board of Trustees of Johns Hopkins University. 

His fifty-seven years of continuous services to the University of Maryland School of Law, of which he is presently Dean Emeritus, besides being President of its Faculty Council. 

He became a member of the teaching faculty of this noted law school in 1882, and continued to teach for a period of forty years; and for twenty-one years also served as the active Dean of the School. 

Moreover, these long years of active teaching flowed from such vast stores of learning, sincerity and kindliness as to have made him a powerful influence in the lives of many past and present leaders of our Bench and Bar. His book on Domestic Relations has been cited repeatedly by the Court of Appeals of Maryland.

His twenty-five years of learned, impartial and gentlemanly services as Chief Judge of the Supreme Bench of Baltimore City.

His many other public services, which we regretfully cannot mention here because of the dearth of both space and time. iii

The Two Chief Objectives of This Book And The Author's Expression of Appreciation 

The labor involved in the building of this book was begun about five years ago with two chief objectives in mind, the first of which is described in the current "Official Publication" 

of the University of Maryland School of Law as follows: 

"Scholarships "In 1922, Mr. Louis S. Ashman, of the Baltimore Bar and an alumnus of the Law School, assigned to the Regents all royaltie's to be derived from the publication of his book 'Prayers and Instructions' in order to provide a fund for the establishment of a scholarship or scholarships * * * "At least one of such scholarships has been awarded in each year since. "For the purpose of continuing these scholarships, Mr. Ashman, in 1935, began the preparation of another book *** the royalties from which have been pre-assigned to the Regents (of the University of Maryland)"

The second objective (of the said two objectives) was to build a text book that would enable our law schools to give adequate courses on the law of directed verdicts, prayers and instructions. In this connection, it should be observed that under the Maryland practice a lawyer is permitted to represent clients in court from the moment of his admission to the Bar.

From the very inception and throughout this five-year adventure, the author was greatly encouraged and benefited by the advice and counsel of Judges T. Scott Offutt, Henry D.

Harlan, Eli Frank and W. Calvin Chesnut. In addition, each of these great jurists and noted public servants engaged in exacting reviews and criticism of different titles or chapters of the author's work, which required vast labor and study on their part.

As may be readily observed, the titles which 

Judges Offutt, Harlan and Frank reviewed, respectively, are listed under the following "Table of Contents."

§§ 1 TITLE 1 § 1. Instructions to Juries are "Called Indifferently Prayers, or 

Instructions" in Md. Courts.

The Court of Appeals of Maryland recently pointed out that -under the Maryland practice the instructions to juries "are called indifferently prayers, or instructions, but however entitled, when granted, they become the instructions of the court, and, as such, are binding upon the jury, or the court sitting as a jury," in civil trials at law.¹

The prayers or instructions in criminal trials are but advis ory.2 

§ 2. History of Instructions to Juries in Md. Civil Trials—“Prayers” -Md. Act of 1642 and Md. Declaration of Rights of 1776-Other States. 

Although the practice of written instructions seems to have been foreign to the common law,3 the General Assembly of the Province of Maryland passed a law in 1642, or within about eight years of the landing of the first small group of Colonists on Maryland soil, which prescribed, among other things, that the "charge" of the trial judge on "the point in issue shall be delivered to the Jury in writing." 4

Cause of Act of 1642 

There are no published records to explain the reason for the passage of the Act of 1642, but the following thought—expressed in the majority opinion of Justice Harlan in the

TITLE 1 Act of 1642 as Genesis of Prayers 

The afore-quoted Act of the Provincial Legislature of Maryland, adopted in 1642, like other statutory laws of that date, was made to last until the next session of the General Assembly or for three years; and it does not appear that it was ever renewed. But it is likely that this Act was the genesis of the existing Maryland system of written instructions, which, in later years, came to be known, in the Maryland practice, as "prayers"; probably in consequence of the fact that counsel, in practice, "prayed" the court to grant the instructions proposed by them.

First Written Instruction in Md. Court 

The first recorded evidence of a written instruction by a Maryland trial judge to a jury, then commonly called a jurors' charge, appears in a slander suit tried in the Provincial 

Court of Maryland in the year 1664, and reads as follows:5 "Whether doctor Luke Barber accuseing Elinor Spinke in saying her oathe was false and malicious those words were spoken by him afore or after she had taken her oathe if spoken before to finde for the defendant, if after to finde for the plaintiff with costs and damages."

First Variance in Md. Courts 

The proceedings of this slander suit against Dr. Barber also contain the first recorded evidence of a variance between the pleadings and the proof in the Maryland courts; for “the process and Judgment against Barber being brought into the howse of Assembly", on appeal, the "first Error" alleged was, in substance, "the difference betweene the writt and declaration". "And the vote of the howse nemine Contradicente was that the error was substantial and not in forme of the declaration only and therefore Vote the Judgment Erroneous and that they both pay their owne Charge." 6

Oral Instructions After Act of 1642 

In the years following the afore-explained expiration of the Act of 1642, the Court of Appeals of Maryland ruled, again and again, that a trial judge could instruct the jury orally or in

writing, or by both methods, although, as is further explained in section 10, the practice of written prayers or instructions is preferred. 

Court Must Not Comment on Evidence 

But the Maryland courts have held, seemingly from their foundation, that a trial judge must not comment or indicate his opinion upon the weight of the evidence or the credibility of the witnesses in respect to an issue of fact which the court could not properly take from the finding of the jury. 

The prevailing Maryland practice of prayers or instructions in civil trials at law, insofar as the practice relates to the preference of written prayers or instructions over oral instructions and in regard to the duty of a Maryland trial court to refrain from commenting upon the weight of the evidence or the credibility of witnesses, is entirely the product of the decisions of the Court of Appeals of Maryland.8

Prayers in Court Trials 

The practice of instructing the jury by written prayers or instructions in the Maryland courts applies, with equal force, to trials where the court itself sits as the jury.9 

Practice of Instructions in Other States 

In 37 States of the nation (as was declared in the address of Chief Judge John J. Parker, published in the 1938 March and April issues of the American Bar Association Journal) the court is forbidden to express an opinion on the facts or to comment upon the evidence, and in 28 of the States the court is forbidden to charge the jury at all except by formal written instructions;10 which practice is guaranteed and

§ 3. History of “Advisory" Instructions to Juries in Criminal Trials 

-Md. Constitution Makes Jury “Judges of Law, as well as of fact.”

Section 5 of article 15 of the prevailing Constitution of Maryland, adopted in 1867, declares (as did the Maryland 

Constitutions of 1851 and 1864) that: "In the trial of all criminal cases, the jury shall be the 

Judges of Law, as well as of fact." 

In Franklin v. State (12 Md. 236, 245)—the Court of Appeals of Maryland pointed out that this Constitutional provision is merely declaratory, and did not alter the pre-existing law regulating the powers of the court and jury in the trial of criminal cases.

Both before and since the constitutional declaration upon the subject, it has been the practice of Judges in some parts of the State to decline to give instructions to the jury in criminal cases under any circumstances; while in other parts of the State it has been the practice for the Judges to give advisory instructions when requested so to do. It seems to have been regarded as entirely a matter of discretion with the Judge, there being no positive duty requiring him to pursue the one course or the other.12 

In Broll v. State (45 Md. 356, 359), the Court of Appeals of

Maryland definitely declared that no trial court in this State can be required by the counsel or jury to give instructions either upon the law or the legal effect of the evidence given at the trial of a criminal case; and that-"This seems to have

When the trial Judge has thought it proper to instruct, it has always been deemed necessary that he should be careful to put the instruction in an advisory form, so that the jury be left entirely free to find their verdict in accordance with their own judgment of the law, as well as the facts. The instruction, when given, goes to the jury simply as a means of enlightenment, and not as a binding and positive rule for their government, as it does in civil cases. The Judge, therefore, cannot, by an instruction given in a criminal case, bind the jury as to the definition of the crime, or as to the legal effect of the evidence before them. He can only bind and conclude the jury as to what evidence shall be considered by them, he being the exclusive judge of what facts or circumstances are admissible for their consideration. 

The practice of instructing the jury, in criminal trials, within the limitations and under the restrictions afore-stated, has repeatedly received the sanction of the Court of Appeals of Maryland.13 

§ 4. Definition of a Prayer-When a Prayer Becomes an In struction.

A prayer, in the first instance, is a request in writing by counsel to the trial court to declare to the jury, or to itself when it sits as both court and jury, one or more of the principles of law that should govern and guide the jury in reaching their findings in respect to one or more of the issues of fact involved in the case on trial.14

A prayer ripens into or acquires the status of a binding instruction only when it is granted by the trial judge.¹ 15 

§ 5. Definition of an Instruction—Opinion or Remarks of Court and/or Counsel as Instructions.

An instruction may be defined as any direction given to the jury by the court in reference to the law of the case. Any

But an opinion or declaration of the trial court that was advanced merely in support of its rulings upon the evidence or in support of its rulings upon the prayers, or in support of its verdict in a case where the court also sat as the jury, is not ordinarily regarded as an instruction,¹7 unless it may reasonably be construed as likely to influence the jury or affect their consideration of the issues submitted to them.18 

A declaration of law by counsel to the jury which the court has refused to restrain, may be construed as an instruction.19 

For a better understanding of when an opinion or a declaration of the trial court or of counsel will, or will not, constitute an instruction upon the law of the case, see Illustrations "A" to "H" of section 6.20

In Sowerwein v. Jones (7 Gill & Johnson, 335, 337, 340, 341)—wherein the trial judge, in giving his reasons for rejecting a prayer of the plaintiff, commented in the presence of the jury upon the legal insufficiency of the evidence to prove a certain point, and announced rules of law as applicable to certain evidence introduced in the casethe Court of Appeals held that these statements of the trial judge, under the circumstances of this case, came within the scope and meaning of the term "instruction", since they were capable of influencing the jury and did control counsel.

Illustration-B 

In Coffin v. Brown (94 Md. 190, 202), the Court of Appeals declared (our paragraphing): "But if we assume that there was sufficient evidence to justify its admission, what the Court said in admitting it was reversible error "The language thus used by the Court, in the presence of the jury, was certainly calculated to affect the jury and thereby injure the defendant. The Court in effect said that the publication of the circular was a natural consequence of the defendant sending the letter to Mr. Vandiver at that time. The circular being admitted with that statement, the jury might very naturally think that that question was settled by the Court while, as we have seen, it was a question for the jury. "If a written instruction had been granted to the effect of what we have quoted, there could be no doubt that it would have been error, and such an oral statement, in the presence of the jury, was calculated to greatly injure the defendant, and perhaps make it useless for his counsel to argue that question before the jury."

"In effect, the jury were told that they could render a verdict for the plaintiff in this action, if they believed from the evidence that Frank Nash had been absent and unheard of for a period of seven years, notwithstanding they did not believe that the body, which was claimed to be that of Nash, was the body of Nash. Illustration-G 

In McCullough v. Biedler (66 Md. 283-285), it was held that the opinion of the trial judge, delivered in support of his conclusion upon a controlling issue of fact, submitted, by consent of the parties, to his determination without the aid of a jury, could not be made the basis of an exception and an appeal, merely because it could be gleaned from the opinion what was thought of the law applicable to a case and evidence such as that under consideration.

The Court of Appeals emphasized that the appeal in this McCullough case would not lie because "the appeal is from the finding and not the Court's ruling on any question of law presented by either side."

In Tinges v. Moale (25 Md. 480, 485), it was said, in part: "The opinion of the Court succinctly states the principle which governed it in the decision, viz: "If a broker who first procures a purchaser, reports his offers to his principal without identifying the person from whom they come, he cannot recover commissions in case of a subsequent sale through another broker at the same price, to the same purchaser, unless it appears in evidence that the seller knew this fact, or that notice was given him by the plaintiff before the completion of the contract and payment of commissions to the second broker.' "We are of opinion that this was a correct exposition of the law in such a case, and that the judgment of the Court should be affirmed. "*** Before leaving this case, it may be proper to observe that in cases like this, of submission to the Court without the aid of a jury, more care or precision should be adopted in raising the questions of law for the decision of the Court below, that upon appeal parties may not lose the benefit of appeal, or this Court be left to gather them from the opinion of the Court below, or the course of the trial there." § 7. Definition of a "Demurrer Prayer”"_"Demurrers to the Evidence"-Prayer for "Directed Verdict" "General" and "Specific” Demurrer Prayers.

A DEMURRER prayer is one that asks the court to peremptorily direct the jury to return their verdict in favor of the proponent of the prayer, or which, in effect, prays the court to take any lesser issue of the case from the consideration of the jury, either upon (a) the assumption of the truth of a certain controlling fact; or (b) upon the assumption, as a fact,

§§ 7-8 TITLE 1 

that there is a want of evidence legally sufficient to sustain the case, claim or defense, as the case may be, that the prayer in question seeks to take from the jury, expressly or in effect.22 

Under the Maryland practice, the offering of prayers to take a case from the jury, in part or whole, is deemed to be equivalent to a demurrer to the evidence. Generally speaking, every demurrer prayer involves consideration of the legal scope or sufficiency of evidence.23

The Maryland decisions speak of demurrer prayers as both demurrers to the evidence and as prayers that seek directed verdicts or other directed findings.24

A GENERAL demurrer prayer is one that embodies a request that the court should peremptorily direct the jury to reach a prescribed verdict or other finding upon the ground that the evidence is not legally sufficient to sustain the case, claim or defense at which the prayer is aimed.25

A SPECIFIC demurrer prayer is one that seeks a directed verdict or other directed finding upon a more specific legal ground than a mere general failure of evidence legally sufficient to sustain the case, claim or defense at which the prayer is aimed.26 

§ 8. Definition of a “Jury Prayer.” 

A JURY prayer is one that predicates or postulates its conclusion upon a hypothesis of facts which are submitted or left to the finding or determination of the jury, or which expressly states a rule of law in hypothetical form, to be applied by the jury only if the jury should find or believe a specified state of

§ 9. 

Definition of a "Variance Prayer."

A VARIANCE prayer is, in relation to the Variance Prayer 

Act of 1914 (Code, article 5, section 11), one that directs the court's attention to a variance between the pleadings and the proof, and prays for an instruction to the jury that is predicated thereupon.28 

§ 10. Oral Instructions-Written Instructions Preferred-Court's Own Instructions-No Duty to Formulate. 

Since the expiration of the Act of 1642 of the Provincial Legislature of Maryland, in 1645, as explained in section 2 of this title, the Maryland courts have not been subjected to any positive rule prohibiting oral instructions.29 

But while the practice of oral instructions is not prohibited in the Maryland courts, and, on the contrary, there may be cases in which that method of instructing the jury may not only be appropriate but essential to any proper performance of the duties imposed upon the court, the ordinary practice is for the trial court to deliver to the jury at the request of the parties such written instructions as were submitted by them and approved by the court, or as modified or altered by the court, or such written instructions as the court formulates of its own motion.30

The Court of Appeals of Maryland recently declared that it is not material whether the jury is instructed as to the law by written instructions offered by the parties, by written in-

§ 11. Form or Requisites of Court's Own Oral or Written Instruc tions-Exceptions.

The propriety of the court's own prepared instructions, whether they be in oral or written form, will be measured by the same standards as those applicable to instructions submitted by the parties.33

Where a trial court assumes the responsibility of rejecting a proper instruction submitted by either of the parties, and itself instructs the jury as to the law under which a recovery may be had or defeated, it is bound to instruct them completely and accurately as to every fact and legal principle material to the question to which the instruction is directed.34 

When oral instructions are given by the trial court to the jury, or when a trial court has made other oral declarations tending to influence the verdict of the jury, it is certainly the right of the party who desires to except thereto, to have them reduced to writing, so that they may be reviewed on appeal; especially since the objectionable part of an oral instruction or other declaration of the trial court must be distinctly indicated in the bill of exceptions.35

§ 12. Practical Value of Md. System of Written Prayers-Federal System of Oral Instructions Not Desirable for Md. Courts. 

Charles McHenry Howard (a member and officer of the noted Council of The American Law Institute), Charles 

Markell and Judge Robert Stanton-all distinguished members of the Baltimore Bar-delivered learned addresses before the Maryland State Bar Association in opposition to the Maryland practice of written instructions, commonly called "prayers," and in favor of the Federal practice of oral instructions, including the right of a Federal trial judge to orally and graphically express to the jury his opinion regarding the weight of the evidence and the credibility of the witnesses.38

At the publication of this work, in the year 1939, its author desires to reiterate, in the main, the opinion expressed in his aforementioned work on "Prayers and Instructions," published in 1923, to the effect that Maryland juries do, on the whole, intelligently apply prayers, except where the jury is confronted with too many prayers; a practice condemned by the 

Court of Appeals of Maryland.40

Moreover, it seems that most of the members of the Maryland Bar are of the opinion that the average Maryland juror

§§ 13-14 TITLE 2 § 13. Trials and Proceedings in which the Practice of Prayers and Instructions is Applicable-In General. 

The Maryland practice of prayers and instructions applies in the following courts, trials and proceedings: (a)—In the trial of criminal cases and civil cases at law, without regard to whether the cases are tried before the court and the usual jury, or before the court sitting as a jury;¹ but in criminal trials the court does not have to grant correct prayers, and the granted prayers or instructions are but advisory to, and so not binding upon, the jury.2 (b)—In trials in the law courts upon agreed statements of fact.3 (c)—In the trial of issues of fact before a chancellor and a jury sitting in a court of equity of Baltimore City.4 (d)-In the trial of issues of fact sent from the Equity courts to the Law courts for determination by jury.5 (e) In the trial of issues of fact sent from the Orphans' courts to the Law courts for determination by jury. (f)—In the trial of issues of fact formulated in the Law courts in Workmen's Compensation cases on appeal from the State Industrial Accident Commission." 

(g)-In the hearing of Mandamus proceedings.8 (h)—In hearings before the State Tax Commission itself, and, seemingly, also in the law courts on appeal from the said Commission.9

Practical Value of Prayers 

In this connection, it should be observed that, except in the trial of a criminal case, a granted prayer becomes a binding instruction by the court to the jury upon some phase of the law of the case, which should guide and control the jury in arriving at their verdict, and that, moreover, counsel may emphasize this important function of the granted prayers in their argument to the jury.12

It should also be borne in mind that the granted prayers of a case go to the jury room, where they may be and frequently are read and re-read by the jury before arriving at their verdict. In this connection, it should be further observed that a prayer generally embodies the theories of law and/or fact which are favorable to its proponent.18 13 The judicious employment of demurrer14 or variance¹5 prayers will often result in directed or mandatory verdicts in favor of their respective proponents. 

Limited Function of Court of Appeals in Law Cases 

After a verdict is rendered, the trial judge may set it aside and grant a new trial, if justice, in his sound discretion, so requires it. But the functions of the Court of Appeals of 

Maryland are much more limited on appeals to it from the law courts of the state. In respect to such appeals, the appellate court has no right to decide on the correctness or incorrectness of the verdict of a jury, or the court sitting as a

Review of Rulings on Motions for New Trials 

So the Court of Appeals is not empowered to review the question whether the trial judge had soundly exercised his discretion in granting or refusing a motion for a new trial.¹7

But while the disposition of a motion for a new trial, whether absolutely or on recognized terms, is within the sound discretion of the trial court and is not a subject for review on appeal, the arbitrary refusal of the trial court to hear a motion for a new trial, as well as the erroneous exclusion of evidence sought to be introduced in support of such motion, may be made the subject of an appeal.¹ 18 An appeal also lies from an order granting a motion for a new trial where the motion is filed after the expiration of the term at which a judgment in the case was rendered, because the effect of the order is to vacate the judgment.¹ 19 

§ 15. Court or Counsel May Initiate the Instructions-Damage Prayers Without Recovery Prayers Not Advisable. 

A Maryland trial court may, but need not, initiate any part or all of the instructions to the jury upon the law of the case. 

However, the long-settled and established practice in the Maryland courts in respect to instructing the jury, or the court sitting as a jury in law cases, is that each party submits in writing, for the consideration and ruling of the trial court, his contentions as to the law of the case. These writings are called "prayers" in the Maryland courts. When the prayers embody, in due form, correct propositions of law that are applicable to the facts and the real issues of the case and necessary for the adequate and proper instruction of the jury, it

May Reject Good Prayer and Instruct in Lieu Thereof 

When a Maryland trial judge chooses not to grant a good and necessary prayer and proceeds, in lieu thereof, to formulate and deliver instructions to the jury of his own—as he should do when he decides to reject a good and necessary prayer he is bound to declare the law accurately, and in terms explicit and intelligible to the jury, upon all the essential points raised by such a rejected prayer.21 However, in such a situation, the trial court is not bound to adopt the exact words of the rejected prayer, if the court's instruction to the jury, given in lieu of the rejected prayer, correctly and substantially cover the propositions of law that were submitted by the rejected prayer.22

§§ 15-16 TITLE 2 Grant of Damage Prayer in Absence of Recovery Prayer Not Advisable 

The established practice of granting a plaintiff's damage prayer which simply informs the jury regarding the measure of damages, if they should find in favor of the plaintiff, is, in the opinion of this author and others, a misleading practice where the jury is left uninstructed regarding what facts they must find before they are at liberty, as a matter of law, to return their verdict in favor of the plaintiff.23a

Form of Court's Own Instructions

§ 16. Need and Form of the Prayers in Court Trials—Court's Fact- Finding Not Reviewable. 

Where the parties to a trial in a court of law waive their right to trial by jury, the court is, by operation of law, substituted for the jury and, thereupon, functions as both court and jury in the trial of the cause.25

Fact-Finding in Law Courts Not Reviewable 

Contrary to the function of the appellate court in the matter of appeals from courts of equity,26 the fact-finding of a court of law sitting as a jury can not be reviewed by the Court of Appeals. § 17. Trial Upon Agreed Statement of Facts-"Case Stated”– Need of Prayers in Such Trials. 

Section 15 of Article 26 of the Code of Public General Laws of Maryland prescribes :33 "Upon all agreed statements of facts, all special cases stated, and all special verdicts, the court shall be at liberty to draw all inferences of facts or law that court or jury could have drawn from the facts so agreed or stated as if the same had been offered in evidence upon a trial before the court or before the court and a jury."

Trial Upon an Agreed Statement of Facts 

This statute does not relieve the parties to a case submitted upon an agreed statement of facts from the necessity of properly presenting the questions of law to be submitted to the ruling of the trial court, if a review thereof by the Court of Appeals is desired.34 In other words, there can be no effective appeal from the mere verdict of the court sitting as a jury, whether the case was submitted to the determination of the court upon an agreed statement of facts, upon testimony, or both, unless the record on appeal shows, at least, that a question of law was raised and ruled upon in the court below, or that the court below exceeded its jurisdiction.35 

Agreed Upon Facts Merely Take Place of Evidence 

An agreed statement of facts filed in a case does nothing more than take the place of evidence offered in the usual way, and does not authorize judgment to be entered for the party entitled thereto, as may be done in such a "special case stated" as is mentioned in the afore-quoted section 15 of article 26 of the Code, in pursuance of the applicable provisions of sections

Need of Prayers in Trial Upon Agreed Facts 

In practice, the questions of law in a case submitted to the determination of the court upon an agreed statement of facts are most often raised by the prayers or instructions of the case;37 although a question of law could arise from a ruling upon a demurrer to a pleading of the case.38 

A party to a case-submitted to the court below for a verdict upon an agreed statement of facts-will not be heard to argue in the Court of Appeals that the lower court should have given him the verdict because the agreed-upon facts were not legally sufficient to entitle his opponent to the verdict, or that the court, in reaching its verdict, should have been controlled and guided by certain principles of law, if these legal contentions were not first raised in the court below by the prayers of the case.39

While the English and Maryland courts of equity are inherently empowered to award issues of fact or law, to be sent to courts of law for trial, to inform the mind of the equity judge, they never exercised the power of summoning juries to try questions or issues of fact under their own direction upon testimony taken ore tenus.44

So the Court of Appeals, in construing the afore-quoted local statute, held that it had conferred a new discretionary power upon the equity courts of Baltimore City by providing for the trial of issues of fact by juries "whenever *** a jury is asked for and allowed, or is desired by the Judge" of the equity court.45 

Since the intervention of a jury, in such a situation, would be nugatory unless the court of equity summoning them had the power to decide all questions of law arising upon the facts offered in evidence, and the competency of evidence offered to prove any fact involved in the issues, it results that the court of equity would have the right to instruct the jury and to admit or exclude the evidence offered.40 But the Court of Appeals is without legislative authority to review the correctness of the instructions given by the trial court to a jury impanelled in a court of equity to hear and determine such issues of fact.47 

However, the presiding chancellor, like the presiding judge in a law court, is empowered to grant a motion for a new trial and to set aside the findings of the jury sitting in a court of equity.48

But the undisturbed findings of the jury in respect to the issues of fact submitted to their determination, are entitled to great consideration by the chancellor in all doubtful caseswhether the issues of fact were heard by the jury in a court of equity or in a court of law-and should be sustained by the chancellor, in reaching his decree, unless the finding of the jury is against the absolute conviction of the chancellor.49

§ 19. Issues Sent from Equity to Law Courts-Need of Prayers in 

Such Trials-Their Form. 

The Maryland courts of equity, like the English courts of equity, are inherently empowered to transmit issues of fact or law to a court of law for determination therein, if and when it pleases the chancellor to do so as a matter of justice.51 

In addition, sections 32 and 48 of article 16 and section 29 of article 9 of the Maryland Code of Public General Laws and Chapter 294 of the Acts of 1939, expressly provide for the sending of issues of fact from courts of equity to the courts of law of the State for determination by jury.52

However, as is explained more fully in section 18 of this title, the answers or findings of the jury upon the issues of fact do not absolutely control the chancellor in arriving at his decree; and this is so without regard to whether the issues of fact were heard by the jury in a court of equity or in a court of law.53

The practice of prayers and instructions is applicable in a court of law to the trial of issues of fact sent thereto from a court of equity for determination by jury.5

Moreover, it is declared by statute (Code, art. 5, sec. 5) that: "In cases of issues sent from the orphans' court or a court of equity to a court of law to be tried, exceptions may be taken to any opinion given by the court before whom such issues shall be tried, and an appeal may be taken on such exceptions; and such appeal, while pending, shall stay all proceedings in the orphans' court touching the matter of such issues." 55

Prior to the trial, in a court of law, of issues of fact received from an Orphans' court, the plaintiff (caveator) may dismiss them as a whole, but not in part; and when the trial upon such issues of fact has once begun, the plaintiff (caveator) is not permitted to dismiss them even in part, or take a non pros, as may be done by a plaintiff in an ordinary civil trial at law in pursuance of section 183 of article 75 of the Code.61

In the trial of issues of fact in a court of law, received from an Orphans' court, both demurrer and jury prayers will be considered defective if they authorize the jury to find a verdict in favor of either the plaintiff (caveator) or the defendant (caveatee); since the function of the jury, in such a trial, is to answer "Yes", or "No", in respect to each of the issues of fact involved in the case.62

Issues in Workmen's Compensation Cases Formulated in Court-Need of Prayers in Such Trials-Their Form. 

The issues of fact that are submitted to the determination or finding of a jury, or to the court sitting as a jury, in Workmen's Compensation cases on appeal from the State Industrial Accident Commission may be formulated de novo in court.85 

Prayers May Restrict Case to Proper Issues 

Where the parties to a Workmen's Compensation case, on appeal from the State Industrial Accident Commission, have submitted the case to the determination or finding of the court sitting as a jury, the court may hear the case without the aid of formal issues of fact, though this practice does not seem desirable. Where a case is tried without the aid of formal issues of fact, by a court sitting as both court and jury, counsel may present prayers to restrict the case to its real or proper issues of fact.66

Function of Jury in Workmen's Compensation Cases The function of the jury in a Workmen's Compensation case is merely to pass on the issues of fact. Accordingly, it is for the court and not the jury to decide whether the State Industrial Accident Commission "has exceeded the powers granted it" by the Act of its creation and "whether it (the Commission) has misconstrued the law and facts applicable to the case decided," and which is the subject of the appeal.67

Where the only real issue in a Workmen's Compensation case was whether the death of the employee-who admittedly was suffering from a heart "disease" prior to the alleged accidentwas accelerated by an accidental injury, it was held that a demurrer prayer of the employer and insurer was bad in form for having asked a directed verdict in their favor upon the ground of the want of evidence legally sufficient to show that the “disease" from which the employee died was the result of an accidental injury.69 But since a majority of the appellate court, in this Workmen's Compensation case, could find no evidence legally sufficient to show that the "death" of the employee was "accelerated" by an "accidental injury", within the meaning of the Workmen's Compensation Law, and, in addition, found that a prayer of the claimant (the widow of the employee) was erroneously granted, the finding of the jury in favor of the claimant was reversed without a new trial.70

It was held that a prayer in a Workmen's Compensation case did not submit a question of law to the finding of the jury merely because it submitted to the finding of the jury the question whether the claimant's existing mental disorder was produced by an "accidental personal injury", without any definition of the term "accidental personal injury.” 71 

§ 22. Mandamus Proceedings-Practice of Prayers When Court 

Also Sits as Jury.

Section 7 of article 60 of the Code of Public General Laws of 

Maryland, applicable to mandamus proceedings, provides for trial by jury of issues of fact in mandamus proceedings, if either party desires it.72 But it is not every question of fact that is a question for the intervention of a jury. The passage

and existence or non-existence of a statute or ordinance is a question of law, and though framed in form as an issue of fact, must, when it arises in the Courts, be decided by them on the evidence legally applicable thereto, without taking the advice of a jury on the subject.73

The practice of prayers and instructions is applicable to the trial of issues of fact in mandamus proceedings.74

When, however, the issues of fact in a mandamus case have been determined by the Judge, sitting without the aid of a jury, the Court of Appeals is not, as in ordinary appeals from a court of law, confined to a review of the rulings on questions of law raised and ruled upon in the court below. Where the trial court has heard a mandamus case without the intervention of the usual jury, the appellate court will inquire whether the writ of mandamus was properly granted or refused, after an inspection of the whole record, and is not restricted to an instruction, or limited to determining whether that instruction was right or wrong. In other words, it is the final order granting or refusing a mandamus which an appeal to the Court of Appeals assails, when the case has been tried by the Judge alone; and, whatever the instructions may be, if there are any, the accuracy or inaccuracy of that order is the thing to be determined.75

Requisites of Prayers in Mandamus Trials 

The form of the prayers in mandamus trials correspond to the form of the prayers in the ordinary civil trial at law.76

TITLE 2 Respective Powers of Commission and Courts in Tax Matters 

To understand the scope of prayers before the State Tax Commission and, again, in the court to which an appeal from the decision or order of the Commission is taken, the following principles must be borne in mind:

The responsibility for the final determination of assessments of all property in the counties, cities and towns of the State of Maryland is specifically conferred upon the State Tax Commission by the Act of its creation, passed in 1914. The valuations are to be made by the Commission according to its best judgment, from the evidence before it, and the courts are without jurisdiction to review any of its fact-finding.79 

The valuation of property is not a judicial function, and a court of law can not be required to act as a board of review in the assessment of property. The court is confined to an examination of the legal principles upon which the State Tax Commission acted, and if there be found no error of law applied by the Commission to the injury of the complaining taxpayer, the court is without power to disturb the assessment.80 

But should it appear from any legitimate source that a valuation had been placed upon the taxpayer's property in a capricious or whimsical or unwarrantable way, the valuation would not be an assessment at all, and the act of the Commission in making it could be reviewed as a matter of law.81 

Requisites of the Prayers Before the Commission and Court- 

Need of Exceptions to Prayers or Order of Commission or Court 

It appears, from an examination of the records on appeal from the State Tax Commission to the trial courts and from the latter to the Court of Appeals, that exceptions are not necessary in these proceedings, either to the prayers or to the final order of the Commission or the court.82

§ 24 

TITLE 3 § 24. Office of "Jury” Prayers-Parties May Request Instructions Upon All Essential Phases of Case. 

The "jury" prayers of a case, as distinguished from demurrer prayers which are also spoken of as prayers for directed findings, are those upon which the issues of fact of the case are left to the decision or finding of the jury, or to the court sitting as a jury. In the Maryland courts, it has been said that the only legitimate and proper purpose of such prayers is to advise the jury as to what the law is governing the facts to be established by them.¹

When Duty of Court to Instruct Jury 

It is the function and the duty of a Maryland trial court, when called upon in the trial of a civil case at law, by either of the parties, to instruct the jury as to the principles of law applicable to the case, and it is the duty of the jury to observe and conform to such instructions.2 And the fact that the verdict is to be rendered by the court, sitting as a jury, does not impair the right of either party to a correct statement of the principles by which the decision of the issues of fact should be controlled.3

Entitled to Grant of All Correct and Necessary Prayers 

Generally speaking, a party to a civil suit in the Maryland courts has a right to have the jury instructed in reference to their proper sphere of action, and to have them told what is legitimately within their province as the triers of the issues submitted to them, and he is entitled to the grant of as many of his prayers as are both correct and necessary for the adequate and proper instruction of the jury upon the law of the case.5

§ 25. Unnecessary Duplication of Prayers-Need Not Grant 

Stronger Law Than is Asked.

The duplication and repeated presentation of the same legal proposition in various prayers-whether done verbatim or by mere transposition of phraseology-are not only unnecessary, but manifestly tend to confuse the jury and to defeat the only legitimate and proper purpose of instructions, namely, to advise the jury what the law is governing the issues of fact involved in the case on trial, and to clearly guide them to a correct verdict, in keeping with the established rules of law.⁹ 

A litigant may not complain of the refusal of a proffered instruction on the law, if the same proposition is sufficiently

Where an instruction covers the whole case, it is no error to refuse other prayers covering the same ground; and this is especially so because a party to a case is not entitled to the grant of prayers that give undue emphasis to his theories of the case.¹ 11 

Need Not Grant Stronger Law Than Asked-Harmless Error

When the instructions given by the court afford to a party the benefit of all the law asked by his own prayers, he cannot object to the instructions because they do not give more. In other words, the trial court is not bound to go beyond the request of the prayer offered, and grant stronger law than is asked, though it might be able to do so if asked.12

While a trial court is always justified in refusing to grant a prayer of a party to a cause that expressly or in effect does no more than to duplicate or repeat one or more of the propositions of law contained in the granted prayers of the party offering the prayer, the action of the trial court in granting a prayer that, in due form, merely duplicates or reduplicates one or more of the correct propositions of law of the granted prayers of the case, will seldom constitute reversible error.13 

§ 26. Md. Courts Must Not Remark or Instruct Jury Upon Weight of Evidence or Credibility of Witnesses. 

By the immemorial practice of the Maryland courts, the jury has an unqualified right to form its judgment on the facts which the court determines to be legally sufficient, without any interference or control on the part of the judge.14 

Judge to be Strictly Impartial

The attitude of the trial judge should be, as between the parties, one of strict impartiality, and he should make no re

Judge Not a Mere Moderator 

However, it has been well emphasized that the trial judge, even in a jurisdiction like Maryland, is not a mere moderator of a town meeting, submitting questions to the jury for determination, nor simply ruling on the admissibility of testimony, but one who stands charged with full responsibility for the just outcome of a trial by confining the trial to the issues presented, excluding irrelevant matters and extraneous influences or considerations; by conducting the proceedings on some consistent theory, on practical lines; and by ruling in accordance with his best judgment on every question raised which is pertinent to the issues.17

Remarks of Court Sitting as Jury 

Where the court also sits as the jury, improper remarks of the judge may not have the same prejudicial and reversible effect as would be the case if the same remarks were made by the court in the presence of the usual jury,18 except, as is explained more fully in sections 5 and 6, when the remarks of the court can be regarded as an instruction upon the law of the case.1 19

§ 26 

TITLE 3 No "Credibility" Prayers 

Instructions to the jury containing legally established rules or statements of tests as to credibility, to be applied by the jury in determining the credibility of witnesses, or in judging the truthfulness of certain of their statements in evidence, though an accepted practice in some States and in the Federal courts, are objectionable to the Maryland practice.20

Among the reasons advanced by the Maryland courts for the rejection of such "credibility" prayers are those that hold that such prayers amount to mere abstractions; that when the evidence has been admitted, the fact of its admission gives the jury the right to consider every fact in the case that is proven to their satisfaction; that it is not the proper office of the court to call the attention of the jury to this or that fact, and inform them what they may take into consideration in making up their verdict; that, upon being granted, such prayers come to the jury with the sanction of the court and are apt to give undue weight and prominence to the fact thus called to their attention; and that such prayers would more likely result in misleading than assisting the jury in arriving at a proper conclusion, especially since they emphasize and thereby center the jury's attention upon the facts that they have so segregated to the exclusion of a just and fair consideration of all of the facts and circumstances in the case.21 

However, the granting of such abstract "credibility" prayers will seldom constitute reversible error.22

Approved Prayer Kindred to "Credibility" Prayer 

Examples of disapproved "credibility" prayers, such as the aforementioned, appear within the opinion of the case of Gilpin v. Somerville (163 Md. 46). 

But such disapproved "credibility" prayers are not to be confused with the approved and somewhat similar "sixth" prayer set out in the case of Davidove v. Duvall (160 Md. 347).

§ 45 

TITLE 3 § 27. Curative Instructions and Need to Move for Mistrial to Off-Set Prejudicial Remarks or Conduct of Judge, Counsel, Etc. 

The Court of Appeals of Maryland recently re-declared that where a trial judge has engaged in remarks that tend to emphasize or minimize the value, weight, or the effect of evidence, a caution by the judge to the jury that it should disregard such expression of opinion by the court, and the further advice to the jury that they are the judges of all questions of fact, will ordinarily be sufficient to cure such improper remarks of court, unless, as sometimes happens, the admonition is worse than the offense.23

If a litigant believes that the remarks or other conduct of the trial court, or of counsel, or of a witness, or of a juror, were so prejudicial as to have really deprived him of a fair and impartial trial, notwithstanding the effort, if any, of the trial court to correct the same, he should promptly move for a mistrial or the withdrawal of a juror, and if this is refused by the trial court, he should note an exception; otherwise, the 

Court of Appeals may not even review such objectionable remarks or misconduct. In any event, a litigant will not be permitted to withhold his objection to such prejudicial remarks or conduct until after he had ascertained whether the verdict was for or against him, provided, of course, that he, or his counsel, was actually aware of the objectionable conduct prior to the rendition of the verdict.24

§ 49 

TITLE 3 Evidence Admitted Subject to Exception 

Where evidence is taken subject to exception, it is incumbent on the party objecting, before or at the close of the evidence, to apply to the trial court, either by motion or prayer, to exclude the portion to which he objects; and if this is not done, the benefit of the original objection cannot be availed of on appeal.34

When a prayer is employed as a motion to strike out evidence admitted subject to exception, or to remove from the consideration of the jury evidence subsequently shown to be inadmissible, the prayer like any other motion to strike out testimony, should be definite, and not too general; for neither a prayer nor a motion to strike out testimony can be granted if phrased, expressly or in effect, to cover admissible as well as inadmissible evidence.35

Effect of Evidence Admitted Without Objection. 

In no event, however, can a prayer be made to perform the office of an objection to inadmissible testimony that has been allowed to come in without objection; and this is so because after evidence has been offered and admitted, without objection, it is too late for the trial court to instruct the jury that it was not admissible, or to grant a motion to strike it out, except where counsel was unaware of the ground of objection. 

When the ground of objection becomes apparent, it at once becomes the duty of counsel to move to strike out the testimony. This rule of law is intended to prevent a party from knowingly withholding his objection until after he discovers the force or effect of proposed testimony.30 36 When testimony is admitted without objection, although if one had been made it would have been excluded as incompetent, it must be treated as properly in the case, and its truth

is accepted in considering a demurrer prayer that challenges the legal sufficiency of the evidence.37 

Evidence Admitted for Limited Purpose.

When an item of testimony is admissible but for a limited purpose, the court is in duty bound to caution the jury against considering such testimony except for the limited purpose of its admission. So where the trial court orally instructed the jury that "these proofs of loss are admitted merely as evidence of the fact that such proofs of loss were filed with the company and not as evidence of any independent fact recited therein," the instruction was held to be both proper and necessary.38

But an instruction to the jury to disregard evidence wrongfully admitted is not always sufficient to cure its admission.39 

Conditional Admission of Written Instrument 

When a written instrument is produced as evidence, and objected to, its execution is to be shown to the court, by prima facie proof, at least, and when that is done it is permitted to go to the jury. But if the preliminary proof is doubtful, the court may allow the jury to take the instrument with the proof in regard to its execution, attended by an instruction that they are to receive it as evidence if they believe it to have been executed, otherwise, they must not consider it as evidence.40 

§ 32. Definitions of Mixed Lay and Technical Terms, Such as 

"Negligence", Etc, May be Given to Jury by Prayers.

When a word or term has a legal meaning only, it should not, as is told more fully in section 65, be employed in a prayer except when accompanied by a definition thereof that is understandable to the jury.

Guilty of Contributory Negligence as a Matter of Law 

Where the evidence, without dispute, shows the injured plaintiff to be guilty of contributory negligence as a matter of law, the defendant may move for a directed verdict in his favor through the medium of a specific demurrer prayer.44 

No Evidence of Contributory Negligence 

Where there is no evidence at all from which a jury could rationally infer that a plaintiff had, by his own negligence, directly contributed to produce the accident complained of by him, he is entitled to the grant of a prayer that so instructs the jury.45

Contributory Negligence of Children 

In a negligence case involving injuries to a young child, the plaintiff is, as a rule, entitled to the grant of a prayer that instructs the jury, in effect, that the injured child was bound to use only that degree of care which ordinarily prudent children of like age and like intelligence are accustomed to use under like circumstances.46

In a negligence case where the injured child was very young at the time of the accident, the defendant may have the jury told, in effect, that the contributory negligence of the parent or guardian of the child is attributable to the child.47

TITLE 3 Contributory Negligence of Passengers or Guests 

Where the injured plaintiff was a mere passenger in the vehicle that figured in the collision that resulted in his injuries, he is, as a rule, entitled to the grant of a prayer that, in effect, instructs the jury that the negligence of the driver of the vehicle in which he was a passenger is not, as a matter of law, imputable to him.48

Burden of Proof Regarding Contributory Negligence 

Where a plaintiff's own evidence in a negligence case does not prove him guilty of contributory negligence as a matter of law, he is entitled to the grant of a prayer that, in effect, instructs the jury that the burden of proof is upon the defendant to show that the plaintiff was guilty of negligence, and that such negligence on the plaintiff's part had directly contributed to produce the injury complained of by him.49 

Doctrine of the Last Clear Chance 

When the evidence in a negligence case is such as to render applicable the doctrine of the last clear chance, the plaintiff is entitled to the grant of a prayer which, in effect, instructs the jury that if the defendant discovered, or by the exercise of ordinary care ought to have discovered the plaintiff's position of peril in time to have enabled the defendant, by the exercise of ordinary care, to have avoided injuring the plaintiff, and the defendant failed to do so, the defendant is liable for the

When the evidence in a negligence case is such as to render applicable the doctrine of the last clear chance, a prayer of the defendant that asks for the verdict in his favor on the ground of the plaintiff's contributory negligence should negative the doctrine of the last clear chance.51

Doctrine of Concurrent Negligence 

When the evidence in a negligence case is such as to render applicable the doctrine of concurrent negligence, it seems that the defendant is entitled to the grant of a prayer which, in effect, tells the jury that if they should believe that the defendant became aware of the plaintiff's position of danger in time to have avoided the injury complained of by him, yet, the verdict of the jury must be in favor of the defendant, provided the jury should also believe that the plaintiff was aware of his position of danger, that he became aware of it in time to have escaped therefrom by the exercise of reasonable care and diligence and that the defendant may reasonably have and did infer that the plaintiff would move to a place of safety in time to have escaped the injury.

And where the evidence is such as to render applicable the doctrine of concurrent negligence, it seems that a prayer of the plaintiff, which seeks the verdict in his favor upon the application of the doctrine of the last clear chance, should negative the doctrine of concurrent negligence.52

§ 55 

TITLE 3 "Right of Way" Between Vehicles-When Not Applicable 

The Maryland statute (Code, article 56, section 209) that prescribes that "all vehicles shall have the right of way over other vehicles approaching at intersecting public roads from the left, and shall give right of way to those approaching from the right"-applies only in appropriate circumstances, that is when the two drivers come to the crossing in such proximity in point of time as to require accommodation of one to the other.

Furthermore, a driver who approaches intersecting highways at a rate of speed prohibited by law, or while engaged in the violation of any other statutory rule of the road, may, therefore, be estopped from asserting the right of way given to him by statute over a driver of a vehicle approaching from his left at interecting public highways. 

For the afore-going and other reasons, the Court of Appeals has repeatedly declared that the propriety of instructions affecting the right of way between vehicles at intersecting public highways must depend in each case upon its special circumstances.5 53 

"Right of Way" Between Pedestrians and Vehicles 

One clause of section 209 of article 56 of the Code prescribes: "All pedestrians shall have the right of way at street crossings in the towns and cities of this State, except where traffic is controlled at crossings by traffic officers. Between street crossings in such towns and cities, vehicles shall have the right of way."

The propriety of instructions affecting the afore-quoted right of way statute, between pedestrians and vehicles, must

§ 36. Prayers and Illustrations Regarding Presumption or Prima Facie Evidence of Negligence From Accident (Res Ipsa Loquitar) or From Statutory Violation. 

Presumption of Negligence From Accident-Res Ipsa Loquitur 

Where the evidence in a negligence case, of either side, is such as to render applicable the maxim or doctrine of res ipsa loquitur, or its equivalent, such as the maxim "so use your own rights or property as to do no injury to those of others,” the plaintiff is ordinarily entitled to the grant of a prayer that, in effect, informs the jury that they may presume or infer negligence from the happening of the accident in question.59

§ 61 

TITLE 3 

The doctrine or maxim res ipsa loquitur is merely a short way of saying that the facts of the occurrence warrant the inference of negligence.60

The doctrine of res ipsa loquitur can never apply where it appears from the plaintiff's own side of the case that his injury may have been caused either by the defendant's negligence, or by some other act for which the defendant is not responsible. For example, while the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur is ordinarly applicable when an injury to a passenger for hire is occasioned by an abnormal condition or happening in the carrier's department of transportation, it is not applicable where the passenger's (plaintiff's) own evidence shows that the carrier's (defendant's) taxicab came in contact with a moving vehicle of a third party. 61 

Presumption of Negligence From Violation of Statute or Ordinance 

A rebuttable presumption or inference of primary or contributory negligence, as the case may be, may also arise, and in most instances does arise by operation of law, from the mere proof of the violation of a penal statute or ordinance enacted for public safety. And this is so because one's failure to observe precautionary rules or regulations established by competent authority to guard against accidents and prevent injuries to others is a want of ordinary care in contemplation of law. 

However, no actionable negligence can arise from the violation of a penal statute or ordinance, either by way of a claim or a defense, if it does not appear that the violation was the which permitted jury to "infer" negligence from "the falling of the dumb-waiter").

Failure to "Stop" at Boulevard

While, generally speaking, the Maryland courts hold that the violation of a penal statute or ordinance constitutes but prima facie evidence of negligence, yet, it would seem that the violation of the statutory rule of the road that requires a motorist to come to a "stop" at a boulevard designated as such by the requisite "stop" signs, may constitute negligence per se even in the Maryland courts.65 

§ 37. "Unavoidable Accident” and Kindred Prayers. 

An unavoidable accident, as a subject of judicial inquiry, is one that could not have been obviated by the exercise of legally requisite care by any of the persons whose responsibility for the occurrence is asserted or denied. Accordingly, if the plaintiff or defendant could have averted the accident by proper care, it could not be said to have been unavoidable; and, in such circumstances, the jury should not be instructed, in effect, that if the accident was unavoidable the plaintiff cannot recover.66

§§ 37-38 TITLE 3 

A prayer that tells the jury that if they "were unable to determine from the evidence how the accident happened, the verdict must be for the defendant," has a somewhat confusing tendency to draw the minds of the jury away from the real issue, since ultimately it is, in most instances, not so much how the accident occurred, as whose fault caused it.67 

A prayer that tells the jury that the defendant is not liable if he could not, with ordinary care, have "arrested" his automobile in time to have avoided the accident in question, tends to distract the minds of the jury from the specific acts of negligence produced in evidence. Besides, the defendant may have approached the scene of the accident at a negligent rate of speed, and so was not able to arrest his automobile and to avoid the accident by the exercise of ordinary care after he discovered the plaintiff's position of peril. And in respect to a night accident, the headlights on the defendant's automobile may have been so inadequate as to have prevented the defendant from seeing the plaintiff in due time.68 

§ 38. That Plaintiff's Rights in Leased Oyster Bed is Subject to the "Paramount Right of Navigation" May be Told to Jury by Prayers— 

Their Form.

In the case of Adams v. Carey (172 Md. 175, 185)-being an action in negligence for damage to plaintiff's leased oyster bed, caused by the efforts of the master of defendant's ferry boat to free it after it had run aground in a fog-it was held that the trial court had committed prejudicial error in refusing to grant the following prayer of the defendant, since, in the absence of this instruction, the jury may not have known that the right of navigation was paramount to the plaintiff's aforesaid right of fishery. 

The said prayer of the defendant says: "The Defendant prays the court to instruct the jury that the land lying under the waters of the Patuxent River and leased by the plaintiff from the Conservation Department of Maryland for the purpose of oyster culture is held by the plaintiff subject to the paramount right of navigation."

§§ 39-41 TITLE 4 Prayer that Scintilla of Evidence is Not Enough 

Where a negligence case is left to the determination of the jury, the court should not instruct them to the effect that a mere scintilla of evidence to show defendant's failure to use due care is not sufficient to justify a verdict for the plaintiff. 

This is so because, as is further explained in section 97, where a party carries the burden of proving an issue of fact, and produces a mere scintilla of evidence in support of it, his opponent is entitled to have that issue taken from the consideration of the jury through the medium of a demurrer prayer.2 

§ 40. When Plaintiff Can Not be Required to Prove "State of Facts 

Alleged in the Declaration."

A prayer should not impose upon the plaintiff the burden of establishing the "state of facts alleged in the declaration," unless the declaration contained no allegation of fact other than those which were essential to the cause of action, and the proof at the end of the trial presented no facts entitling the plaintiff to a recovery other than those alleged in the declaration.

In other words, a prayer is erroneous when it requires a plaintiff to prove all the allegations of a declaration that contains unessential or redundant allegations, as is found, for example, in declarations such as those that relate to traffic accidents and which charge the defendant with a number of negligent acts, any one of which, if established to the satisfaction of the jury, would entitle the plaintiff to the verdict.³ 

§ 41. Burden of Proof Prayers Must Not Exact Higher Standard of Proof than Law Exacts-Fair Preponderance of "Affirmative" or "Positive" Evidence, Etc.

A party who is charged, as a matter of law, with the burden of proof in respect to a particular issue of fact, claim, or defense, must not be required to prove the same by a higher and different standard of proof than the law exacts. So in the ordinary civil case, a party bearing the burden of proof cannot be required to sustain it by "positive" evidence, testi-

But one who carries the burden of proof in respect to a case, or any lesser issue of fact thereof, may be required to "prove" or "establish" it by a "fair preponderance" of "affirmative" evidence, or "testimony", or "proof." The use of words "fair preponderance of affirmative evidence", in defining the burden of proof, has been repeatedly sanctioned by the Court of

§ 42. Charges of Fraud and Criminality Must be Sustained by More than a Mere Preponderance of the Evidence-Presumption of 

Innocence. 

When fraud or criminal conduct involving moral turpitude is charged in a civil case, the charge must be proven by something more than a mere preponderance of evidence. 

Accordingly—in a suit on a fire insurance policy which was defended on the ground of arson allegedly committed in pursuance of a conspiracy between the mortgagor and the mortgagee of the burned automobile, the Court of Appeals apparently approved the following 3rd prayer of the plaintiff : "The Jury is instructed that the burden of proof is on the Defendant to establish its defense or defenses by a preponderance of the evidence; and by preponderance of evidence is meant not only that the evidence in favor of the Defendant must, in the minds of the Jury, be more weighty and more satisfactory than the evidence of the plaintiff on the same point, but that where the defense is conspiring to set and setting fire to insured property by the plaintiff, the evidence of the Defendant on that point must also to the minds of the Jury clearly and satisfactorily overcome the presumption of innocence which attaches to the person or persons to or against whom the charge of conspiring to set and setting fire to insured property is made."

§§ 43-44 TITLE 4 § 43. Burden of Proof Prayers in Suits to Recover for Services- Effect of the Presumption of Liability for Accepted Services. 

In the case of services rendered to deceased by one not a member of deceased's family, the law implies a promise to pay therefor, and the burden is upon the party resisting payment to show that no charge was to be made. 

Accordingly-in a case involving an action for services rendered to defendant's (administratrix's) decedent by plaintiff, who was not a member of decedent's family-it was held that the trial court had properly refused a prayer of the defendant that asked the court to instruct the jury that the "burden of proof is on the plaintiff to prove his case by preponderance of the evidence", instead of limiting the plaintiff's burden of proof (a) to the rendition of the services by the plaintiff; (b) non-payment therefor; and (c) the representative character of the defendant."

Burden of Proof Prayers Regarding Defenses in Actions Ex 

Where a defendant has affirmed and relied upon facts collateral to or dehors the contract as a defense, the burden of proving such facts is upon him; but this obligation of the defendant does not relieve the plaintiff of the burden of proving his own case.8

So in a case where the plaintiff (corporation) sued to recover the purchase price of the two oil burners described in a written contract which contained an express warranty as to their quality and fitness for a particular purpose, and alleged in its declaration that it had in all respects complied with the terms and provisions of the contract-it was held that the defendant could not be deprived of the "ordinary burden of proof prayer" by the mere fact that the defendant controverted the plaintiff's evidence regarding its compliance with the said terms of the said sales contract, since the plaintiff was bound to prove its

Where a defendant carried the burden of proof in respect to his defense that his failure to deliver the amount of canned tomatoes named in the contract was occasioned by a partial crop failure, except such as were required by the Government, it was held that the plaintiff was entitled to the grant of a prayer which, among other things, placed the burden of proof upon the defendant in regard to said defense; and that, therefore, the defendant was not entitled to the grant of a prayer that placed "the burden of proof upon the plaintiff to establish his case by a preponderance of evidence"; since, in the absence of some qualification, the jury might have been misled as to the burden of proof in respect to the said crop failure defense.10 

§ 45. When Defendant Carries the Burden of Proving Plaintiff's Contributory Negligence-Approved Form of Such a Prayer. 

As is further told in sections 33 and 176, where the plaintiff in a negligence case does not prove himself guilty of contributory negligence as a matter of law, he is ordinarily entitled to the grant of a prayer which reads such as the following: 11 "The court instructs the jury that in order to defeat a recovery in this suit, on the ground of contributory negligence on the part of the plaintiff, the burden of proof is upon the defendant to show that the plaintiff was guilty of negligence, and that such negligence on his part contributed to produce such injury, but in passing upon the question of contributory negligence, the jury is at liberty to consider all the testimony produced in the case." 

§ 46. Effect of the Doctrine of Res Ipsa Loquitur upon Burden of Proof Prayers in Negligence Cases. 

Where a prayer of a defendant in a negligence case, in which the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur was held applicable, placed the burden of proof upon the plaintiff to show that the accident

§ 47. When Prayer Should Not Tell Jury that Plaintiff Must Show that Defendant's Negligence was the "Sole" Cause of Plaintiff's Injury.

Since one is liable if he, by his own negligence, had merely contributed to produce an injury to another free of fault, a defendant in a case involving a collision between his vehicle and that of a third party (other than the plaintiff) is not entitled to ask for the grant of a prayer that tells the jury expressly or impliedly that the burden of proof is on the plaintiff to show that the negligence of the defendant was the "sole" cause of the plaintiff's injury.14 § 48.  as Applies to Burden of

The Maryland rule is that a guest in an inn or hotel who shows that he lost his baggage or money by a fire on the premises, has produced a prima facie case against the proprietor, who, thereupon, has the burden of showing his freedom from negligence causing the fire.15

Where the jurisdiction of the State Industrial Accident Com mission was sustained by a preponderance of the evidence-it was held that no harm could have resulted from the possible error in the prayer of the employee which placed on the employer the burden of proving the residence of the claimant. 

The employee carried the burden of proof in respect to this issue because he was the appellant from the adverse decision of the Commission.16 

Where the declaration in a negligence case alleged in detail the injury sustained by the plaintiff, and his proof sustained the allegations on that subject without any contradiction—it was held that no ground for reversal arose from a granted prayer of the defendant which instructed the jury that the plaintiff had the burden of establishing "the state of facts alleged in the declaration." 17

Where a granted prayer of the plaintiff needlessly imposed upon himself the burden of showing a fact of which there was no legally sufficient evidence, it was held that no possible injury arose therefrom to the defendant.18

Ordinarily, however, either the refusal to grant a correct burden of proof, or the granting of a prayer of the appellee which imposed, upon the appellant, a higher burden or standard of proof than was exacted of him by law, will constitute reversible error.19

§§ 49-50 TITLE 5 Need of Explicit Instructions Regarding Measure of Damages 

Indeed, it has been repeatedly said that it is of the utmost importance that juries should be explicitly instructed as to the rules by which they are to be governed in estimating damages.2 

So it was held-in an action in tort against a common carrier for the wrongful refusal of passage to the plaintiff upon its railroad train-that the trial court had committed a fatal error in granting a prayer that told the jury that if they found for the plaintiff he "is entitled to such damages as the jury may find would, under all the circumstances, compensate him for such refusal"; since this prayer "left the whole question of damages at large, without definition by the Court, to the discretion of the jury, and without any criterion to guide them." 3

A defendant is always entitled to the grant of prayers that correctly define or restrict the damages that the jury may award to the plaintiff.4 

§ 50. Right to Submit Case Upon Damage Prayers Alone. 

A plaintiff may limit his request for instructions to the jury to that of a damage prayer, predicated upon the finding of the verdict in his favor.5

Moreover, as is told more fully in sections 15 and 24, a litigant is not bound to submit any prayer whatsoever.

TITLE 5 § 51. Right to Prayers Which Restrict the Verdict to "Nominal” 

Damages or Which Exclude "Punitive" Damages or "Permanent” Injury.

Where the state of the evidence warrants it, as is told more fully in section 100, a defendant may be entitled to the grant of a demurrer prayer which peremptorily instructs the jury that their verdict cannot include more than nominal damages; or that the jury must not allow "punitive" damages; or that there is no evidence legally sufficient to show that plaintiff sustained any "permanent" injury.8 

§ 52. Right to Confine the Damages to the Express and Implied Allegations of the Pleadings-Variances. 

If a party regards a granted prayer as not confining the jury to the claims or issues of damage as made by the pleadings, and he desires to narrow the inquiry or to obtain a more explicit instruction, setting out the facts in detail, he may do so through the medium of prayers submitted at the trial table.⁹

Moreover, as is explained in sections 87 and 91, a litigant may interpose a variance special exception in regard to any prayer of his opponent that seeks to recover damages which, though finding legally sufficient support in the evidence, are expressly or impliedly at variance with the state of the pleadings.

TITLE 6 § 57. Minimum Requisites of Any Prayer—“Jury” Prayer Must Not Predicate the Verdict Upon an Indefinite Proposition of Facts. 

Every prayer which is phrased in terms too general, vague, or indefinite to submit a legal proposition, or in terms too vague or indefinite to form the basis of a legal proposition, is defective.¹

With special reference to demurrer prayers, it has been said, again and again, that a prayer is defective when it does not point out any particular ground upon which the right to recover is asserted or denied, and does not direct attention to any particular error or omission of proof, or raise any definite question as to its sufficiency.2

A jury prayer is defective when it predicates the verdict or other conclusion-that it seeks to attain in favor of its proponent-upon the finding by the jury of an uncertain or indistinct or vague hypothesis of facts, since a prayer so phrased is incapable of submitting a legal proposition for the consideration of the court, besides offering no guide for the jury in arriving at a proper verdict.3 

§ 58. Illustrations of Prayers Which are Too General and Indefi nite to Submit a Legal Proposition, Etc.

(161 Md. 249, 264-265-second appeal)-being a suit by a mortgagee on a fire insurance policy that was contested on the defense of arson-it was said that the mortgagee's 1st, 7th and 8th prayers "were predicated upon a common hypothesis that no evidence had been offered in the case to show a confederation between *** and *** to burn the Light Street Garage for the purpose of collecting the insurance on automobiles stored there." They were based upon a general failure of evidence, and raised no question as to its legal sufficiency. Illustration-B 

In Rent-A-Car Co. v. Fire Ins. Co. (158 Md. 169, 185-first appeal), it was said (our paragraphing): "The mortgagee was entitled to have its contention that the mortgagor set the property on fire without the mortgagee's privity and consent submitted to the jury. "The defendant did not object to the prayers presenting this theory on the ground of any formal defect, but the three prayers referred to should have been more explicit and clear, as they permit the argument that the mortgagee could not have become responsible for the fire by command, connivance, or conspiracy as well as by direct participation in its physical preparation and start."

Illustration-C 

In Brown v. Patterson (141 Md. 293, 295, 298), the 1st prayer of the plaintiff read as follows: 

"The plaintiff prays the court to instruct the jury that if they shall find from the evidence that the plaintiff was struck by an automobile operated by the defendant, and was injured; and if the jury shall further find that such injury to the plaintiff was caused by the want of ordinary care and prudence of the defendant, and not from the want of ordinary care and prudence on the part of the plaintiff, directly contributing to the injury, then the verdict of the jury must be in favor of the plaintiff."

With reference to the afore-quoted prayer, the Court of Appeals said it "has been granted and approved over and over again in negligence cases, although, of course, there may be circumstances in a case making such a prayer too general, or for other reasons objectionable.
