§ 59. What Constitutes an "Approved" Prayer-Safety and Risk in Following Approved Prayers and Language From Opinion of Court. 

What Constitutes an "Approved" Prayer 

The Court of Appeals of Maryland recently re-emphasized that the mere fact of its affirmance of a judgment below does not imply approval of all prayers granted on behalf of one side or the other.

Moreover, since the appellate court is not ordinarly called upon to review the correctness of the rulings of the trial court which were favorable to the appellant, the mere mention, in the opinion of the case, of a granted prayer of the appellant without disapproval, may not be construed as an approval of

$ 59 

TITLE 6 

the prayer for the purpose of a subsequent case in which a similar prayer is offered.5

It should also be borne in mind-when reading an opinion of the appellate court to determine whether a certain prayer in the case was actually approved-that the appellate court is expressly estopped, by statute and rules of its own making, from considering whether a prayer which was actually granted in the court below was defective for having assumed a disputed fact, or for having submitted a fact to the finding of the jury that was without legally sufficient support in the evidence, or for having submitted a question of law to the decision of the jury, if the defect was not pointed out, at least, at the trial table by the mode of a special exception. This is further explained in sections 62 to 66 and in sections 136 to 148.

Safety and Risk in Following Approved Prayers 

Generally speaking, a prayer which was clearly approved by the Court of Appeals, both as to form and substance, may be safely followed or employed in another or later case, provided, of course, that the proof and the real issues of the later case correspond, in legal effect, to the proof and the real issues of the earlier case in which the prayer was approved, and also provided that the law as declared in the prayer of the earlier case was not changed in the meantime.6

TITLE 6 Rulings on Prayers on Retrial of Same Case 

A ruling upon a prayer, which the appellate court approved on appeal from the first trial of the case, may not apply in the second or retrial of the case, if the second trial produced a substantial change in the evidence or in the real issues of the case."

Following Language of Court Opinions 

The reasoning of courts in opinions is not addressed to juries, and is not always adapted to use in instructions to them. So the incorporation into a prayer of a rule of law in the language stated in an opinion of the Court does not necessarily help to establish the prayer as an approved one. Besides, the Court of Appeals has more than once warned that expressions in an opinion should not be bodily incorporated in a prayer and presented as abstract propositions. 

§ 60. Phraseology, Size and Paragraphing of Prayers-Facts to be 

Stated in Elementary Form-Incomplete Erasures and Foreign Footnotes on Prayers. 

Phraseology of Prayers

The sole purpose of instructing the jury is to aid and enlighten them in their duty, so far as it is competent for the court to assist them. Therefore, the prayers of a case, and especially the jury prayers, should be composed in terms explicit and intelligible to the jury.⁹ but is fixed, definite and certain, and while the manner of its application changes with difffering facts its principles and rules remain invariable.").

TITLE 6 

Involved Facts-Facts to be Stated in Elementary Form Early in the development of the Maryland practice of written instructions to juries, commonly called prayers, the Court of Appeals declared that it is much to be desired that propositions for the court or for the jury, should be as precise and distinct as possible; and that if counsel present to the trial court a complicated and involved statement which it will be difficult for the jury to understand distinctly, it will be sufficient ground upon which the court should refuse to give a direction or instruction in the terms asked for. And the Court of Appeals further emphasized that few instances will be found in which a transaction however ramified in its details, may not be reduced into something like elementary and distinct parts or points, each readily to be comprehended by minds of ordinary intelligence.10 

Brevity, Clarity and Paragraphing of Prayers-Harmless Error

In other words, the prayers of a case should be drawn with as much brevity as is consistent with a clear and accurate statement of the law applicable to the facts of the case, since undue prolixity or unnecessary repetition tend rather to confuse, than to enlighten the jury.11

The Court of Appeals has generally discouraged prayers of extreme length, as well as those which contain more than one paragraph, as not adapted to aid and enlighten the jury. 

However, the error attached to the granting of an unusually long prayer, or to the granting of a prayer which was unnecessarily divided into paragraphs will seldom, of itself, con-

Incomplete Erasures and Foreign Footnotes on Prayers 

The meaning of a prayer should not be clouded or confused by the addition of the citation of authorities in support thereof, or by an incomplete erasure, or by an indistinct modification or alteration of the prayer, or othewise. However, an objection to an instruction on any such ground should be promptly and definitely pointed out at the trial table, so as to afford an opportunity to the draftsman of the prayer to rectify the mistake.15 

§ 61. Form of the Introductory and Closing Clauses of Prayers— Need of Repeating "If the Jury Shall Find" After Each Fact.

Marking Court's Instruction as "Court's Own" An instruction proposed by the trial court itself was declared not to be open to valid criticism simply because it was headed-"Court's instruction"-and marked "Granted as

Opening Language of Body of Prayer 

Regardless of the form of its heading or titling, the body or text of a prayer should and in practice generally does start with either one of the following three forms of introductory 

(1) "The plaintiff (or defendant) prays the Court to instruct the jury that * * #99 (2) "The Court instructs the jury that * ** ?? #99 (This (3) "The plaintiff (or defendant) prays the Court to rule (or declare) as a matter of law that clause is generally employed where the court sits as both court and jury.)

Closing Language of Prayer-Premise and Conclusion 

There should be an intelligible connection between the premise and the conclusion of a prayer.1 19 Where the author of a prayer is entitled to the verdict if the jury should find or believe the elements or hypotheses of fact enumerated in the prayer, the prayer may and in practice does end or conclude with a clause such as the last clause of the following prayer: "The Court instructs the jury that if they shall find that ***, that * * * and that * ** then their verdict must (or should) be in favor of the plaintiff (or the defendant).” 20

But such a prayer must not end or conclude with a clause reading such as "and their verdict must be for the defendant;" for this clause is clearly a non sequitur, calculated to mislead or confuse the jury, and so vitiates the prayer.21

TITLE 6 Need of Repeating-"If the Jury Shall Find That * * *99 

A prayer which, at its beginning, submits its enumerated facts to the finding of the jury by the hypothetical clause reading "if the jury shall find that ***"-need not ordinarily repeat this clause, or its equivalent, either before or after each enumerated fact.22

When, however, a fact in a prayer is so misphrased as to violate the rule against the assumption of a disputed fact in a prayer, which rule is discussed in section 62, the insertion of the proviso or clause, just before such a misphrased fact, reading "and if the jury shall further find that," or the insertion of the proviso or clause just after such misphrased fact, reading-"if the jury shall so find"-will sometimes have the effect of avoiding the violation of the said rule. On the other hand, the unnecessary repetition of such hypothetical provisions or clauses throughout a prayer may tend to confuse the jury.28 

§ 62. Assumption in a Prayer of a Disputed Fact or Hypothesis Not Permissible-Prayer Should Not Say That Jury "Ought" to Infer a Fact-Need of Special Exception. 

It has been long-settled in the Maryland courts that a prayer is defective in its structure if it either expressly or inferentially assumes as proved a fact in controversy or conflict, especially when the burden of proving that fact is upon the author of the prayer.24

TITLE 6 What Language May Constitute the Assumption of a Fact

The rule against the assumption of a disputed fact or hypothesis in a prayer or instruction applies with equal force to a case where the court sits as both court and jury.25 And it may also apply-as is explained in section 26-to a remark of the trial judge regarding the weight or credibility of the evidence, if made in the presence of the jury.

Implied Submission of Facts to Finding of Jury 

As is further explained in section 77, an issue of fact, composed of several distinct elements or parts, may have been impliedly submitted to the finding of the jury by the submission to their finding of a certain other fact.27

The assumption, in a granted prayer, of a material fact in conflict between the parties, constitutes an objection not less fatal than would be the exclusion from such a prayer of a disputed fact that is necessary and material to support the instruction sought, for in either case the tendency is to force a verdict on facts, the finding of which is taken from the jury.31 

When, however, it cannot be gleaned from the record of the case, as a whole, that the appellant was likely injured by the grant of such an erroneous prayer, the appellate court will not reverse the judgment.32

In Peterson's Exc'rs. v. Ellicott (9 Md. 52, 53, 54, 64), the defendant's third prayer told the jury that if they should believe the facts enumerated in the prayer, "then the jury may and ought to find that the plaintiff at the death of the said Peterson had no just claim against the said Peterson on account of the education and support of said granddaughter, notwithstanding the jury may find the acknowledgments of said Peterson as given in evidence."

In regard to this prayer, it was said (according to the syllabus): "Where the presumption asked by a prayer to be drawn is only one of fact, and not of law imperatively binding upon the jury, an instruction that if the jury believed the facts stated in it 'then they may and ought to find for the defendant,' is erroneous, because the term 'ought,' makes it imperative upon the jury so to find.”

Illustration-B 

In Cooke v. Kell (13 Md. 469, 494), it was held that a prayer which instructed the jury-"That, by the deed of 1792, the grantor conveyed to the grantees, therein named, the property therein described," etc.was defective for having thus assumed the existence of the deed of 1792.

Illustration-C In Denmead v. Coburn (15 Md. 29, 30, 45), it was held that a prayer that told the jury that the plaintiff was entitled to recover the value of the materials "used" by the defendant, etc., was erroneously granted because it assumed that such materials were used. Illustration-D In Am. Straw Board Co. v. Smith (94 Md.

19, 20), it was said (syllabus): "That another prayer offered by the defendant, founded upon the hypothesis that the driver was not bound to anticipate the likelihood of the plaintiff's being hidden among the weeds, and that it was not negligence not to see plaintiff so hidden, was also properly refused, because it likewise assumes as a fact that the plaintiff was hiding in the weeds to escape observation and fails to require the jury to find whether the driver was free from negligence in driving through the blinding dust on the foot-path of the highway where pedestrians were accustomed to walk."

As drawn, the prayer does assume that to some extent at least the injuries complained of did disable the plaintiff, etc., and if the verdict had been for a nominal amount, there would have been force in the objection, but as it was for substantial damages, it is apparent that that error did not injure the appellant."

A prayer may submit to the finding of the jury a fact, hypothesis or theory that the jury may rationally infer only from some other fact in evidence.48

A litigant will not, as a rule, be heard to complain that there is a want of evidence legally sufficient to support an issue or hypothesis of fact that was submitted to the finding of the jury by a prayer of his opponent, if a prayer of his own offering submitted a similar issue or hypothesis of fact to the finding of the jury.44

Where a party expressly or impliedly concedes a prayer of his opponent that submits an issue of the case to the finding of the jury, he may not, as a rule, thereafter contend that there is a want of evidence legally sufficient to sustain that issue.45

A fact founded in common knowledge, or one of which the court could properly take judicial notice or knowledge, may become the foundation of an instruction.46

§ 101 

TITLE 6 Proof Arising From Inadmissible Testimony 

While an instruction of a case may be based upon inadmissible testimony which was actually admitted into the evidence of the case by the trial judge, none should be based upon testimony excluded by the trial court. But where the inadmissible testimony, which was actually admitted, was made the subject of an exception at the trial of the case, and is ruled out on appeal, an instruction predicated thereupon would obviously fall.47

Presumption on Appeal Regarding Sufficiency of the Proof 

When there is a want of evidence in the record legally sufficient to sustain a material fact sought to be left to the finding of the jury by a rejected prayer, the appellate court will presume that the prayer was rejected because of this inherent defect. Need of Special Exception 

As is further explained in sections 136 to 147, while the appellate court may and will review a rejected prayer to determine if it had submitted a fact or hypothesis to the finding of the jury that was without legally sufficient support in the evidence even in the absence of a special exception thereto in the court below, the appellate court may not and will not do so, in the absence of a special exception, if it be a prayer that was actually granted by the trial court.49 

A granted prayer, of the appellee, which predicated the verdict of the jury in his favor upon a fact or hypothesis that was without legally sufficient support in the evidence, and which was made the subject of a special exception, will result in a reversal of the judgment, if it may be gleaned from the record of the case, as a whole, that the appellant was likely prejudiced by this error in the prayer.50 § 65. § 65 

TITLE 6 Need of Special Exception 

As is further explained in sections 136 to 146, while the appellate court may and will review a rejected prayer to determine if it had submitted, expressly or inferentially, a question of law to the finding or determination of the jury even in the absence of a special exception thereto in the court below, the appellate court may not and will not do so, in the absence of a special exception, if it be a prayer that was actually granted by the trial court." 78 

A prayer of the appellee which has submitted a question of law to the determination of the jury, or to the court sitting as the jury, will result in a reversal of the judgment if it may be surmised from the record of the case, as a whole, that the appellant was likely injured thereby.79

Duty to Grant Both Prayers When One Defines "Waiver" 

Where plaintiff's first prayer submitted his defense of waiver to the finding of the court sitting as a jury, without stating the facts in evidence which, if believed by the jury, would constitute the waiver, while his second prayer did do so, it was held that the trial court should not have rejected these complemental prayers, but should have granted them expressly in connection with each other.80 used in such contract, the evidence as to the meaning of such phrase having been directed to the time of the execution of the contract).

§ 109 

TITLE 6 

§ 66. mit Questions of Law to the Determination of the Jury.

Illustrations of Prayers Which Expressly or Impliedly Sub- 

The following are case illustrations of prayers which were adjudged to have submitted, expressly or inferentially, a question of law to the finding or decision of the jury, and also of prayers which were adjudged not to have done so.81 

Also see the text of section 65, and the case illustrations in some of the footnotes to this section. 

81 See sec. 65, and the case illustrations within the text of this sec. Illustration-A 

In A. & P. Co. v. Noppenberger (171 Md. 378, 395-397), it was said (our paragraphing): "The plaintiff's first prayer, which was granted, instructed the jury that the mere fact that the automobile operated by Carter at the time of the accident did not belong to defendant would not bar the right of the plaintiff to recover if they found that 'the use' had been authorized 'expressly or impliedly' by the defendant. "That prayer was granted in connection with defendant's fifth prayer, which stated the converse of that proposition. It is true the (plaintiff's) prayer did submit to the jury an hypothesis of which there was no legally sufficient evidence, that of express authority, but, in the absence of a special exception, that objection is not open in this court. 

"The defendant also specially excepted to the prayer on the ground that it submitted a question of law to the jury. That exception should have been sustained. "The whole question in the case was whether certain facts were legally sufficient to permit an inference of implied authority. Whether the facts existed was for the jury, whether if they existed such an inference might be deduced from them, was not only a question of law, but the most important legal question in the case, and was for the court. "The principal argument in this case was whether the facts justified an inference of implied authortiy. It was asking a great deal of a jury to expect them to answer that question without some guidance or direction from the court, and yet that was the effect of the prayer, for it left it to the jury to determine whether the use of the automobile was 'authorized either expressly or impliedly.' "The special exception should therefore have been sustained and the prayer refused."

§ 66 

TITLE 6 Illustration-B 

In Engineering & Machine Co. v. Swindell (161 Md. 571, 594-595), it

Iwas held that the grant of a prayer based on the hypothesis of a finding by the jury that defendant agreed to construct for plaintiff a machine which would make merchantable bottles in "merchantable quantities" was erroneous, since, in the absence of some explanation to the jury, the expression "merchantable" was meaningless as applies to the capacity of the machine.

Illustration-C 

In Hambleton & Co. v. Union Nat. Bank (161 Md. 318, 328), it was held that the defendant's first prayer, which submitted, to the court sitting as a jury, the question whether the employment in question was "permanently terminated", did not submit a question of law to the finding of the jury, but, rather, "a matter of fact from the evidence." 

Illustration-D 

In Shriver Co. v. Interocean Co. (157 Md. 341, 352-353), which was a suit on a contract, a prayer erroneously left, to the finding of the jury, the question whether there had been a "waiver" of a stipulation as to time' of payment, without telling the jury what facts in evidence, if believed by them, would constitute the "waiver".

In this connection, the Court of Appeals said, in part (our paragraphing): "When payments have been customarily received later than a day specified and the dealer decides to disallow any further grace, in order to put himself in position to rescind for failure to pay on time he must give the debtor notice that the terms of the contract must be observed, or that no further delays will be tolerated. "This is the rule laid down in the instruction approved by this court in Sullivan v. Boswell, 122 Md. 539, 544, which is as follows: "If the court as a jury shall find that the plaintiffs from time to time accepted payments for coal after the stipulated times and thereafter shipped more coal, then these are facts from which the court as jury may find that the plaintiffs had waived and lost the right to rescind for breaches of said term theretofore made, and the law is that they could not after such waiver, if such be found, recover the right to rescind for future breaches of said term as to payment without some notice to defendant that they intended thereafter to strictly enforce such term, and opportunity after said notice to the defendant to comply strictly with said term."

TITLE 6 Illustration-E 

In State v. Phillinger (142 Md. 365), being a negligence case, it was held that a prayer of the defendant was not defective because it failed to explain what was meant by "the scope of his employment." 

Illustration-F 

In Doggett v. Tatham (116 Md. 147, 154), where the trial court modified the prayer in question by the addition of the words "provided, however, that the jury must also find that the defendant was not in fault under said contract", it was said: "This addition to the prayer was unfortunate, because it submitted to the jury not only to find what constituted the contract, but what the proper interpretation of that contract was, and the interpretation of a contract is always a matter of law to be ruled upon by the 

* it submitted to them questions for their determination which it was proper should have been passed upon by the Court. 

Roberts v. Bonaparte, 73 Md. 191.”

Illustration-G 

In Commercial Realty & Constr. Co. v. Dorsey (114 Md. 172, 180), it was held that a prayer is erroneous which submits to the jury the question whether a contract "was duly cancelled", this being an issue of law.

Illustration-H 

In Meyer v. Frenkil (113 Md. 36, 43, 44), it was held that the first prayer of the appellee (plaintiff), set out on page 43 of the opinion, "does not, as urged by the appellant, submit to the jury the construction of the written agreement dated November 7th, 1904. It merely requires the jury to find what the contract between the parties was. 

And this under the conflicting evidence was a proper question to be determined by the jury."

Illustration-I 

In Roth v. Shupp (94 Md. 55), it was held, in an action for false imprisonment that a prayer leaving it to the jury to find whether the plaintiff was "illegally imprisoned" is erroneous because it submits to their finding a question of law. 

Illustration-J 

In Cooper v. Holmes (71 Md. 20, 29), it was held that prayers leaving it to the jury to find if proceedings under a tax sale' were regular or if the collector's advertisement was sufficient, are erroneous in submitting questions of law to the jury.

§ 67 

TITLE 6 § 67. Abstract or Irrelevant Propositions of Law or Fact Have No Place in Prayers-Should Be Addressed to the Real Issues of the Case. 

Every prayer should expressly or inferentially embody or submit some question of law, for the ruling of the court and the guidance of the jury, with reference to some real or sincere issue of fact, finding legally sufficient support in the evidence. 

So prayers which embody mere abstract propositions of law or fact are erroneous regardless of their soundness or purity as legal abstractions.82

Obviously, if a prayer embodies a proposition of law that is bad even as a mere abstract legal proposition, the prayer is fundamentally defective without regard to whether it was framed with reference to any real issue of fact of the case on trial.83

Effect of the Pleadings and Statement of Counsel 

Except where the court's attention is, in due form, directed to the pleadings, as is further explained in sections 81 to 93, the testimony and the authorized statements of counsel will be looked to for a determination of what constitutes the real issues of the case, without reference to the pleadings.84

§ 113 

TITLE 6 Illustrations of Abstract Prayers 

So where the merits of an action at law depended, in every aspect of it, upon the true construction of an agreement, every prayer which went to the right of action, and kept out of view the effect of the agreement, and so did not involve the true point of controversy between the parties, was adjudged as wholly abstract.85 

And, again, in a negligence case, involving fatal injuries to a passenger in an automobile that collided with a street car of the defendant, and in which all the evidence related to the negligence vel non of the defendant in relation to this collision, without evidence of any kind as to the operation of the automobile after the collision, except that of the driver of the automobile who said that the street car "drove" him into the building a prayer of the defendant was adjudged misleading because it sought to submit to the finding of the jury the issue whether the said passenger met his death when he fell or was thrown from the automobile as a result "of the said automobile either striking the curb, or colliding with the building mentioned in the evidence." 86

Skeleton Rules of Statutory or Case Law 

The practice of embodying a mere skeleton rule of statutory or case law in a prayer, without any specific guide for its application to any real issue of fact of the case on trial, is a practice that more often tends to confuse and mislead the jury than to aid them in arriving at a proper verdict.87

But it is sometimes permissible for a prayer to inform the jury of a simple provision of law-such as the rule of the road relating to the "right of way" between automobiles approaching intersecting public highways-in the very language of the statute, without defining its meaning or limiting its application to any specific phase of the case on trial.88

§§ 67-68 TITLE 6 

It has been repeatedly adjudicated that prayers which embody mere abstract propositions of law or fact, should not be granted because they tend to confuse, perplex, or mislead the jury and to distract their attention from the real issues of the case on trial.89 But the actual granting of abstract prayers will not always produce a reversal of the judgment, and this is especially so in regard to a prayer which did nothing more than submit a correct rule of law in language intelligible to the jury, although not strictly relevant to the sincere issues of the case.90 

§ 68. Inconsistent or Repugnant Prayers Should Not Be Granted. 

It is the aim of the courts to harmonize their instructions so as to avoid confusion in the minds of the jury regarding the principles of law that should guide and control them in reaching their verdict upon the issues of fact which the court has left to their finding or determination. Accordingly, prayers which, among themselves, are inconsistent, contradictory, repugnant or conflicting should not be granted, regardless of their individual soundness.91

TITLE 6 

Nor should a prayer be granted if it, within itself, embodies conflicting or unrelated propositions of law or fact.92 

A prayer which comprises two conflicting propositions, either one of which, if finding legally sufficient support in the evidence, would present a good cause of action, but both of which, because conflicting, can not be combined in one and the same instruction, should not be granted.⁹ 93 But where the evidence warrants another view than that presented by a prayer of one of the parties, and where his opponent is entitled to have that other view presented in a separate prayer, there is no error in joining the two views in one instruction of the court itself, as the converse of each other, or as in any way qualifying the one or the other, and instructing the jury to find accordingly, as they may find or believe the facts to be.94

Prayers are not in conflict, in the sense of being inconsistent, simply because they are based or predicated upon a different hypothesis of facts finding support in the evidence of the case. For example, where the plaintiff's and the defendant's prayers were addressed to their respective and conflicting theories, as applied to the relative positions of the cab and the truck involved in the accident in question, and to the corresponding duty of each driver in that particular situation in which the jury might find the drivers and vehicles were before the collision, the two prayers were adjudged to be complemental and not conflicting.95

Such varying prayers are sometimes described as qualifying prayers, and not inconsistent or contradictory.96

Inconsistency Due to Error in Prayer of Complaining Party 

Where there was a want of evidence legally sufficient to show that the City of Baltimore (a co-defendant in a negli gence case) had actual notice of the hole along side of the street car track, and where, nevertheless, a granted prayer of the plaintiff submitted to the finding of the jury the hypothesis or theory of both actual and constructive notice on the part of the City, it was held that the plaintiff could not properly complain that a granted prayer of the City, which informed the jury that there had been offered no evidence "legally sufficient to prove that the City had actual notice of the condition of said street," was repugnant to his said prayer.99

TITLE 6 § 69. Argumentative or Discursive Prayers Should Not Be Granted. 

Since a Maryland trial judge is not permitted to express, directly or indirectly, an opinion upon the weight or credibility of testimony that the court admitted into evidence and should have left to the finding of the jury, the prayers or instructions should not embody statements in the nature of an argument or discussion.100 

Although it is thoroughly settled that argumentative or discursive prayers have no rightful place in the Maryland practice, and that such prayers generally tend to confuse and embarrass the jury, and should be rejected, nevertheless, it would seem that the granting of such an erroneous prayer will seldom constitute reversible error; and this applies to "credibility" prayers, which have no rightful place in the Maryland practice of prayers or instructions.101 

§ 70. Misleading, Confusing, Obscure or Ambiguous Prayers 

Should Not Be Granted.

Obviously, any prayer that is phrased in terms which are involved, or obscure, or ambiguous, or indefinite, or which are otherwise unintelligible, tends to confuse and embarrass and thereby mislead the jury.103

§ 121 

TITLE 7 § 71. Definitions of Prayers That (a) Omit or (b) Segregate or 

(c) Assume a Fact, and of a Prayer That (d) Submits an Unproven Fact.

The Maryland decisions speak of prayers which (a) omitted facts, or (b) segregated facts, or (c) assumed facts, and also of prayers which (d) submitted unproven or insufficiently proven facts to the finding of the jury. 

Prayer Which Omitted a Fact 

When a prayer tells the jury that their verdict should be in favor of its proponent, if the jury should believe the hypotheses or elements of fact enumerated in the prayer, and when the facts, as enumerated in the prayer, do not constitute a legally adequate basis or foundation for the finding of the verdict mentioned in the prayer, even assuming the truth of the facts, the prayer has omitted a fact material and necessary to support the instruction that it sought. This may be better observed from a connected reading of sections 72, 73, 79 and 80. 

Prayer Which Segregated a Fact 

A prayer which has enumerated some but not all of the material facts in evidence, is one that has segregated a fact. 

This may be better observed from a connected reading of sections 74, 75 and 80. 

Prayer Which Assumed a Fact

The conclusion of every sound demurrer prayer, as is told more fully in section 7, is based, expressly or impliedly, upon the assumption of either the existence or the non-existence of a fact. A jury prayer, as is told more fully in sections 62 and 

63, assumes a fact by referring to it, expressly or inferentially, without leaving it to the finding of the jury. 

Prayer Which Submitted an Unproven Fact 

As is told more fully in section 64, a prayer which has submitted a fact to the finding of the jury that is without any support whatsoever in the evidence, or which is without legally sufficient support in the evidence, is one that has, in contemplation of law, submitted an unproven fact to the finding of the jury.

§§ 72-73 TITLE 7 § 72. A Prayer That Misstates the Law Independently of the Evidence Can Never State Law of Case Correctly. 

A prayer which incorrectly states the law independently of the evidence cannot be regarded as correctly stating the law in relation to the evidence. In this connection, it was said that the law does not change with every new combination of facts to which it can be applied, but is fixed, definite and certain, and while the manner of its application changes with differing facts, its principles and rules remain invariable.¹ § 73. Prayer Must Base Verdict That It Seeks Upon an Adequate 

Foundation of Facts-Must Not Impose Too Many Facts-Case Illus trations. 

A prayer going or concluding to a recovery is defective if it fails to instruct the jury that, before they can render a verdict in accordance with its mandate, they must first find every fact essential to that result.2

Generally speaking, a prayer impliedly misstates the law when it omits a fact necessary and material to support the instruction that it seeks. For example, a prayer is ordinarily defective when it predicates the verdict, which it seeks to attain in favor of its proponent, upon a foundation or hypothesis of facts which, even if found to be true, would not support the verdict as a matter of law. Moreover, such a defective prayer will not ordinarily be cured by the circumstance that there are disputed facts in evidence, besides those recited in

On the other hand, as is further explained and illustrated in section 75, a prayer may prove to be fatally defective even where it claimed the verdict, for its proponent, upon a legally adequate foundation of facts as was recited in the prayer itself, if the prayer failed to negative or otherwise allow for a countervailing fact, claim or defense of the opposite party finding legally sufficient support in the evidence.5 

A prayer of one side, is also defective when it requires the jury to find more facts than the law exacts before they are permitted to render their verdict in favor of the other side.

In Adams v. In reference to the afore-mentioned prayer in the Adam's Case, it was said, in part, (our paragraphing): "The plaintiff's prayer which was granted was faulty, because it failed to require the jury to find that defendant or his servants operating the ferry boat had or should have had knowledge of the fact that oysters were or might be planted in the area which might be affected by the operation of the boat, or that its operation could inflict damages upon the property of another. Illustration-B 

In Louis v. Johnson (146 Md. 115, 119, 121), being an action against the owner of an automobile and its driver for injuries received in a collision, wherein the owner contended that the driver was not acting as his agent at the time of the plaintiff's injury, it was held that a granted prayer, submitted by the plaintiff-which told the jury that their verdict should be in his favor against the owner of the automobile if they believed the facts enumerated in the prayer-was fatally defective because it omitted the issue of fact regarding the said agency of the driver, especially since the owner produced evidence in support of this defense.

Illustration-C 

In Clark v. Banks (158 Md. 24, 31-32), being an action for the recovery of brokerage commissions, which was resisted upon the defense of an estoppel in pais, the defendants sought to have the jury instructed to the effect that the plaintiff was not entitled to recover "if the jury should find that the husband promised O. B. McLean to pay him full commissions if he procured a purchaser, and that the plaintiff was present at this promise and at the negotiations which led up to the sale of the property to a purchaser produced by McLean, but remained quiet and permitted the transaction to be closed without asserting any claim to commission." 

In regard to this desired instruction, it was said, in part (our paragraphing): "The pleader rests the estoppel in pais on the presence, silence, and inaction of the plaintiff. "These elements are too narrow a foundation, since the trinity are without legal significance if they are not coupled with a knowledge, either actual or constructive, of the plaintiff of what was happening. Herman on Estoppel, sec. 1062. "The duty to speak or to act opportunely does not spring merely from a presence at negotiations, unless there be a knowledge of something occurring which, with respect to others, makes it a duty of the party to act or to speak. "Under these circumstances, the court supplied a patent defect of the prayer by incorporating in the prayer the indispensable element of knowledge on the part of the plaintiff, by concluding the prayer with this clause: "'provided the jury believe from the evidence that Linwood L. Clark was justified from the plaintiff's conduct and actions

125 

TITLE 7 

and her knowledge of the terms of the contract of sale, in assuming that plaintiff looked to McLean and not to him for commissions, before paying all commissions to McLean.' "In other words, the party estopped must act with knowledge, and the reliance of the one who asserts the estoppel upon the silence and inaction of the party to be estopped must be reasonable, when measured by the exercise of reasonable prudence, and must not be because the one claiming the estoppel closes his mind to cautionary or inconsistent circumstances.” 

§ 74. Prayers That Segregate or Emphasize a Fact, or Which Designate a Witness, Are Not Favored. 

While it is true that a party may sometimes segregate a portion of the facts offered in proof and ask an instruction upon them, as is explained hereinbelow and in section 75, such prayers are not generally favored. It is a practice liable to abuse, and to mislead, due to the following causes:

Grounds for Disfavor of Prayers Which Segregate Facts 

When the evidence has been admitted the fact of its admission gives the jury the right to consider every fact in the case that is proven to their satisfaction. It is not the proper office of the Court to call the attention of the jury to this or that fact, and inform them that they may take it into consideration in making up their verdict. Such instructions coming from the Court, are apt to give undue weight and prominence to the facts thus called to their attention.7 

Moreover, a Maryland trial court must not, as is further explained in section 26, grant any instruction or make any comment that would tend to emphasize or minimize the value, weight, or effect of evidence, or which would furnish credibility tests for the jury to apply to the testimony of any witness.8

§ 74 

TITLE 7 Prayer that Concludes to a Recovery Must Submit Whole Case 

A prayer concluding with the right of either party to recover must submit the whole case, and the conclusion reached upon the facts stated must be correct notwithstanding all other facts and circumstances in evidence.⁹ 

Undue Emphasis of a Fact in a Prayer

Even where it is permissible for a prayer to segregate a fact in evidence and predicate an instruction upon it, the statement of the fact should not be arranged or presented in the prayer in such a manner as would give the fact undue emphasis or prominence in the eyes of the jury.10 Nor should a prayer segregate facts in derogation of their proper relation to the issue.11

Prayer Should Not Single Out the Testimony of Any Witness 

Where a defendant's prayer, in a negligence case, told the jury that if they "believed the accident happened as described by the defendant's witness, Gilbert Porter, then the verdict of the jury must be for the defendant," it was held that the prayer was properly refused because it would be an exceedingly dangerous practice to adopt, for the following reasons:

In the first place, if the jurors, or any of them, knew Mr. 

Porter and believed him to be a truthful man, they would hesitate to render a verdict for the plaintiff because they might regard the prayer as requiring them to pass on his veracity, and not simply on his recollection or opportunity to see and comprehend all that occurred. It would have the effect of bringing his testimony into more prominence than that of any other witness, and moreover the jury might not remember all of his testimony.12

When Prayer May Base the Verdict on the Testimony of a Certain Witness But where an occurrence, as testified to by the witness designated in the prayer, was so controlling, in contemplation

§ 75. When Prayers May and May Not Segregate Facts and Ignore Claims or Defenses of the Opposite Party-Case Illustrations. 

It is long-settled in the Maryland courts that a party may segregate one or more of the facts produced in evidence and ask an instruction upon it or them. But when so segregated the conclusion arrived at in the instruction must be consistent with the truth of all the other facts produced in evidence. In other words, if found to be true the facts so segregated must support the theory of the prayer, non obstante the truth of other facts produced in evidence.14

Prayer Going to a Verdict for Plaintiff Since a prayer which instructs the jury that the plaintiff is entitled to recover if certain facts are found to exist, has the effect of withdrawing from the consideration of the jury all facts other than those specified, the rule is that the prayer is erroneous, if the facts which it excludes admit of a conclusion different from the one to which it is directed.15

§ 75 

TITLE 7 Prayer Going to a Verdict for Defendant 

Any prayer denying plaintiff's right to recover, or directing a verdict for defendant, upon the finding by the jury of a segregated group of facts is bad, if there are in the case other facts not included in that group which may properly and validly be given the effect of qualifying or destroying the conclusion stated in the prayer.16

Prayer Going to a Verdict On a Central Fact 

A prayer may segregate one question of fact, finding legally sufficient support in the evidence, and may ask the court to instruct the jury that if they should believe that fact, their verdict must be in favor of the proponent of the prayer, provided, however, that the segregated fact was a central and controlling one and that, if believed by the jury, it was sufficient, in contemplation of law, to entitle the proponent of the prayer to the verdict, without consideration by the jury of the facts in the case not mentioned in the prayer.¹ 17 

Basing Legal Proposition On a Segregated Fact 

The practice of segregating facts in prayers which tell the jury what the law is if they should find or believe the specified facts is common to the Maryland courts.18

Care Due Passengers Boarding Moving Car

Passengers Not Chargeable With Negligence of Driver 

And, again, where a prayer tells the jury, in effect, as it may do in appropriate situations, that while the plaintiff is responsible for his own want of ordinary care, he is not chargeable, as a matter of law, with the negligence of the driver of the automobile in which the plaintiff was a passenger at the time of the collision in question, if the jury should find that the plaintiff neither owned the automobile nor had any control over its driver, the prayer obviously segregates this phase of the plaintiff's case.20

Must Negative Countervailing Claim or Defense of Opponent 

Generally speaking, it may be said that a prayer which asks the court to instruct the jury that their verdict must be in favor of its proponent, if the jury should find or believe the hypotheses or elements of fact enumerated in the prayer, should not be granted if the prayer has failed to negative or otherwise submit to the consideration of the jury those claims or defenses of the opponent which find legally sufficient support in the evidence and which, if believed by the jury, would be sufficient, in contemplation of law, to defeat, nullify or modify the verdict as was allowed by the prayer.21

TITLE 7 Not Necessary to Negative Mere Denial Testimony 

But it is not legally necessary for a prayer of a plaintiff, even where it goes or concludes to a verdict upon the finding by the jury of the facts postulated in it, to negative or otherwise allow for the evidence of the defendant which, in contemplation of law, amounts to but a denial of one or more of the facts that were postulated in the prayer of the plaintiff.22 

And, under similar factual situations, the same rule of law applies to a prayer of a defendant, even where it goes or concludes to a verdict upon the facts postulated in it.23 

Effect of Granting a Segregated Prayer “In Connection" 

As is further explained in section 129, a granted prayer which had erroneously segregated a fact may sometimes be saved, from producing reversible error, by being granted expressly in connection with another prayer which submitted to the finding of the jury the issues of fact excluded from the segregated prayer.24

Illustration-A 

As is further told in section 33, where there are circumstances in a negligence case from which the jury could rationally infer that the plaintiff had, by his own negligence, directly contributed to produce the injury complained of by him, no prayer of the plaintiff that goes or concludes to a recovery or verdict should ordinarily fail to exclude or negative the theory of his own contributory negligence.

§ 131 

TITLE 7 Illustration-B 

As is further told in section 33, where the evidence in a negligence case is such as to render applicable the doctrine of the last clear chance, no prayer of the defendant that goes or concludes to a verdict upon the supposition of the plaintiff's contributory negligence should fail to exclude or negative the theory of the last clear chance.

In Bode v. Coal Co. (172 Md. 406)—involving an intersectional collision between Doctor Bode's automobile and a truck of the defendantit was said that the trial court had erred in granting a prayer, submitted by the defendant, which offered a complete guide to a verdict on a segregated fact whose isolation by the prayer excluded other countervailing facts, such as the plaintiff's "right of way", which the jury could have found, and which, if found, would have prevented the fact thus segregated from being sufficient to bar a recovery by plaintiff, especially since there was no express requirement by the court that this deficient prayer of the defendant be read in connection with correct instructions granted on plaintiff's behalf. 

Illustration-D 

In the second appeal in the case of Creamery Co. v. Friedman (160 

Md. 526-first appeal Friedman v. Hendler Creamery Co., 158 Md. 131) —involving an action on account of a collision between motor vehicles at a street intersection, in which the evidence showed that each driver had violated some rule of the road-it was held that a prayer of the defendant, which instructed the jury that the plaintiff could not recover if they found that the plaintiff's failure to yield the right of way was the direct and proximate cause of the accident, was not defective because it failed to tell the jury that the plaintiff could recover if they found that the defendant's violation of another rule of the road was the direct and proximate cause of the accident, since a finding by the jury that the plaintiff's failure to yield the right of way was the proximate cause of the collision would constitute a complete bar to the plaintiff's right of recovery and necessarily excluded the said theory of the plaintiff.

In May Oil Burner Corp. v. Munger (159 Md. 605)-involving an action for the purchase price of two oil burners-prayers of the defendant which allowed her the verdict if the jury should find that the oil burners were defective and not as warranted-were adjudged to be erroneous, because these prayers ignored the evidence that showed that the defendant had accepted the oil burners with the full knowledge of the alleged defects; since where one accepts an article

§ 75 

TITLE 7 

sold to her, with full knowledge of defects therein, she can not thereafter rescind the contract of sale, but her remedy on account of the defects is to bring suit for breach of warranty, or to assert such breach by way of recoupment, or even in the extinction of the purchase price, when sued therefor.

Illustration-F 

In Phillipsborn Co. v. Fineman (148 Md. 188)-involving an action for the recovery of the price of curtains, made especially by the plaintiff for the defendant-it was held that the jury was erroneously instructed, in effect, “that if the curtains were retained by the defendant an unreasonable time the plaintiff could recover the full contract price, even if the jury should find a breach of contract on his part", especially since this defective prayer, even as amended, ignored the testimony which showed that the plaintiff had promised to correct the defects in the curtains, and since the defendant was entitled, in any event, to recoup for the breach of the warranty which the evidence showed.

Illustration-G 

In Cohen v. Fink Piano Co. (160 Md. 440, 443)—involving an action for the price of a radio-a prayer of the plaintiff, which told the jury that their verdict must be for the plaintiff, if they should find that the defendant had ample opportunity to examine the various radios sent to him on approval and that he finally accepted the last one and unconditionally paid a deposit thereupon, was adjudged to be correct, since "no question of recoupment" was involved, and since "the proposition of law in the prayer is correct, as applied to plaintiff's testimony; and no defense set up by the defendant was excluded from the consideration of the jury."

Illustration-H In Home Credit Co. v. Fouch (155 Md. 384)—involving an action on a note by an endorsee thereof-a prayer of the defendants (makers), which told the jury that if they should find that defendants' names were forged to the note, then the verdict of the jury must be in their favor, was adjudged to be defective because it excluded from the prayer facts in evidence which, if believed by the jury to be true, would show such an estoppel as would defeat this defense of forgery.

§ 76. Factual Sufficiency of “General” Primary and Contributory Negligence Prayers-Approved Forms of Such Prayers. 

Except where a single definite act of negligence is relied upon by a plaintiff, the question of the defendant's primary negligence may ordinarily be submitted to the determination of the jury by a general negligence prayer, such as one which requires the jury to decide whether "the plaintiff's injuries resulted from the want of ordinary care and prudence on the part of the defendant," without informing the jury as to which of the defendant's acts, shown in evidence, would, if believed by the jury, show a want of due care on defendant's part.25 

Right to "General" and "Specific" Primary Negligence Prayers

In a case where but a single definite act of negligence was relied upon by the plaintiff, it was held that the action of the trial court, in granting plaintiff's general negligence prayer, such as the afore-described, would not constitute reversible error, since such general negligence prayers have been accredited by repeated approval on appeal, and because, if a defendant regards a granted prayer as not confining the jury to the issue of negligence as made by the pleadings or the evidence, and he desires to narrow the inquiry or to obtain a more explicit instruction, setting out the facts in detail, he may submit such prayers at the trial table. Right to and Form of General Contributory Negligence Prayers 

The question of a plaintiff's contributory negligence may always be submitted to the determination of the jury by general contributory negligence prayers such as the following:27 (1) "The jury are instructed that if they believe from the evidence that the plaintiff could have avoided the accident by the use of ordinary care on his part, their verdict must be for the defendants." (Lynch v. Baltimore, 169 Md. 623). (2) "The jury are instructed that even though they believe from the evidence that the plaintiff tripped in a hole in the street near the street car tracks, nevertheless, if they further believe that the plaintiff could have avoided stepping in the hole by the use of ordinary care on his part, then their verdict must be for the defendants." (Lynch v. Baltimore, 169 Md. 623). (3) The Court instructs the jury that "Notwithstanding the jury shall believe from the evidence that the defendant was guilty of negligence, yet if they shall further believe from the evidence that the plaintiff, Pillard, was also guilty of negligence, and that the accident was directly caused partly by the defendant's negligence and partly by the plaintiff's negligence, then the verdict of the jury must be for the defendant, without regard to whose negligence was the greater." (Pillard v. Ches. Steam. Co., 124 Md., 468, 471-472-this and other approved forms of contributory negligence prayers are set out in sections 620 to 634 of Ashman's (1923) Prayers and Instructions.)

TITLE 7 Right to "Specific" Contributory Negligence Prayers 

Such general contributory negligence prayers are always proper, if there is any proof, express or implied, of contributory negligence, because, as phrased, they allow the jury to take into consideration all the facts and circumstances in evidence bearing upon this question, and do not segregate and give undue emphasis to particular facts of the case, as obviously applies to specific contributory negligence prayers.28

When, however, a plaintiff would be considered guilty of contributory negligence as a matter of law, if the jury believed a certain disputed fact in evidence, regardless of all other facts in proof bearing upon the question of his contributory negligence, the defendant is entitled to the grant of a prayer which submits that certain fact to the finding of the jury and which instructs them that, if they should find or believe that certain fact, then their verdict must be for the defendant.29 

§ 77. When the Submission by a Prayer of One Fact to Finding of Jury Impliedly Submits Another-When Prayer Refers to "All of the 

Circumstances."

The exclusion from a prayer of a fact necessary and material to support the instruction sought, constitutes an objection not less fatal than would be the assumption of the same fact, for in either case the tendency is to force a verdict on facts, the finding of which is taken from the jury. But that objection does not present itself, however, when the exclusion or omission is only of some element or constituent part of a fact, the finding of which, as a whole, is properly left to the jury,80

For example, it was held that the following approved prayer had, in effect, also submitted to the finding of the jury the question of the agent's authority to execute the agreement for and on behalf of the defendants:32 "The Court instructs the jury, that if they believe from the evidence in the cause, that the defendants signed and executed the agreement bearing date 31st December 1856, and that pursuant to said agreement, the referees therein chosen made their award, bearing date the 3rd of January 1857, and that a copy of said award was furnished to each of said parties, and the money awarded to the plaintiff has not been paid, then they must find for the plaintiff."

Effect of Reference in Prayer to "All of the Circumstances" 

On the other hand, in an action to recover for the death of a passenger in an automobile, who was killed when the automobile struck a telephone pole while avoiding defendant's train on a City street, it was held that a prayer of the plaintiff had erroneously segregated and emphasized certain facts in evidence, such as the absence of lights on the defendant's train and its movement at a speed greater than that permitted by an ordinance (four miles per hour), without submitting to the finding of the jury countervailing facts in evidence such as that the street was brilliantly lighted. Moreover, this omission in the prayer was not cured by the addition of the words "taking into consideration all the circumstances attending the movement of said car as shown by the evidence." " 33

In Buehner v. Selhorst, (149 Md. 474, 479, 481), being an action against the endorsers on a note, the 3rd prayer of the defendants asked the court, sitting as a jury, to rule as a matter of law that "unless the note was presented to the maker for payment and dishonored, and notice of non-payment by the maker was given to the endorsers, the verdict must be for the defendants";-but the court modified the prayer by the addition of the proviso- "Unless the Court as jury shall find that the defendants waived such notice and unless it shall further find that said note was a note signed by" the maker "for the accommodation of the defendants * *99 This modification was declared to be erroneous because either one of these facts would, as a matter of law, dispense with the necessity of presentment and notice. 

In other words, the mere insertion in the aforesaid prayer of the above italicized word "and" where the word "or" seemingly belonged, required the court sitting as a jury to find more facts than was necessary as a condition precedent to the plaintiff's right of recovery, and so the prayer impliedly misstated the law of the case.

Need of Special Exception 

As is more fully explained in sections 62 and in sections 136 to 145, the appellate court will review a granted prayer, as well as a rejected prayer, to determine if it had erroneously omitted a fact essential to the verdict or other conclusion as was allowed by the prayer, although it may not and will not do so, in the absence of a special exception, in regard to a granted prayer which assumed a fact. In other words, a special exception is never required against a prayer which omitted, rather than assumed, an essential fact.44

§ 81 TITLE 8 § 81. Right to Confine the Proof to the Pleadings-Why the Allegata and Probata Should Correspond. 

It is a fundamental rule of law that the evidence must correspond with the allegations, and be confined to the issues of fact as made by the pleadings.¹ 

In other words, every litigant may be required to prove his case according to the allegata and probata²—that is to prosecute or defend his case not upon the evidence alone, but upon the pleadings and the evidence applicable to the pleadings. 8

Variances Due to the Form of the Action or the Pleas 

Moreover, the doctrine of allegata and probata, as applies to the pleadings and the proof of a case, extends with equal force to such of the proof as is not, in contemplation of law, in harmony with the pleadings because of the form of the

Why the Allegata and Probata Should Correspond 

The Court of Appeals has emphasized that it is essential to keep in mind the reason and object of the rule that the allegata and probata must corrspond; which rule is intended to answer the double purpose of distinctly and specifically advising the opposite party of what he is called upon to answer, so as to enable him properly to make out his case and to prevent being taken by surprise in the testimony at the trial, and of preserving an unerring record of the cause of action as a protection against another proceeding based upon the same cause.8

Immaterial Variances 

However, the strict rule that once prevailed, in regard to variances between the pleadings and the proof, has been considerably relaxed in order to rid the administration of justice of superfluous technicalities, and this applies even in actions ex contractu, where the rule is more rigidly enforced than in actions ex delicto; and, although the probata must still con-

§ 82. Purpose of "Variance Prayer Act" of 1914-Present Effect of a General Reference to the Pleadings by a Demurrer Prayer. 

The Act of 1914 (Code, art. 5, sec. 11-originally sec. 9A), which relates merely to the form of raising, by a prayer, the question of a variance between the pleadings and the proof, and which we are designating as the "Variance Prayer Act" of 1914, to distinguish it from the "Variance Pleadings Act" of 1914, discussed in section 83, prescribes:11 "The fact that a prayer or instruction which refers in general terms to the pleadings, was granted or refused by the Court below, shall not be sufficient to show that the point or question of a variance between the pleadings and the evidence was tried and decided in the Court below, as required by section 10; and the question of such a variance shall not be considered as having been raised by any prayer or instruction below, unless such prayer or instruction shall state specifically the points wherein it is claimed that such variance exists."

Design of Variance Prayer Act of 1914 

This Act of 1914 was designed to obviate the mischief of the following pre-existing practice. Before this Act went into effect, if any prayer of a case referred to the pleadings, even in but mere general terms, it became the duty of the court to examine the pleadings and to determine if there was a vari- 9 See footnote 8 to this sec.; see case illustrations in text of secs.

§ 83. Purpose of "Pleadings Prayer Act” of 1914-Right to Demar to Deficient Evidence Rather Than to Deficient Declaration. 

The Act of 1914 (Code, art. 75, sec. 97), which in effect prescribes that a prayer cannot be employed to question the sufficiency of the pleadings, though available to challenge the legal sufficiency of the evidence, and which we have designated as the "Pleadings Prayer Act" of 1914, to distinguish it from the "Variance Prayer Act" of 1914, discussed in the preceding section hereof, prescribes.18 "In the trial of all actions at law in the courts of this State no question as to the sufficiency of the pleadings, as stating a cause of action or a defense, as the case may be, which might have been raised by demurrer, shall be raised by prayer or instruction at the trial; provided, however, that nothing in this section shall be held to prevent the court from passing on the question of the legal sufficiency of the evidence to establish a cause of action or defense, although the determination of such question may involve the decision of questions of law which might be raised by demurrer."

Design of "Pleadings Prayer Act" of 1914 

This statute was obviously designed to abrogate the preexisting case law of Maryland, which held that when a prayer referred to the pleadings, the court was permitted to inquire into the legal sufficiency of the declaration.19

TITLE 8 Presumption That Proof Conformed to Pleadings-Review of Pleadings 

Without Evidence

The Court of Appeals will ordinarily review a demurrer to the pleadings even where the evidence, taken at the trial of the case, is omitted from the record on appeal; and this is so because, in the absence of anything in the record to the contrary, it must be assumed that the trial below proceeded in harmony with the pleadings, and that the proof admitted conformed to them. Besides, the evidence cannot supply omissions or correct defects in the pleadings.2 20 .

Demurring to Deficient Evidence Rather Than to Deficient Declaration The failure of a defendant to demur to a deficient declaration does not deprive him of the right to demur to the correspondingly deficient evidence, produced in support of the allegations of the declaration.21

On the other hand, a plaintiff is privileged to produce, in evidence, stronger statements of fact, in contemplation of law, than those contained in his deficient declaration, which was left free of demurrer, provided that the statements as produced in evidence were not materially at variance with the allegations of the declaration or the form of the action.22 

Advantages and Disadvantages in Demurring to Bad Declaration In considering whether or not to demur to a deficient declaration, counsel should also bear in mind the following related rules of law or practice: (1) In filing a demurrer to a declaration, it is necessary, in consequence of the statute applicable to Speedy Judgment Acts or in consequence of local rules of court applicable to demurrers to all pleadings at law, to point out, in effect, the deficient allegations of the declaration.28

§ 84. Amendments to Pleadings to Avoid Variances-Liberal Code Provisions Therefor-Which Pleadings Are Not Amendable. 

Section 35 and sections 39 to 49, inclusive, of article 75 of the Code of Public General Laws of Maryland, contain liberal provisions for the allowance of amendments to the pleadings, in the sound discretion of the court, up to "any time before the jury retire to make up their verdict in cases of jury trial; and in cases of demurrer and other trials before the court, at any time before judgment is entered." 28

Amendments Regarding Parties—“Entire New Parties" Not Permissible Section 45 of article 75 of the Code prescribes.30 

"In amendments for non-joinder or misjoinder entire new parties, either plaintiffs or defendants, cannot be introduced, but some one of the original plaintiffs and some one of the original defendants must remain parties to the action; and in no case of amendment can entire new parties, either plaintiffs or defendants, be made."

Pleas of Limitations, Abatement and Dilatory Pleas Not Amendable Section 47 of article 75 of the Code prescribes :31 

"Nothing in the preceding sections of this article relating to amendments shall affect any plea of limitations, in abatement, to the jurisdiction or other dilatory plea."

Continuance of the Trial Where Amendment Was Allowed Section 48 of article 75 of the Code prescribes :32 

"Where an amendment is allowed after the jury is sworn and the court shall consider a continuance necessary to a fair trial for the cause a juror shall be withdrawn, but if the court considers that a continuance is not necessary to a fair administration of justice the jury may proceed and try the case after the amendment."

When Action of Court in Refusing or Granting Amendment is Reviewable

Generally speaking, however, the Court of Appeals will not review the action of the trial court in either allowing or refusing to allow an amendment to the pleadings, except where the action of the court was contrary to fixed provisions of law, such as the statutes discussed hereinabove.38 

§ 85. Construing Prayers of Case Without Reference to the Pleadings-When Permissible Judicial Notice of Orphans' Court Issues, 

The first clause of section 10 (formerly 9) of article 5 of the Code, at times mentioned as the Act of 1825, expressly enjoins the Court of Appeals from deciding "any point or question which does not plainly appear by the record to have been tried and decided by the court below." In view of this statutory clause, the appellate court soon ruled that if either party designs to raise any question of pleading by a prayer, 36 Code, art. 75, sec. 28 (109); Penn. R. Co. v. And it has been held, ever since, that when a prayer does not refer to the pleadings, its correctness is determined by reference to the evidence alone.39

Where the prayers offered in a case make no reference to the pleadings, and no jury prayer was subjected to a variance special exception, the plaintiff's right to recover, and the defendant's right to defend, does not depend upon the allegations of the pleadings, or upon the form of the action, or the form of pleas, but upon the case as made by the evidence. 40 

As is further explained in section 82, the Variance Prayer Act of 1914 made no change in the pre-existing law of variances, except in relation to the form or method of raising the question of a variance by a prayer. In substance and effect, this statute abolished the pre-existing practice of raising the question of a variance by a mere general reference to the pleadings in a prayer, and further prescribes that the exact point or question of the variance, between the pleadings and the proof, should be stated in any prayer which aims to raise the question of a variance.41

So a prayer which attempts to raise the question of a variance, between the pleadings and the proof, by any general reference to the pleadings, will be construed only in relation to the evidence, irrespective of the pleadings.42

§ 86. Joint Plaintiffs and Defendants-When Variance Arises From Failure to Show a Joint Liability or a Joint Right of Recovery. 

Section 12 of article 50 of the Code of Public General Laws, prescribes:

Not Necessary to Prove Joint Liability in Contract or Tort Cases 

"In suits brought against alleged joint debtors in actions ex contractu it shall not be necessary for the plaintiff to prove their joint liability as alleged in order to maintain his action; but he shall be entitled to recover as in actions ex delicto against such one or more of the defendants as shall be shown by the evidence to be indebted to him; and judgment shall be entered in his favor against such one or more of said defendants as fully as if the defendant or defendants against whom he shall fail to establish his claim had not been joined in the suit." 44

In view of the provisions of the afore-quoted statute, it was held, in an action ex contractu against the defendants, that the fact that the evidence failed to show a joint liability in both defendants could not prevent the plaintiff from recovering severally against the one shown to be liable.45

§ 87 TITLE 8 When Voluntary Bill of Particulars is Not Binding 

But it was held that an account which was voluntarily filed with a declaration that was not brought under the Speedy Judgment Act, did not restrict the plaintiff's proof to the account as filed.54

Bill of Particulars May Spoil But Not Cure Declaration 

A bill of particulars to a declaration, when properly called for and filed in response to the call, becomes a part of the declaration, and the parties are restricted in their evidence to the claim thus presented, but it is not so far a part of the declaration as to cure any substantial defect in it that would be bad on general demurrer to the declaration, although it may serve to show an infirmity in the claim, and so make the declaration open to a demurrer which, in the absence of a bill of particulars, would not have been so exposed.55

Bill of Particulars Can Spoil Good Common Counts 

In other words, a bill of particulars can spoil a good declaration, but cannot cure a bad one.

Accordingly, a bill of particulars, duly filed, will open good common counts to demurrer when the bill of particulars shows that the claim, as disclosed in the bill of particulars, is not recoverable under the common counts.56
