§ 88. Illustrations of Variances in Actions Ex Contractu. 

The following are illustrations of actions ex contractu in which it was held either that the variance between the pleadings and the proof was material, or immaterial, or that there was no variance at all between the pleadings and the proof: 

A-Illustration of a Material Variance in an Action Ex Contractu 

In Piper v. Wells (175 Md. 326), being a suit for commissions growing out of the sale of the property mentioned in the standard "listing agreement" between the plaintiff and defendant, which the defendant breached before the sale of her property took place-it was said, in part: "This brings us to a consideration of the prayers. As previously observed, the suit was not for breach of the contract, but for commissions under a supposedly subsisting contract * * * "By her (defendant's) B prayer, which was (properly) granted, the Court was asked to rule as a matter of law that in view of the fact that under the pleadings the suit was not one for damages for breach of contract, but a suit for the payment of a liquidated sum due and owing the plaintiffs, there was no legally sufficient evidence to entitle them to recover under the pleadings, and the verdict of the 

Court, sitting as a jury, must be for the defendant."

B-Illustration of a Material Variance in an Action Ex Contractu 

In Citizens' Nat. Bank v. Custis (153 Md. 235, 245), the declaration stated that the note, which was the subject of the suit, was "payable to the said Bertha D. Custis on demand."

In speaking of this note, it was said, in part (our italicizing and paragraphing): "The instrument produced proved to be payable to the order of 

Bertha D. Custis, and, although sealed, was negotiable in form.

§ 88 

TITLE 8 

"As the instrument declared upon was stated (in effect) to be a nonnegotiable writing obligatory, the variance was material, and the paper writing was inadmissible under the pleadings."

C-Illustration of a Material Variance in an Action Ex Contractu 

In Aitz Chaim Cong. v. Butterhoff (141 Md. 267, 276-277), it was said, in part (our paragraphing): "It is contended by the appellants that as the above account contains no item for loss of profit to the appellee, caused by the appellants' breach of the contract, he could not, under the statute (Code, art. 75, sec. 24, sub-sec. 107), recover such profit in these proceedings *** "We cannot in this case escape the conclusion that under the statute mentioned, this evidence was inadmissible. "The account, set out with the particularity of a bill of particulars, in effect became a bill of particulars, and like a bill of particulars, the plaintiff was, under the statute, restricted in his evidence to the proof of the items therein set out."

D-Illustration of a Material Variance in an Action Ex Contractu 

In W., B. & A. Elec. R. R. Co. v. Moss (130 Md. 198, 207), involving a suit in assumpsit to recover for services rendered in securing a lease for the defendant and in surrendering the plaintiff's own lease, it was said, in part (our paragraphing): "The defendant's fifth, sixth and seventh prayers should have been granted. "These prayers instructed the jury that the plaintiff could not recover any damages sustained by loss of alleged profits, in either the grocery store business or the boarding house business. "The suit was not for loss of profits but for services rendered in securing the lease and in surrendering the plaintiff's own lease * * *”

E-Illustration of a Material Variance in an Action Ex Contractu 

In White Automobile Co. v. Dorsey (119 Md. 251, 259), it was said, in part (our paragraphing): "The fifth count declared on an express warranty of the automobile by the appellant. "It was essential to the plaintiff's right to recover that he establish by competent evidence to the satisfaction of the jury some one of the material representations alleged. "Evidence of other and different warranties were manifestly inadmissible under the pleadings."

F-Illustration of No Variance in an Action Ex Contractu 

In Wilson v. Kelso (115 Md. 162, 170), it was said, in part (our paragraphing): "The objection to the introduction of the note in evidence is that it discloses a variance between the allegation and the proof *

§ 159 

TITLE 8 

"As the plaintiff elected to hold the defendant separately liable, and as the note was evidence of that liability, there was no variance, notwithstanding the fact that the note when produced showed that there were other joint and several makers whom the plaintiff might have sued. "To hold otherwise would be to tell the holder of such an instrument as the one sued on that he is at liberty to sue any one of the makers separately, and then deprive him of the power to prove his case by the application of the rule of evidence mentioned." 

G-Illustration of No Variance in an Action Ex Contractu 

In Mut. Fire Ins. Co. v. Ritter (113 Md. 163, 172-173), it was said, in part (our paragraphing): "The language of the policy is 'do insure the said H. F. Ritter agreeably to the terms and conditions of the said company hereunto annexed, to the amount of $595,' while the language of the declaration is 'did insure said plaintiff agreeably to the terms and conditions of said company for five hundred and ninety-five dollars.'" 

46 * * we cannot discover any error in the ruling of the Court admitting the policy in evidence."

H-Illustration of a Material Variance in an Action Ex Contractu 

In the syllabus to Richardson v. Anderson (109 Md. 641, 642), it was said: "While a set-off must be specially pleaded and evidence in support of it is not admissible unless so pleaded, yet, when such evidence has been produced without objection, and the prayers do not confine the right to recover to the pleadings and evidence, the jury may find the existence of a set-off in favor of the defendant." 

I-Illustration of a Material Variance in an Action Ex Contractu 

In State v. Wilson (107 Md. 129, 130, 133), being an action on a bond of a tax collector, the declaration alleged its condition to be that the collector "should well and faithfully execute his office and the several duties required of him by law and would well and truly account for and pay all moneys which might be received by him as said collector and be answerable for by law at such times as the law may direct." 

The condition of the bond, as filed with the declaration, was that he "shall well and faithfully execute his office and the several duties required of him by law, and shall well and truly account for and pay to the county commissioners of Kent county or their order, the several sums of money which he shall receive for the county or be answerable for by law at such time as the law shall direct."

Accordingly, it was held that there is a variance between the condition set forth in the declaration and that in the bond, and that therefore a demurer to the declaration should be sustained.

§§ 88-89 TITLE 8 J-Illustration of a Material Variance in an Action Ex Contractu 

In the syllabus to Sounder v. Home Friendly Society (72 Md. 511); it was said: "In an action to recover on life certificates issued to the plaintiff by the defendant insurance company, the declaration alleged that the certificates were made payable to the plaintiff on the death of the insured, and that the defendant was bound to pay the sum of $1,000 on each of them by means of an assessment, &c., whereas they were payable to the plaintiff if living at the death of the insured, and the agreement, was to pay within ninety days after satisfactory proof of death: HELD: 

"That this constituted a variance.”

K-Illustration of No Variance in an Action Ex Contractu 

In Weber v. Fickey (52 Md. 500, 512), it was said (our paragraphing): "The only ground of objection urged against its admissibility is that the record of the judgment shows that it was recovered by Frederick Fickey, Jr., while the amended narr. in this case names the plaintiff as Frederick Fickey. "It was contended that this is such a variance as to make the record inadmissible *** "It has been held in various cases, that 'Jr.' is no part of a man's name "The record of the judgment was properly admitted." 

L-Illustration of a Material Variance in an Action Ex Contractu 

In the syllabus to Norris v. Graham (33 Md. 56), it is said: "If in an action brought to recover money alleged to be due for wood furnished a third party 'on the credit and guaranty of the defendant,' the evidence shows that the defendant contracted with and purchased the wood from the plaintiff, and was to pay for it, there is a variance between the allegata and probata, and the plaintiff cannot recover."

M-Illustration of a Material Variance in an Action Ex Contractu 

In the syllabus to Penna., etc., v. Dandridge (8 G. & J., 248), it is said: "A declaration which alleges a contract to tow a vessel and cargo out, safely and securely, is not supported by proof of a contract to tow out free from a particular description of danger. "In the one case, the contract would cover a loss from any and every cause, while in the other, there could be no recovery, unless the loss arose from the danger particularly named in the contract." 

§ 89. Illustrations of Variances in Negligence Cases. 

The following are illustrations of negligence cases in which it was held either that the variance between the pleadings and

§ 161 

TITLE 8 

the proof was material, or immaterial, or that there was no variance at all between the pleadings and the proof: 

A-Illustration of a Material Variance in a Negligence Case 

In Toy v. Atlantic G. & P. Co. (176 Md. 4 A. (2d) 757, 766-767), being a negligence case to recover against a dredging company for damages sustained by plaintiffs when mass of earth, which had been dredged from canal, under Federal supervision, slid into pond, and deprived plaintiffs of access to their land, etc., it was said (our paragraphing): "As set forth in Dicey on Parties to Actions the general rule is that a husband may sue either alone or jointly with his wife for all injuries done during coverture to real property of which the husband and wife are seized, or to which they are entitled in right of the wife. "Should the husband sue with his wife where she neither must nor may be joined, the error is fatal *** "The declaration alleges that the plaintiffs are husband and wife and as such are the owners in fee simple of the tract of land which was injured by the wrongs alleged. "The testimony proved that the land affected is owned in severalty by the husband, which is a variance but not a question on this record, as it is not raised by an appropriate prayer."

B-Illustration of No Variance in a Negligence Case 

In Longenecker v. Zanghi (175 Md. 307), it was said, in part (our paragraphing): "The second ground of (special) exception (to the plaintiff's prayer) is that the pleadings did not permit recovery based upon the doctrine of last clear chance. "The plaintiff declared in an action for injuries which directly resulted from the careless, reckless and negligent manner in which the defendant was operating her automobile at the time of the accident, and which was not due to any negligence on the part of the plaintiff directly contributing thereto. "So, any form of negligence on the part of the defendant in the operation of the automobile which was the proximate and exclusive cause of the plaintiff's injury was within the pleadings."

C-Illustration of a Material Variance in a Negligence Case 

In Thompson v. Sun Cab Co. (170 Md. 299, 301-303), it was said, in part (our paragraphing): "*** the single question is the propriety of the court's action in granting, at the close of the plaintiff's case, a prayer instructing the jury that the plaintiff had offered no evidence legally sufficient to entitle him to recover against the defendants ***”

$ 89

TITLE 8 

"The non-liability of one of the joint tort-feasors did not appear until the close of the plaintiff's case, and objection could then be made as a variance ✶ ✶✶” 

"The prayer offered put the plaintiff to his election. "He could have amended his declaration by asking leave of the court to strike out the defendant against whom his proof had failed, and the cause would then have proceeded against the remaining defendant ** **" 

D-Illustration of No Variance in a Negligence Case 

In Miller v. Hall (161 Md. 111, 114), it was said, in part (our paragraphing): "It is objected that as, concerning the right of way, the declaration filed in the case did not specify violation of the law (Code, art. 56, sec. 209) as a ground of liability, the question of violation is not within the issues on which the parties went to trial, and proof on it is therefore not admissible *** "A charge of negligence in a collision of vehicles approaching each other at right angles at a street crossing by its very nature brings up a question of yielding the right of way, and gives notice of the pertinency of evidence on that question." 

E-Illustration of No Variance in a Negligence Case 

In Coplan v. Warner (158 Md. 463, 468), it was said, in part (our paragraphing): "The court refused a prayer of the defendant for an instruction that, as there was no evidence of driving carelessly, negligently, and at a high rate of speed, as was charged in the declaration, the plaintiff was not entitled to recover, and the purpose of the prayer was, as stated by counsel, to raise a question of variance between the declaration and the proof on the charge of driving at a high rate of speed * * * "The essential allegation is that of driving carelessly and negligently * "As we have said, we are of opinion that there was evidence from which a jury might legally find negligent driving." 

F-Illustration of an Immaterial Variance in a Negligence Case 

In the syllabus to Hochschild, Kohn & Co. v. Murdock (154 Md. 

575, 576), it is said: "That, while the declaration alleged that a revolving door in defendant's store was insecurely folded and suffered to remain in the center of the entrance, without sufficient stays to keep it in place, the evidence tended to show negligence in causing the folding of the door rather than in the lack of a secure fastening, did not show a prejudicial variance."

163 

TITLE 8 G-Illustration of a Material Variance in a Negligence Case 

In Nelson v. Seiler (154 Md. 63, 70), it was said, in part (our paragraphing): "An offer was made to prove that the father of the present appellant, owner of the automobile and a co-defendant, knew of the convictions and arrests of his son alluded to, and it was argued that upon such proof liability might be placed upon the father for entrusting his automobile to an incompetent or dangerous driver * * * "In this situation the evidence was rightly rejected, in so far as its purpose was to establish negligence in the father as stated. "And this court concludes that it should have been rejected, even considered as offered to impeach the witness' veracity." 

H-Illustration of a Material Variance in a Negligence Case 

In M. & C. C. of Balto. v. Stalfort (123 Md. 269, 279-280, 282), it was said, in part (our paragraphing): "In his prayer (plaintiff's 1st) no allusion is made to the defects in the repaving of the gutter mentioned and described in the declaration, but by it the Court is asked to instruct the jury if it finds other conditions existing which are attributed to the negligence of the 

"In the case before us, like the case from which we have just quoted, the facts alleged in the declaration in respect to the cause of the alleged injury to plaintiff's property, are altogether different from the facts stated in the plaintiff's prayer upon which he asked to recover "For the reasons we have stated, we think the Court was in error in granting the plaintiff's first prayer-and in not granting the defendant's first prayer asking that the case be taken from the jury because of the want of legally sufficient evidence, under the pleadings, to entitle the plaintiff to recover."

I-Illustration of a Material Variance in a Negligence Case 

In the syllabus to Joyce v. Flanigan (111 Md. 481), it is said: "A party has the right to have the evidence confined to the issue made by the pleadings, and consequently, when a declaration alleges that the defendant negligently failed to ascertain the presence of poisonous gases in a sewer trench being dug, or to remove them, or notify a workman of their presence, evidence as to the provision of means of egress from the trench is not admissible." 

J-Illustration of a Material Variance in a Negligence Case 

In the syllabus to Western Md. R. Co. v. Shirk (95 Md. 638), it is said: "When the declaration alleges only negligence in regard to the inspection of a car, the broken axle of which was the efficient cause of the injury sued for, it is error to enlarge the issue thus made by

$$ 89-90

TITLE 8 

requiring the jury to find, in order to exonerate the defendant, not only that it made a careful and competent inspection of the car, but also that it exercised due care in all subsidiary arrangements necessary to the safety of the passenger."

K-Illustration of an Immaterial Variance in a Negligence Case 

In the syllabus to Ryan and McDonald v. Gross (68 Md. 377, 378), it is said: "Where the plaintiff charges that his property was destroyed by sparks of fire from a certain 'steam shovel plough' or 'steam engine' operated by the defendants, and the proof shows that the fire was caused by sparks from a steam engine used by the defendants in working a shovel plough, there is no substantial variance between the allegation and the proof. "It is enough if the substance of the issue is proved, and variance in form merely, or in matter immaterial, will not be regarded." 

§ 90. Illustrations of Variances in Actions Ex Delicto (Except 

Negligence).

The following are illustrations of actions ex delicto (except negligence) in which it was held either that the variance between the pleadings and the proof was material, or immaterial:

A-Illustration of a Material Variance in an Action Ex Delicto 

In Real Estate Etc. Corp. v. Water Co. (167 Md. 191, 193), it was said, in part (our paragraphing):

The plaintiff sued in ejectment and so was obliged to prove that it held the legal title to the land that was the subject of the suit. At the trial, however, the plaintiff produced deeds that showed it to be the owner of "only certain water rights and privileges incident thereto"; which "rights are clearly only easements. * * *” 

So it was held : "If any rights of appellant (plaintiff) have been invaded by appellee * * appellant's remedy is in an action on the case and not in ejectment."

And it was also held that the trial court had properly granted the defendant's third prayer, approved as a variance prayer. 

B-Illustration of a Material Variance in an Action Ex Delicto 

In Pugaczewska v. Maszko (163 Md. 355, 357-360), it was said, in part (our paragraphing): "The declaration is against Michael and Leokadya Pugaczewska as for a joint tort. "There was evidence in the case to support the hypothesis that Michael and Leokadya had each been guilty of a several and inde-

§ 165 

TITLE 8 

pendent assault and battery upon Mrs. Maszko, but no evidence of any kind that they had committed a joint assault upon her. "But the only theory on which the plaintiff was entitled to recover under the declaration was that Michael and Leokadya Pugaczewska had jointly assaulted and beat her, and that is what the verdict of the jury decided * * *” "We find no error in the refusal of appellant's demurrer prayer. 

It made no reference to the pleadings, so that the question it submitted was whether there was any evidence legally sufficient to entitle the plaintiff to recover against Leokadya Pugaczewska. The only question raised by such a prayer is whether, upon the evidence apart from the pleadings, the plaintiff is entitled to recover in any form of action." 

C-Illustration of a Material Variance in an Action Ex Delicto 

In Tea Company v. Roch (160 Md. 189, 190-193), being a suit "against the proprietor of a grocery store on account of nervous shock caused by plaintiff's receipt from the store of a package containing a dead rat * **", it was said, in part (our paragraphing): "The declaration as drawn presents a case against the defendant *** for injuries sustained by the plaintiff as a result of a practical joke perpetrated by * * *” the defendant. "All of the evidence which fits the declaration makes of the incident a practical joke perpetrated by West, the manager, for which the defendant could not have been held. "What made this case different from *** was the testimony of the plaintiff's husband that West said to him shortly after the boy delivered package: 'I am sorry, Mr. Roch, I made a mistake. I sent your wife a wrong package'; which was substantially the same statement made to her mother. "If this admission had not gotten into the case there would have been nothing to tie the act complained of to the defendant." 

D-Illustration of an Immaterial Variance in an Action Ex Delicto 

In the syllabus to Stanton v. Lapp (113 Md. 324), it is said: "If the description of the land in the declaration in an action of trespass is substantially the same as that contained in the lease, a mere variance in form between the two descriptions is immaterial, and the lease is admissible in evidence." 

E-Illustration of an Immaterial Variance in an Action Ex Delicto 

In the syllabus to Shafer v. Smith (7 H. & J. 67, 68), it is said: "But in no case can damages be recovered in one action for an independent substantive injury for which another form of action is prescribed. "The declaration alleging the well to be the plaintiff's and the evidence showing it to be the defendant's, the variance was held to be fatal."

§ 91 

TITLE 8 § 91. Three Ways of Confining the Proof, Claims, Defenses and the Prayers of a Case to the State of the Pleadings. 

In the Maryland courts the question of a variance between the pleadings and the proof may be raised by any or all of the following three methods, viz:59 (1) By an objection to evidence that is expressly or impliedly at variance with the state of the pleadings, or with the form of the action, or with the form of the pleas.60 (2) By a variance prayer that states specifically the points of variance between the pleadings and the proof.61 (3) By a variance special exception against a jury prayer that seeks to recover or defend, as the case may be, upon a claim or defense that is materially at variance with a material allegation of the pleadings, or with the form of the action, or with the form of the pleas.02 

Objection to Evidence Directs Court to Pleadings Where an objection is raised to the admissibility of evidence offered generally at the trial of the case, the attention of the court is necessarily called to the pleadings in the cause, as the admissibility of the evidence is entirely dependent on them, and the court cannot judge of the pertinence or materiality of the evidence except by reference to the pleadings.63

§ 92. Approved Forms of Variance Prayers in Relation to the Vari ance Prayer Act of 1914 (Code, art. 5, sec. 11). 

The following prayers appear to have been expressly or im pliedly approved as variance prayers in relation to the Variance Prayer Act of 1914 (Code, article 5, section 11-set out in section 82 hereof):

A-Illustration of a Variance Prayer-Expressly Approved 

(Piper v. Wells, 175 Md. 326) "The Court rules as a matter of law that in view of the fact that under the pleadings this is not a suit for damages for breach of contract, but a suit for the payment of a liquidated sum due and owing the plaintiffs, there is no evidence legally sufficient to entitle the plaintiffs to recover under said pleadings, and the verdict of the Court, sitting as a jury, must be for the defendant."

B-Illustration of a Variance Prayer-Expressly Approved 

(Real Estate Etc. Corp. v. Water Co., 167 Md. 191-193) "The Court instructs itself, sitting as a jury, that there is no evidence in this case legally sufficient to show that title to the land described and claimed in the declaration is in the plaintiff, and hence the verdict of the Court, sitting as a jury, must be for the defendant." 

C-Illustration of a Variance Prayer-Seemingly Approved 

(Coplan v. Warner, 158 Md. 463, 468) "The Court instructs the Jury that it is alleged in the declaration that the defendant, his agents or servants carelessly and negligently and at a high rate of speed operated and managed an automobile so that it collided with the plaintiff, causing him injury. That there is no evidence in this case legally sufficient to show that the defendant, his agents or servants, operated and managed said automoible carelessly and negligently and at a high rate of speed and that, therefore, under the pleadings in this case, the verdict of the Jury must be for the defendant."

§§ 92-93 TITLE 8 D-Illustration of a Variance Prayer-Seemingly Approved 

(Hochschild, Kohn & Co. v. Murdock, 154 Md. 575, 576, 580) "The Court instructs the jury that no evidence has been offered in this case legally sufficient to prove the allegation contained in the Declaration that the revolving door referred to therein was insecurely folded or suffered or permitted to remain in the center of the entrance without efficient, or adequate brakes or stays to hold or keep it in place, and that, therefore, their verdict shall be in favor of the defendant, Hochschild, Kohn & Company, Inc."

E-Illustration of a Variance Prayer-Expressly Approved (Isaac Benesch & Sons, Inc. v. Ferkler, 153 Md. 680, 682) 

"The Court instructs the jury that the plaintiff's proof as adduced in this case varies from the allegations contained in the declaration, in that there is no legally sufficient evidence in the case tending to support the averment that the plaintiff 'was caused to slip and fall due to the floor having been freshly oiled and the failure of the said defendant to allow sufficient time to elapse for the proper drying of the oil that had been placed thereon' and that because of such variance between the probata and allegata the verdict of the jury shall be for the defendant."

And that, under the pleadings in this case the plaintiff is precluded from relying upon the doctrine of last clear chance which is the basis of the said prayer."

§ 169 

TITLE 8 Approved Form of "Last Clear Chance" Prayer 

The afore-quoted variance special exception was addressed to the following approved prayer of the plaintiff, involving the doctrine of the last clear chance: "The Court instructs the Jury that even if they find that there was want of ordinary care and prudence on the part of the plaintiff, yet he is entitled to recover provided the defendant could have avoided the accident by the exercise of ordinary care after she saw, or by the use of ordinary care might have seen, that the plaintiff's truck was entering the intersection of Jarrettsville Road and Paper Mill Road in the path of her automobile and in danger of being struck by it." 

B-Illustration of an Oral Variance Special Exception-Expressly Approved 

(Davidson Chem. Co. v. Miller, 122 Md. 134, 138)

In this Davidson Chem. Co. case, the plaintiff submitted a prayer which, in effect, required the jury to decide whether he was indebted to the defendant, under the latter's plea of set-off, which was, however, withdrawn at the trial with leave of court.

Whereupon the defendant's counsel orally objected to the said prayer of the plaintiff "upon the ground that its (defendant's) claim of set-off having been withdrawn by leave of court and the pleading amended by striking out such plea, there was no longer any such issue in the case to be submitted to the jury."

TITLE 9 § 94. Power of Maryland Court to Take Civil Case or Any Part 

Thereof From the Jury-Duty of the Jury to Obey Directed Verdict. 

It has been held in Maryland, as an axiom of the law ever since the institution of courts of justice, that it is the exclusive province of the jury to decide on the credibility of witnesses and to determine the weight of testimony.¹ On the other hand, it is equally well settled, in civil trials, that the court is inherently empowered to determine whether the evidence is legally sufficient to sustain the whole or any part of the case on trial, of either the plaintiff or defendant.2 

In other words, it is the settled law of Maryland, as well as in England, that the legal sufficiency of evidence is a question of law for the court, but the comparative weight and value of the testimony is a question exclusively for the jury, under proper instructions from the court.3 

Taking Case From Jury Via Demurrer Prayers 

Accordingly, it is always competent, in civil trials at law, for either of the parties to submit demurrer prayers which, in effect, pray the court to take from the jury, or from the court sitting as a jury, the opponent's case, in whole or part, because of the undisputed existence of a certain controlling fact, or because of a general want of evidence legally sufficient to sustain the case, claim or defense, as the case may be, to which the demurrer prayer under consideration was addressed.4 

Taking Case From Jury Via Variance Prayers 

As is further explained in sections 81 to 93, a case may also be taken from the jury, through the medium of a variance prayer, because the evidence is at variance with the pleadings.

§§ 94-95 TITLE 9 

Jury Must Obey Directed Verdict

Where the court grants a demurrer prayer or variance prayer that directs the jury to render a verdict in favor of the plaintiff or the defendant, as the case may be, the jury has no duty but to obey.5

Court Cannot Take Criminal Case From Jury 

In criminal trials, however, as is further explained in section 160, the court cannot grant demurrer prayers, due to the unique provision in the Maryland Constitution that perpetuated the jury in all criminal trials as "Judges of the Law, as well as of fact." 

Two Stages For Offering Defendant's Demurer Prayers— Waiver of Exception by Defendant's Production of Testimony. 

Section 96 of Article 75 of the Code of Public General Laws of Maryland, originally enacted in 1894, reads (as amended): "If the defendant in the trial of any action in a court of law, including issues from another court, shall, at the close of the plaintiff's evidence and before offering any evidence or defense, pray the court to instruct the jury that the plaintiff in such action has offered no evidence legally sufficient to entitle the plaintiff to a verdict on any one or more counts or issues, or offer a prayer to the same effect, and the court shall reject such prayer, the defendant shall not be precluded from offerng evidence of defense, but such defendant may offer evidence of defense as fully and to the same extent as though such prayer had not been offered."

Design of Act of 1894 

The Act of 1894 was clearly designed to change the following pre-existing practice. Before the passage of this Act (Code, art. 75, sec. 96), if at the close of the plaintiff's case, the defendant submitted a demurrer prayer to take the plaintiff's case from the jury, and if such prayer was refused, the defendant was estopped, by certain rules of court, from producing testimony in defense, and so the case then went to the jury on the plaintiff's testimony alone." 

5 Harris v. Hipsley, 122 Md. 418, 427. 

6 Schwanteck v. Berner, 96 Md. 138, 143-144; Barabasz v. Kabat, 91 Md. 53, 60.

§§ 95 

173 

TITLE 9 

The reference in the said Act of 1894, as amended, to "issues from another court," is seemingly intended to apply to Orphans' court issues."

Defendant's Waiver of Exception by Producing Testimony 

A defendant who has produced any testimony whatsoever, following the court's refusal of his demurrer prayers submitted at the close of the plaintiff's case, has, thereby, conclusively waived his exception to the said action of the court, although he is privileged to renew his exception to the refusal of any of his demurrer prayers, as well as his jury prayers, at the close of the whole case.8

In this connection, however, it should be borne in mind that, in passing upon a demurrer to the evidence at the close of the whole case, the court cannot, as a rule, consider evidence produced on behalf of the defendant except where it tends to cure a defect in the proof of the plaintiff."

In other words, the court cannot, ordinarily, grant a demurrer prayer which, in effect, calls for a directed finding in favor of the litigant who carried the burden of proving the issue of fact which the prayer under consideration sought to take from the jury.11 

Rule Against a Directed Verdict in Favor of a Plaintiff Accordingly, there exists in the Maryland courts the rule against a directed verdict in favor of a plaintiff. Moreover, this rule ordinarily applies even where the defendant has produced no evidence in contradiction of the plaintiff's case. This is so because the court cannot, ordinarily, deprive the jury of their inherent power to refuse to give credence even to uncontradicted testimony, and to pass upon its credibility and weight.12 "Uncontroverted" Rather Than "Uncontradicted" Facts

It is when the facts are virtually uncontested or uncontroverted, rather than when the testimony in regard thereto is virtually uncontradicted, that the court can determine, as a question of law, whether they do or do not sustain the claim or defense, as the case may be, which the demurrer prayer under consideration sought, in effect, to take from the jury.13 

When Directed Verdict in Favor of Plaintiff is Permissible In other words, where the facts of a case have been ascertained and agreed upon by the parties, or are virtually undisputed or uncontroverted, and there is no dispute as to the inferences to be drawn from the facts, the question becomes one of law and may be decided as such by the court. § 177 

TITLE 9 

When "Slightest Evidence" Is Sufficient

It is the settled law of Maryland that if there be the slightest evidence in any case, no matter how weak, derived from a legal source and pertinent to the issue, the jury alone are entitled to have it and to judge of it.18 

Mere "Conjecture" or "Scintilla of Evidence" Not Sufficient

But a party who carries the burden of proving an issue of fact, does not sustain it by the production of testimony that is lacking either in probative force or evidential value; and he cannot sustain it by evidence amounting to mere surmise, conjecture or possibility.¹ 19 Nor can the party bearing the burden of proof sustain his claim or defense, as the case may be, by a mere scintilla of evidence.20

TITLE 9 

The Court of Appeals of Maryland has said, again and again, that in matters of proof the Courts are not justified in inferring from mere possibilities the existence of facts.21 

Criterion by Which to Determine Legal Sufficiency of Evidence 

The criterion by which to determine whether the evidence is sufficient to be submitted to the jury is whether it is of such probative force as to enable an ordinarily intelligent mind to draw a rational conclusion therefrom in support of the proposition sought to be manifested by it.22 

Effect of Evidence Produced by Proponent of Demurrer Prayer 

In viewing the evidence on a demurrer prayer, the court must ordinarily disregard the evidence that was produced in behalf of the proponent of the prayer, except insofar as his evidence may help the case of his opponent.28 

Opponent's Evidence Must Be Accepted as True 

It is axiomatic that, in passing upon a prayer that seeks a directed verdict, which means a demurrer prayer, the evidence of the party whose case the prayer seeks to take from the jury must be accepted as true, and the court must also assume all legitimate inferences deductible therefrom and place thereon that construction which is most favorable to leaving the case to the determination of the jury.24

TITLE 9 When Demurrer Prayer Refers to Pleadings But Generally 

As is explained more fully in sections 82 and 85, relating to variance prayers, where a general demurrer prayer of a defendant does not refer to the pleadings, or where it refers to the pleadings in but general terms, the prayer cannot be granted, if there be evidence legally sufficient to entitle the plaintiff to recover in any form of action, whatsoever, without reference to or regard for the express or the implied allegations of the pleadings in the case.25

Mere Supporting Issue of Fact Arising From the Evidence 

Where a litigant proceeds to introduce evidence of an item of fact which tends to support a dominant issue of fact, and fails to produce evidence legally sufficient to sustain the supporting item of fact, his opponent is entitled to the grant of a demurrer prayer that informs the jury of the failure of the evidence regarding the supporting fact.34

Example of Failure of Evidence Regarding Mere Supporting Fact 

For example, where it was shown that the box which was attached to the hoisting engine, containing a load of stone, fell out of control and caused the plaintiff to be injured, and where it was further shown that a "tooth had been broken out of a ratchet on the drum on the hoisting engine," without showing, except speculatively, that this caused the fall of the said box, it was held that the trial court properly instructed the jury to the effect "that there was no evidence in the case legally sufficient to prove that the broken cog had caused the accident." 85

§ 100 

TITLE 9 Restricting Case to "Nominal" Damages 

Where there is a want of evidence legally sufficient to show that a plaintiff had sustained any actual or material damage or loss, and where the plaintiff is, nevertheless, entitled to recover nominal damages, as applies to an action for the breach of a contract,37 or to an action in trespass,38 and to other situations,89 the jury may be instructed, through the medium of demurrer prayers, to allow but nominal damages, if their verdict should be in favor of the plaintiff.40 

Excluding "Permanent" Injury 

Where there is a want of evidence legally sufficient to show that a plaintiff had sustained any permanent injury, the jury may be so instructed, through the medium of demurrer prayers; and also through the medium of special exceptions addressed to jury prayers which submitted, either expressly or inferentially, the question of permanent injury to the finding of the jury.41

Excluding "Punitive" Damages 

Where there is a want of evidence legally sufficient to show that a plaintiff is entitled to recover punitive damages, the jury may be so instructed, through the medium of demurrer prayers; and also through the medium of special exceptions addressed to jury prayers which submitted, either expressly or impliedly, the question of punitive damages to the finding of the jury.42

§ 185 

TITLE 9 Implied Partnership By Holding Out As Such 

One who holds himself out to the world as a partner, or permits others to do so, may be liable as such to one dealing with him or the firm, in the reasonable belief that he is a member of the partnership firm, if credit was, to some extent, induced by this belief, and if the holding out of the partnership was by the authority or with the knowledge of the person sought to be charged as a partner.48 

Where a contract or transaction, in the name of an individual partner, is shown to be connected with the business of the firm and within the apparent scope of its business, the transaction is binding on the firm and on all the partners who consented to, or acquiesced in, such use of the partner's individual name in the transactions of the firm.49

Whether one so held himself out as a partner, is ordinarily a question of fact and not of law.50

Liability of Partners For Torts of Each Other 

The liability of one copartner for the tortious acts of another is analogous to the liability of a principal for the acts of his agent, since each partner acts both as principal and as the agent of the other as to acts done within the apparent scope of the business and purpose of the partnership and for its benefit. The test of the liability of the partnership and of the several members thereof for the torts of any one partner is whether the wrongful act was done within what may be reasonably found to be the scope of the business of the partnership and for its benefit.51

§ 101 

TITLE 9 Liability of Partners For Each Other's Willful Torts 

So where one partner commits a willful and malicious tort not within the scope of the agency or the common business of the partnership, to which the other members have not consented and which has not been ratified, they are not liable for harm thereby caused.52 But if a wrongful act is done by one partner for the benefit of the firm, and the firm afterwards takes advantage of it and adopts the transaction, all the members of the firm may then become responsible.53 

Liability For Acts of Agents 

To hold an alleged principal liable for an act of his alleged agent or servant, it is necessary to show that the latter was the agent or servant of the former at the time of the act in question and that it was an act which came, expressly or impliedly, within the course or scope of the agent's or servant's authority or employment.54

Implied Authority From Agent's Position or Relationship 

The implied authority of an agent will often depend on the agent's position or relationship with or to the party who is sought to be charged with his acts of commission or omission, as the case may be.5 55 

Questions of Agency For Jury-Burden of Proof 

Where there is any evidence of agency, the weight of the evidence is for the jury. However, where the relation of the agency is dependent upon the acts of the parties, the law makes no presumption of agency, and then it is always a fact to be proved, with the burden of proof resting upon the person alleging the agency to show not only the fact of its existence, but also its nature and extent.56

§ 187 

TITLE 9 Presumption of Agency and Scope of Employment 

But the proof of the existence of the agency and that the agent was acting within the scope of his employment, may arise from some recognized rebuttable presumption of law or fact, as applies to one found to be driving the vehicle of another.57

Burden of Proof Regarding Termination of Agency 

When an agency has been shown to exist, the burden of proving the termination of the agency is upon the one relying on that fact.58

Agent's Secret Interest in Contract-Burden of Proof 

One who makes a contract with another through such other's known agent, and gives the agent a secret interest in the contract, cannot recover against the principal for breach of the contract, unless the latter, with full knowledge of the situation, ratifies the agreement. However, the burden of proving that the principal had full knowledge of the agent's antagonistic interest is upon the party enforcing the contract.59

Corporation Not Bound by Antagonistic Acts of Officers 

While the acts of a corporate officer, acting within the scope of his authority and on behalf of and in the interest of the corporation, are binding on the corporation, a corporation is not ordinarily bound by the concealed knowledge or acts of its officers which were not concealed or done in furtherance of the business of the corporation, nor intended for its benefit and advantage.60

TITLE 10 § 102. Burden of Proof and Presumptions as They Affect Demurrers to the Evidence or Directed Findings-Defense of Suicide. 

The law of presumptions and burden of proof, as is discussed in this section, is addressed entirely to its effect upon demurrers to the evidence, or, in other words to its effect upon directed findings. Moreover, this section should be read especially in conjunction with section 96, relating to directed verdicts in favor of plaintiffs and other parties who are ordinarily charged with the burden of proof, and also in conjunction with other sections, such as those which discuss the law of presumptions and burden of proof in relation to demurrers to the evidence or directed findings in specific types of cases.1 

Meaning of the Term "Burden of Proof" 

The term "burden of proof," sometimes distinguished from the "burden of evidence," means finally the obligation to go forward, or that he who asserts a fact either by way of complaint or defense assumes the burden of proving it. In other words, the term "burden of proof," especially when considered in relation to demurrers to the evidence or to prayers for directed findings, is generally employed to determine the side that was affirmatively bound to sustain, by legally sufficient proof, the case, claim, defense or issue of fact which the demurrer prayer under consideration requested the court, in effect, to take from the jury.2 

Does Burden of Proof "Shift"? 

When, if ever, does the burden of proof "shift"? Neither the courts nor textwriters appear to be in harmony in regard to their answers to this question. It does not, as a rule, 1 See secs. 39 to 48, and also the many case illustrations set out in footnotes 1 to 1Z of sec. 39, regarding the law of "burden of proof", especially as it relates to instructions to the juries upon this subject.

Burden of Proof Arising From Shift of Testimony 

A party may be required, by law, to bear the burden of proof in regard to a particular claim or defense, as the case may be, in mere consequence of a certain shift in the state of the testimony. This is explained by former Chief Judge 

James P. Gorter, who taught the law of evidence at the University of Maryland School of Law for many years, as follows 

(on page 61 of his 2nd edition of the Law of Evidence): 

Shift in Burden of Proof in Suit on Note "In a suit by an endorsee of a promissory note against the maker, the plaintiff first offers the note in evidence; the defendant offers proof that the note was obtained by the payee by fraud. This throws the burden upon the plaintiff of showing he was a bona fide holder for value without notice of the fraud; but when he has offered evidence to show this, viz; that he was a purchaser for value without notice, if there be no evidence to the contrary, the court will instruct the jury that there is no legal evidence from which they can find notice of knowledge of fraud, and that their verdict should be for the plaintiff."

Burden of Proof Regarding Affirmative Defenses 

It seems to be well settled that a defendant who sets up an affirmative defense, either in his pleadings or in his evidence, which amounts to something more than a mere denial of the plaintiff's evidence in support of his case, ordinarily carries the burden of proving the defense as a matter of law.6

Directed Findings in Regard to Affirmative Defenses

Sections 98 and 99 are devoted to a discussion of the circumstances under which an affirmative defense may be taken from the jury, in pursuance of a demurrer prayer, because there was offered no legally sufficient evidence in support of the defense. Generally speaking, a party who carries the burden of proof in regard to his affirmative defense, is not entitled to a directed finding, in his favor, in respect thereto; and this is ordinarily so even where the plaintiff had offered no evidence whatsoever in contradiction or denial of defendant's proof in support of the defense; for a Maryland court is not ordinarily empowered to deprive the jury of their inherent prerogative to refuse to believe even uncontradicted testimony.12

Directed Finding on Question of Suicide in Insurance Cases 

When may a Maryland court, in an action on an insurance policy, decide as a matter of law that the evidence showed conclusively that the insured had committed suicide? In this connection, it is important to bear in mind the vital distinction between a suit on an accident insurance policy which does not cover loss for self-inflicted injuries while sane or insane, and a suit on a life insurance policy which contains the proviso that the company will not be liable in case of suicide. 

Without regard to whether the suit was brought on a life insurance policy or an accident insurance policy, the presumption of law is that the death of the insured was due to accident or natural causes; but the burden of proof rules are not the same.14

In a suit on a life insurance policy which contains the proviso that the company will not be liable in case of suicide, the burden of proof is upon the defendant to show by a preponderance of evidence that the death of the insured was not accidental, since this proviso creates an exception to liability on the part of the insurance company, which is a matter of defense. In a suit on such a life insurance policy the beneficiary

In a suit on an accident insurance policy, which does not cover loss for self-inflicted injuries while sane or insane, the beneficiary, in order to recover on account of the death of the insured, must allege and show that the death was caused directly and exclusively by bodily injury sustained solely through accidental means.16 

In view of the fact that the insurance company carries the burden of proof in regard to the defense of suicide, if it be an action on a life insurance policy which embodies a proviso that relieves the company of liability in the case of suicide, and in view of the rebuttable presumption of law that holds that the death of the insured was due to accident or natural causes, no Maryland case has held, as a matter of law, that the defense of suicide, in the particular action then before the court, was conclusively established. However, the opinion in the leading Maryland case which referred to this unbroken chain of decisions, also indicates that, just as in the case of the defense of contributory negligence, a directed verdict would be warranted, as a matter of law, if the undisputed evidence as produced on behalf of the plaintiff established the suicide, "or where evidence from other sources amounted to demonstration." 17

In the leading Maryland case, and seemingly the only one to pass upon the defense of suicide in a suit on an accident insurance policy, of the kind afore-described, rather than on a life insurance policy, it was held-notwithstanding the evidentiary presumption of law to the effect that the death of the insured was due to accident or natural causes-that the "undisputed" proof in the case, regarding the circumstances under which the insured fell from the window of the hospital, did not entitle the plaintiff (beneficiary) to the grant of prayers which, in effect, instructed the jury that the burden of proof was upon the insurance company (defendant) to show that the said fatal fall of the insured was not accidental.

§ 103. Circumstantial Evidence and Negative Testimony as They 

Affect Demurrers to the Evidence.

It is well settled that a fact in issue may be established either by direct or circumstantial evidence, or both.19 

In the Maryland courts it has been said, again and again, that in mere civil disputes, where no violation of the law is in question, and no legal presumption operates in favor of either party, the preponderance of probability, due regard being had to the burden of proof, may constitute sufficient ground for a verdict.20

While there is strong authority for the proposition that a well connected train of circumstances is as cogent of the existence of fact as any array of direct evidence, and frequently outweighs opposing testimony, it seems to be thoroughly settled that, to constitute a basis for a claim or defense, the circumstances must amount to more than a mere surmise of the claim or defense, as the case may be.21

Circumstantial Evidence of Both Fatal Collision and Negligence 

It was held that the jury could rationally infer that the fatally injured pedestrian was struck by the defendant's automobile, and also that the defendant was negligent, from a chain of minute circumstances such as that three hairs of the color of the pedestrian's hair were found upon the broken glass of the windshield of the defendant's automobile and that broken glass was found near the point where the pedestrian was found lying, supplemented by the defendant's admission that the windshield of his automobile was broken by a crash which occurred near the same point, immediately after the defendant had passed another automobile, the lights of which obscured his view; although no one testified that the defendant had participated in this fatal accident, and the defendant emphatically denied any knowledge thereof.23

Negative Testimony as Proof—Not Hearing Horn or Bell 

Whether negative testimony, such as the statement of a witness that he did not hear the ringing of the bell of the engine, or that he did not hear the blowing of the horn of the automobile, will be accepted as proof that the bell was not sounded or that the horn was not blown at the time of the accident in question, will depend, in a large measure, upon the position that the witness was then occupying and upon the surrounding circumstances in general, as concerned the hearing facilities of the witness.25

Judicial Knowledge 

While it is the general rule, as is explained more fully in sections 82 and 85, that unless the court's attention is, in due form, directed to the pleadings of the case, the prayers thereof will be construed entirely in relation to the evidence, without reference to or regard for the state of the pleadings, yet, since a trial court is bound to take into consideration every fact of which it is allowed to take judicial notice or knowledge, it seems that the court could not, in passing upon a demurrer prayer, ignore a fact that was admitted in consequence of the provisions of a statute such as the afore-quoted, merely because the court's attention was not especially directed to the statute and to the pleadings of the case on trial.28

§ 105. Admissions by Parties and Their Agents as Substantive Proof-Evidence From Contradiction of Witness Not Substantive Proof -Admissions During Compromise Negotiations. 

Admissions of Parties 

Where the evidence in a case shows that a party thereto had admitted the existence of a fact in issue, he is not entitled to the grant of a demurrer prayer which expressly or impliedly asks the court to rule that there is a want of evidence legally sufficient to prove or sustain that fact.29 

Admissions of Agents-Res Gestae 

And this applies with equal force to a fact that was admitted merely by an agent of the proponent of such a demurrer prayer, provided, of course, that the agent, at the time of the making of the admission under consideration, was acting within the course or scope of his authority or employment, in contemplation of law.30 

Whether an admission of fact by an agent, or servant, or an attorney, will or will not bind his principal, employer or

§ 105 

TITLE 10 

When however, an admission of fact by an agent becomes admissible for such a purpose only, and not because it could be and was construed as a part of the res gestae, the admission of fact cannot be considered by the court in ruling upon the legal sufficiency of the evidence, in pursuance of a demurrer prayer. In other words, an admission of an agent that rightfully came into evidence merely for the purpose of contradicting or impeaching the credibility of the testimony of the agent upon the point of the admission, cannot be regarded as affirmative or substantive proof of the fact that was alleged to have been admitted by the agent.34 

But an admission of an agent in a position of authority may sometimes be regarded as affirmative or substantive proof even where the admission came into evidence only through testimony given in contradiction of the agent's evidence upon the subject of the admission.35

Admissions During Compromise Negotiations 

While an offer of compromise is not admissible as an admission that a debt is due and owing, admissions of particular facts may be received as evidence of such facts, even though the admissions accompany an offer of compromise, except where they are inseparably connected therewith, or are made as a concession to induce a compromise, or are stated to be made without prejudice.36

Admission From Failure to Deny Accusation 

The rule that holds, in effect, that one's failure to deny a definite statement, made in his presence and understood by him as charging him with fault or wrongful conduct, may be construed as an admission of the truth of the statementcannot ordinarily be extended to include the mere opinion of a third person as to the weight and significance of facts previously admitted by the declarant.37

§ 203 

TITLE 10 Need of Repeating Exact Words of Admission 

Neither an admission nor a confession has to be repeated verbatim; for the substance or effect of the actual words spoken by the person sought to be charged therewith will ordinarily suffice in both civil and criminal cases.38 

When is Admission Broad Enough to Take Case to Jury? 

In any event, before an admission can take an issue of fact to the jury, the admission under consideration must furnish some legally sufficient proof of the issue of fact under consideration.39 

For example, in a negligence suit against a dentist, by a former patient, it was held that alleged admissions of the dentist to the effect that he should have taken an X-ray before filling plaintiff's tooth, and that he should not have filled it, did not furnish legally sufficient evidence of the want of reasonable care in filling the tooth, or that there existed conditions from which the injury complained of might have been anticipated; since an admission, to be sufficient in such a case, must be an admission of negligence or of lack of the skill ordinarily required for the performance of the work undertaken.40 

On the other hand, it was held that a letter from the defendant's attorney to the plaintiff-written within three years before the latter filed his suit for surgical serviceswhich referred to the defendant's previous offer of $300 in full settlement, and which stated that the defendant was still willing to pay that amount, and that he was informed that the offer was a liberal one "for the services rendered," contained an admission which was sufficient, in contemplation of law, to warrant the rejection of the defendant's demurrer prayer that sought a directed verdict in his favor upon the ground that there was no evidence in the case legally sufficient to remove the bar of the statute of limitations.41

§§ 105-107 TITLE 10 Effect of Admissions in a Pevious Trial 

In passing upon a demurrer to the evidence, the Court of Appeals very recently ruled that statements made in a previous trial, while testifying, are admissible at a subsequent trial only for the purpose of impeaching the witness who made them, and not as substantive evidence.42 

§ 106. Inadmissible Testimony as It Affects Demurrers to the Evidence When Hearsay Testimony is Admissible. 

As is further explained in sections 31 and 64, when a court is asked to rule upon the legal sufficiency of the evidence, in passing on a demurrer prayer, it must consider objectionable evidence that was admitted without objection to the same extent as proper evidence. In other words, objectionable evidence admitted without objection has the force and effect of proper evidence.43

It is also settled that evidence introduced without limitation of purpose is in for all purposes.44 

When Hearsay Testimony is Admissible

In this connection, it should be observed that in certain classes of cases, such as workmen's compensation cases, hearsay evidence is sometimes admissible as of right.45 § 107. "Incredible" Testimony-“Uncontradicted” and “Self-Contradictory" Testimony-Looking Without Seeing-Their Effect Upon 

Demurrers to the Evidence.

§ 205 

TITLE 10 Incredible, Vague and Self-Contradictory Testimony 

The "invariable" Maryland rule which declares, for the purpose of a defendant's demurrer prayer, that the court musı assume as true all of the plaintiff's testimony, and its reasonable inferences, insofar as they tend to support the plaintiff's right of action, cannot be extended to require the acceptance as true of the testimony of a witness when that testimony is so vague, indefinite and self-contradictory as to be plainly of no probative value.47

On the other hand, it has been said, again and again, that where the plaintiff's testimony as given in the case involved in the appeal entitles him to a verdict, his right to have the jury decide as to its credibility is not affected by the circumstance that he had previously made statements inconsistent therewith. In other words, it is ordinarily the function of the jury to determine whether the revision by a witness of his previous statements and his explanation therefor in the case at bar were credible.48

§ 109. Jury's Inspection of Premises-Its Effect Upon Demurrers to the Evidence.

That the jury viewed the locus in quo will not of itself prevent the court from taking the case from the jury in pursuance of a demurrer prayer. If the premises, as existent at the time of its inspection by the jury, disclose a condition that is relevant to an issue of fact of the case on trial, evidence of this condition should be presented in open court.68

But it was held, while ruling upon a demurrer to the evidence in a negligence case, that the court could take into consideration the fact that the jury had viewed the premises, and could thereby get a better understanding of the conditions, if evidence as to them had been offered before the court and jury, but could not be as clearly presented by photographs and oral testimony as by the aid of a view of the premises themselves.69 

In Eminent Domain proceedings, it was said that the jury goes upon the land for the purpose of ascertaining its value, and their view should have more effect than in ordinary cases where they are generally and primarily permitted to go to the locus in quo so as to better understand and apply the evidence.70

§ 110 

TITLE 10 Proof of Fraud in Obtaining a Written Instrument 

And it has been held that it is error to submit a question of fraud to the jury upon slight parol evidence to overturn a written instrument;72 and also that evidence of fraud, to warrant a court in submitting a case to the jury as to the invalidity of an instrument under seal, must be clear, direct, and satisfactory.73

Proof of Crime in Civil Cases-Presumption of Innocence 

There is a well-recognized distinction in regard to the degree or quantity of proof in the trial of civil and criminal cases. In criminal trials the presumption of innocence is so strong that the law in favor of life and liberty requires the fact of criminality to be established, to the exclusion of every other reasonable hypothesis, or, in other words, to a moral certainty.74 

But in civil disputes where no violation of law is in question, and no legal presumption operates in favor of either party, the preponderance of probability, due regard being had to the burden of proof, may constitute sufficient ground for a verdict.75

When Mere Preponderance of Evidence is Not Sufficient 

When fraud or criminal conduct is charged or imputed in a civil case, something more than a mere preponderance of evidence must be produced; and the proof in support of such a charge must be clear and satisfactory; though, as is explained in section 103, the supporting proof may consist of circumstantial evidence.76

TITLE 11 

Requisites and Scope of a "General" Demurrer Prayer Due to Act of 1825-Need of "Specific" Demurrer Prayers. 

The first clause of section 10 of article 5 of the Code (known as the Act of 1825) prescribes :¹ "In no case shall the Court of Appeals decide any point or question which does not plainly appear by the record to have been tried and decided by the court below * * " General Demurrer Prayers which are Too General General prayers, such as one which asks the court to rule that "under pleadings and evidence in the case the verdict of the jury must be for the defendant," 2 or one which asks the court to rule "that no evidence had been offered in the case to show a confederation," 3 do not satisfy the requirements of the said Act of 1825. Moreover, such general prayers are deemed to be too indefinite and general to submit a legal proposition to the ruling of the court. This is explained in section 57 and illustrated in section 58. 

"Precise" Question Raised by Good General Demurrer Prayer 

Until 1902, when the opinion in the leading case of Parr v. 

City Trust Co. (95 Md. 291, 297-299) was filed, the form of a general demurrer prayer, in view of the requirements of the said Act of 1825, was not clearly and finally approved. Since then, however, it is well-settled that a prayer, reading such as the following, is a good general demurrer prayer, and that

Approved Form of a General Demurrer Prayer 

"The defendant prays the court to instruct the jury that there has been offered no evidence in this case legally sufficient to entitle the plaintiff to recover, and, therefore, the verdict of the jury must be in favor of the defendant.” 

Not All Legal Questions or Defects in Proof are Reached by a 

General Demurrer Prayer 

But the ultimate scope or range of a general demurrer prayer, in view of the requirements of the said Act of 1825, has yet to be defined by the Court of Appeals. In other words, the appellate court has not yet defined all the legal grounds or defenses that it will take cognizance of when passing upon the action of the lower court in refusing or granting, as the case may be, a general demurrer prayer. 

Defense of Statute of Frauds Not Reached by General Demurrer Prayer 

For example, in view of the Act of 1825 (being the first clause of section 10 of article 5 of the Code), and in view of the fact that, independent of the prayer, the question did not appear to have been raised below, the appellate court recently ruled that a good general demurrer prayer, which challenged the evidence as being legally insufficient to entitle the plaintiff to recover, did not itself have the effect of raising the defense that the contract of sale in suit was unenforceable under the Statute of Frauds, due to the failure of the contract to state the price."

But, in arriving at the said conclusion, the appellate court pointed out that contracts that fail to meet the requirements of the Statute of Frauds are not void, but only voidable at the option of the parties sought to be charged by them.7ª 

Broad Scope or Range of a General Demurrer Prayer 

It appears, however, that a good general demurrer prayer is inherently possessed of sufficient scope or range to raise, in effect, the question of the legal sufficiency of the evidence to sustain each and every element of fact which the plaintiff was bound to sustain by affirmative evidence as a condition precedent to his right of recovery.8

Need of Specific Demurrer Prayers 

But because the scope or range of a general demurrer prayer has yet to be definitely defined, it seems advisable, and at times also necessary, to employ specific demurrer prayers. 

Either of the parties to a case is at liberty to seek a directed verdict in his favor through the medium of a general demurrer prayer or a specific demurrer prayer, or both."

So it has been repeatedly held that a demurrer prayer of a defendant which was offered after he had produced testimony in defense, is defective if it asked the court to instruct the jury that the plaintiff had offered no evidence legally sufficient to entitle him to recover. A prayer, offered at the close of the evidence on both sides, and which instructed the jury-"that upon plaintiff's own evidence, her own want of ordinary care and caution directly contributing to the injuries which she received, and, therefore, the verdict of the jury must be for the defendant❞—was held not to be open to the objection that it segregates the testimony of the plaintiff herself and ignores that of other witnesses; and, furthermore, the prayer was construed as having been addressed to all of the evidence produced on the part of the plaintiff.12

A demurrer prayer must submit its propositions of law to the ruling of the trial court, and so it is defective if it assumes them.13

A prayer which declared that "under the pleadings in this case, the plaintiff has offered no evidence herein legally sufficient to remove the bar of the Statute of Limitations," and that the verdict must, therefore, be for the defendants, was adjudged to be erroneous for having assumed that the cause of action was barred by the statute and requires some evidence to remove the bar.14

A prayer which asked for a directed verdict in favor of the defendant upon the ground that the evidence did not show that "the negligence of the defendant's chauffeur was the proximate cause of the accident," was adjudged to be defective for having assumed negligence on the part of the chauffeur and asking the court to say as a matter of law that such negligence was not the proximate cause of the accident.15 

§ 114. Effect of Demurrer Prayer That Refers to the Pleadings in but Mere General Terms.

Since the passage of the Variance Prayer Act of 1914 (Code, article 5, section 11), a general demurrer prayer which refers to the pleadings in but mere general terms, cannot be accepted as a variance prayer. It is accepted, however, as a general demurrer prayer.16 

§ 115. Approved Forms of Defendant's and Plaintiff's Contributory Negligence Demurrer Prayers. 

Neither a general demurrer prayer which challenges the evidence as being legally insufficient to entitle the plaintiff to recover, nor a specific demurrer prayer which challenges the evidence as being legally insufficient to show negligence on the part of the defendant, has the effect of raising the question of contributory negligence.17

TITLE 11 § 117. Approved Forms of "General" and "Specific" Demurrer 

Prayers to Direct Finding in Favor of "Defendant" as to a "Part" of the Case. 

Need to Take Directed Verdict as to Count Where a granted demurrer prayer of a defendant was addressed to a count of the plaintiff's declaration and asked for a directed verdict in regard thereto, it was held that it was not necessary to actually take the verdict of the jury in regard to that count, and that the prayer would have been adequate if it had not concluded with such a request, since the jury is presumed to have heeded the instruction of the court, and to have found for the defendant in regard to the count mentioned in the said prayer.21

§ 122. Approved Forms of Demurrer Prayers of Joint Defendants. 

When Demurrer Prayer of Joint Defendant is Defective 

A demurrer prayer of a joint defendant that challenges the evidence as being legally insufficient to entitle the plaintiff to recover is erroneous, if there is any evidence in the case legally sufficient to entitle the plaintiff to recover against either of the defendants.27

TITLE 11 

§ 125.

Right of Plaintiff to Take "Non Pros" After the Grant of 

Defendant's Demurrer Prayer-Effect upon Plea of Set-Off. 

Because of the provisions of section 183 of article 75 of the Code, as re-enacted by Acts of 1920, which prescribes, among other things, that a plaintiff may submit to a voluntary judg ment of non pros up to the time when argument upon the facts has begun, a plaintiff may take a non pros following the grant of the defendant's demurrer prayer, for a directed verdict in his favor, and before the actual rendition of the verdict by the jury in obedience to the mandate of such a prayer.31

But a plaintiff's right of non pros cannot interfere with the defendant's right of recovery upon his plea of set-off. However, this rule of statutory law is not applicable to a judgment of non pros entered on defendant's motion and contrary to plaintiff's wishes, as when based on plaintiff's failure to comply with the rule security for costs.32

In a trial where the court also sat as the jury, it was held that the plaintiff could not take a non pros after the argument on both the law and facts.33 

§ 126.  Regarding Demurrer Prayers. 

Generally speaking, it seems that a case will not be reversed because of an erroneous ruling upon a demurrer prayer by the trial court, if the verdict as rendered does not appear to be unjust to the appellant.34

So it has been repeatedly held that a case will not be returned to the lower court for re-trial merely because it was taken from the jury in pursuance of a defective demurrer prayer or upon an erroneous legal ground, if it appears that

For example, where it appeared that the case should not have been taken from the jury in pursuance of a demurrer prayer that alleged a want of evidence legally sufficient to show the existence of primary negligence, but could have been properly taken from the jury on the ground of contributory negligence, if a demurrer prayer upon that ground had been presented in the lower court, the appellate court refused to reverse the judgment and grant a new trial.85

§ 127 

TITLE 12 § 127. Time for Offering, Giving, Recalling or Adding to the Prayers or Instructions of a Case-Rules of Court Regarding Same. 

Rule No. 31 of the Rules of the Supreme Bench of Balti more City prescribes (our paragraphing):1 "After all the evidence intended to be offered by plaintiff and defendant shall have been introduced the court will expect to be furnished with all the prayers which the parties respectively propose to found thereon. "The plaintiff, if he shall have submitted any material proposition not admitted by the defendant shall be entitled to open and conclude on the prayers. "The court upon the whole case will give such instructions as may appear requisite to place the case fully before the jury. "Copies of such prayers as have been prepared out of court must be furnished each side by the other immediately after the evidence on both sides is in, and counsel will be expected to prepare their prayers out of court whenever it is possible to do so." 

By virtue of the Act of 1894 (Code, article 75, section 96), a defendant is entitled to present demurrer prayers at the close of the plaintiff's case and, again, at the close of all the testimony, if he produced testimony following the refusal of his demurrer prayer at the close of the plaintiff's case.2 

May Change Instructions Up to Rendition of Verdict 

At any time up to the actual rendition of the verdict, the trial court is empowered, in its sole discretion, to recall, alter or add to its instructions to the jury, to the end that the jury may be properly instructed regarding the law of the case.3

But out of regard for the orderly administration of justice and for the rules of court enacted in furtherance thereof, the trial courts are reluctant to disturb and rarely do disturb the

Duty to Correct Given Instructions or Remarks of Counsel 

When, however, the attention of the trial court is called, at any stage of the trial, to any alleged ambiguity, or claim that instructions already granted are susceptible of different interpretations, it at once becomes the duty of the court to remove the ambiguity and to make the meaning of the instruction plain.5 And it seems that this duty of the court also arises when its attention has been directed to a misstatement of the law of the case by counsel in argument to the jury.

Instructing Jury in Presence of Counsel 

In order to give counsel the opportunity to except to the action of the court in giving additional instructions to the jury, and also to file special exceptions thereto where that seems necessary, the courts should aim to give the additional instructions only in the presence of opposing counsel." 

As is further explained in section 167, the instructions in criminal trials involving felony or treason must not be given to the jury out of the presence of the accused.8

§§ 127-128 TITLE 12 Need of Preparing Prayers "Out of Court" 

Since a slight change in the testimony on either side, from that anticipated by counsel, might readily render a previously prepared prayer fatally defective, it would seem that the provision of the afore-quoted Rule of Court regarding the preparation of the "prayers out of court whenever it is possible" should be cautiously enforced.10 In this connection, the legal profession might well bear in mind the policy of the Maryland courts as was expressed in the comparatively recent case of Winslow v. Atz (168 Md. 246): 

In that case the Court of Appeals of Maryland declared (our paragraphing):

Court Must Take Time to Consider the Prayers 

"It is suggested on behalf of the appellee that the prayers offered by the defendant were 'so unreasonably long, involved and numerous for a case of this kind that it was really not incumbent on attorney for the plaintiff and the trial court to stop the proceedings indefinitely to study them in detail * * *' "The primary reason for courts is the administration of justice, but that end can not well be served if the theories and contentions of the parties made in good faith are to be ignored because it is not convenient to take time for their consideration." 

§ 128. Duty of Court to Reject Bad Prayers and to Grant Good Prayers-Right to Modify Prayers-Need of Special Exceptions. 

It may be said, as a rule, that it is the duty of the trial court to reject every prayer that is not sanctioned by the rules of law, whether the defect in the prayer be one of form or of substance,11 or that is unnecessary.12 And this duty extends to any prayer that cannot be granted in its entirety.18

Duty to Reject Bad Prayer in Absence of Objection Thereto The duty that rests upon the trial court to reject every defective prayer, unless it be a conceded prayer,14 exists without regard to whether or not the defective prayer was made the subject of a general or special exception at the trial of the case. But while the appellate court-as is told more fully in other sections-will review a rejected prayer for any defect whatsoever even where the prayer was not subjected to a special exception in the court below, it is estopped by statute, in the absence of such a special exception, from reviewing certain classes of defects in prayers which were actually granted.15

Court May but Need Not Modify Prayer 

A Maryland trial court is not bound to modify, amend or in any manner fashion the prayers submitted to it by counsel so as to bring them within the rules of law.16 The court is, however, fully empowered to do so.17 In other words, while a 

Maryland trial judge is fully empowered to modify or amend any prayer that does not conform to the rules of law, the judge may, if he sees fit to do so, content himself with a simple refusal thereof.18

For example, where the trial court had rejected a prayer defining malice because it was incorrect, it was held that it was not bound, ex mero motu, to give any definition of it.19 

Where a party refused to consent to a proper modification of his prayer as suggested by the trial court, it was held that the trial court did not err in refusing the prayer instead of
