§ 129. Effect of Granting Prayers "In Connection With" Each 

Other.

While the practice of granting a prayer of one side expressly "in connection with" a prayer of the other side is well established in the Maryland courts, it is a practice that properly applies to but limited situations.22 A prayer should not be so restrictively granted, but should be granted unconditionally, when it contains within itself a sound and complete instruction to the jury, which had not omitted or ignored any claim or defense of the opposite party that could have the effect of nullifying or qualifying the instruction to the jury as was given by the prayer.23

When Prayers Should and Should Not be Granted Connectedly 

For example, where a prayer tells the jury that their verdict must be in favor of its proponent, if they should believe the elements or hypotheses of fact enumerated in the prayer, 20 Conservation Co. v. Stimpson, 136 Md. 314, 329.

In a case where the plaintiff brought suit for the breach of a contract of sale, and where the defendant set up the defense of a verbal agreement of cancellation of the contract, it was held that the trial court had properly granted a prayer of the plaintiff, which had ignored the said defense, expressly in connection with prayers of the defendant which submitted the facts regarding this defense to the finding of the jury; but it was also held that the court, in granting these prayers of the defendant, should not have noted upon them that they were granted in connection with the said prayer of the plaintiff; since the facts stated in the prayers of the defendant, if true, constituted a complete bar to recovery by the plaintiff.26 

Effect of Granting Prayers Connectedly 

And, in the aforesaid case, the appellate court further declared that the effect of granting the said prayer of the plaintiff expressly in connection with the said prayers of the defendant was to call the jury's attention to the evidence relied on by the defendant, and to instruct them that notwithstanding they found the facts set out in the plaintiff's prayer, if they also found the facts stated in the defendant's prayers, their verdict should be for the defendant.27

When Prayers of Same Side Should be Granted Connectedly

The practice of granting one prayer expressly in connection with another is also applicable to prayers of the same side.28 For example-where the first prayer of the plaintiff was defective because it submitted his claim of waiver, of a certain provision of the contract in suit, to the finding of the jury without informing the jury as to what acts or facts in evidence would constitute the waiver, and where the second prayer of the plaintiff did tell this to the jury—it was held that the trial court had erred in rejecting the first prayer, since it could and should have been granted in connection with the said second prayer of the plaintiff.29

When Connecting Prayer Tends to Confuse 

A prayer should not be granted in connection with another that tends to confuse or contradict it, rather than to supplement it.30

How to Grant Prayers Connectedly 

When it is intended to qualify or limit one prayer by another, the correct practice is to refer to the other in such terms as the jury will see that it is so intended, for otherwise they may be misled or may overlook the effect of the qualifying one.3 31 

When a Prayer Refers to Another Prayer 

Where a prayer in itself makes a general reference to another prayer, it may have the same effect as though it were expressly granted in connection with such other prayer.32

§ 130. Modification of Prayer Should be Clear, Consistent, and Correct in Relation to Its Own Factual Hypothesis or Theory. 

Early in Maryland judicial history it was declared that where the court undertakes of its own motion to add a qualification to a prayer, the qualification must be consistent with the original prayer, and not leave it doubtful or difficult to determine what was the scope or design of the entire instruction. This salutary principle has never been relaxed.34 

Modification Should Be Consistent With Proposition Submitted by 

Prayer The modification should not be inconsistent with the proposition asked for by the prayer, and the intent of the prayer, as modified and granted, should be readily comprehensible to a jury composed of laymen.35

Modified Law Must Fit Facts of Prayer 

Moreover, the law as embodied in the modification of a prayer, must be correct in relation to the factual hypothesis or theory as was submitted by the prayer itself. For example, where the doctrine of the last clear chance was applicable, as a matter of law, if the fatally injured pedestrian was

§ 131. Implied Modification of Granted Prayer-Effect of Re marks of Court or Unrestrained Argument of Counsel. 

The modification of a granted prayer may sometimes arise impliedly, as, for example, where the trial judge undertakes to express, in the presence of the jury, his opinion regarding the meaning or effect of a granted prayer of the case.37 

As is indicated in section 129, the mere act of the trial court in granting one prayer in connection with another prayer may have the effect of modifying or qualifying either or both of the prayers.

And it seems that a modification of a granted prayer of the case might arise from the refusal of the court to restrain counsel from arguing to the jury in opposition to a proposition thereof.38 

§ 132. How to Except to the Modification of a Prayer-How Same 

Must be Shown on Appeal-Harmless Modifications.

Record Must Show Original and Modified Prayer 

The appellate court will not review the action of the lower court in modifying prayers, if the record does not show how

Need of Two Exceptions When Prayer is Modified 

Morever, the appellate court may not review the action of the trial court in modifying a prayer of the appellant, unless the bill of exceptions shows that the appellant had noted, at the trial, an exception to the refusal of the prayer as offered and, also, to the court's modification thereof.40 

When Modification Affects Form Only 

The modification of a prayer by the trial court presents no reversible error when the modification is a change in form only and does not modify any statement of the law.41 

Harmless Modification of Prayers 

Where the trial court would have been justified in rejecting a prayer altogether by reason of erroneous matter therein, it was held that its modification of the prayer to the extent of eliminating the objectionable part was not ground for reversal.42 Nor will a litigant be heard to complain that a prayer submitted by him which was inherently bad was so modified as to render it somewhat less objectionable.43 

And, as is explained more fully in section 134, an appellant will not be heard to complain of an erroneous modification of a prayer by the trial court, if the same error was embodied in a prayer as submitted by the appellant. 

§ 133. Conceded Prayers-What Constitutes Same Their Effect Upon Demurrer Prayers, Etc. 

A conceded prayer is one which the trial court granted with the assent, express or implied, of the opposing party.44

§ 133 

TITLE 12 Effect of Failure to Except to Modification of One's Own Prayer 

It seems that a conceded prayer may sometimes arise from the mere failure of the proponent of prayer to except to its modification by the court. For example, where a prayer of a defendant in a malicious prosecution suit told the jury that their verdict must be in his favor, if they found that he did not swear out the warrant of arrest, and the court modified this prayer-without any objection or exception-by submitting to the jury the additional question whether the defendant had otherwise participated in the prosecution of the plaintiff, it was held, therefore, that the defendant was not entitled to the grant of another prayer which told the jury that the burden of proof was upon the plaintiff to show that the defendant swore out the warrant of arrest, and that if they found that this burden was not met, then their verdict must be for the defendant.45

Effect of Failure to Except to Grant of Opponent's Prayers 

The mere failure to note an exception to the grant of a prayer of the opposite party will not ordinarily elevate the prayer to the legal status of a conceded prayer. For example, where the trial court had announced that it would reject the demurrer prayers of the defendants, which sought a directed verdict in their favor, and where the defendants' counsel answered "no" to a question by the court whether he had any objection to plaintiff's prayers submitting the case to the jury, it was held that this occurrence did not elevate the plaintiff's prayers to the legal status of conceded prayers, so as to prevent the defendants from relying upon their exception to the refusal of their said demurrer prayers.46

Waiving Own Demurrer Prayer by Conceding Opponent's Jury Prayer 

But where the defendant, in a negligence case, conceded a prayer of the plaintiff which submitted to the finding of the jury the questions of the defendant's primary negligence and of the plaintiff's contributory negligence-it was held that the demurrer prayers of the defendant, to the effect that there is no legally sufficient evidence of negligence on its part, and to the effect that the plaintiff was guilty of contributory negligence as a matter of law, were properly refused, since it is

Since 1859 Conceded Prayer Becomes Binding Law of Case 

It has been held in the Maryland courts, by an unbroken chain of decisions since 1859, that a conceded prayer becomes the law of the case even when it embodies wrong propositions of law or fact, and that a conceded prayer is binding alike upon the parties and the court.48

Prayer Inconsistent with Conceded Prayer Not Grantable 

Consequently, any prayer offered in the case which is shown to be inconsistent with such a conceded prayer cannot be granted.49

Conceded Prayers On Retrial of Case 

On the second trial of the case the parties are not ordinarily bound by instructions to the jury conceded at the first trial.52 

§ 134. Side Responsible for Errors in Prayers-When Appellant's 

Prayers have Reproduced Mistakes of Appellee's Prayers-Estoppel. 

It has been said, again and again, upon the plainest principles of justice, that the appellant will not be heard to complain that the trial court, in granting or modifying a prayer of the case, adopted or repeated a proposition of law or fact which was advanced by him in his own prayers. In other words, a party will ordinarily be estopped from complaining, in effect, that the trial court had accepted as sound a proposition of his own production.53

Accordingly, the appellate court held, in effect, as follows: (a) That the grant of claimant's prayer, permitting the jury to decide whether an order of the commission was correct, was not the subject of complaint by the employer and insurer, since they submitted for the jury an issue, which was granted by the court, involving this identical question.54 (b) That where the court would have been justified in rejecting a prayer altogether because of erroneous matter therein, a modification of the prayer that eliminated the objectionable part was not ground for reversal.55 (c) That a party cannot complain that a prayer submitted by him, which was inherently bad, was so modified as to render it somewhat less objectionable.56

52 Sittig v. Birkenstack, 38 Md. 158. 

53 See footnotes 55 to 60 of this sec.; Clark v. Banks, 158 Md. 24, 32; United Rys. Co. v. Carneal, 110 Md. 211, 232-233.

§ 257 

TITLE 13 § 135. 

Jurisdiction of Court of Appeals in Law Cases-Need of General Exceptions at Least. 

No matter how patently and grossly wrong a verdict, judgment or sentence of a court of law may appear to be, the Court of Appeals of Maryland is absolutely enjoined-by several legislative enactments and by a long line of judicial pronouncement of its own making—from reviewing, setting aside or correcting the verdict, judgment or sentence, if the record on appeal does not disclose, at least, a ruling by the court below on some question of law;¹ unless there appeared to be a want of inherent jurisdiction in the court below to hear the case, or to enter the verdict or judgment under con sideration.2 Need of Exceptions 

Moreover, as may be observed from the following illustrations, some rulings of the court below cannot be reviewed by the Court of Appeals, if the appellant did not, in the court below, note a general exception, at least, to the ruling.3

§ 135 

TITLE 13 

“General” and Sometimes "Special" Exceptions Necessary to

Rulings on Prayers 

(a) A general exception is necessary to a ruling by the trial court upon a prayer or instruction of the case. It should also be observed, as is explained in sections 62 to 66 and in sections 136, 137 and 139, that certain objections to a granted prayer cannot be reviewed by the Court of Appeals in the absence of a special exception thereto and general exceptions to both the granting of the prayer and the refusal of the special exception.4 

General Exception Necessary to Ruling on Evidence 

(b) A general exception is necessary to a ruling by the trial court upon the admissibility of evidence.5 

General Exception Necessary to Ruling On Motion to Declare Mistrial 

(c) A general exception is necessary to a ruling by the trial court upon a motion to declare a mistrial, based upon the misconduct, or what amounts thereto in technical contemplation of law, of a witness, or of the judge, or of the jury, or of counsel, or of anyone else.

No Exception Necessary to Ruling On Pleadings 

(d) No exception is necessary to a ruling by the court below upon a demurrer to the pleadings." 

No Exception Necessary to Ruling On Workmen's Compensation Issues 

(e) No exception is necessary to a ruling by the court below upon the propriety of the issues in the trial of an appeal from the State Industrial Accident Commission.8

§ 136 

TITLE 13 Special Exception Never Necessary to a "Rejected" Prayer 

In the case of a rejected prayer, the appellate court will review it for every material defect, whether it relates to the form or the substance of the prayer, if the record on appeal merely shows that a general exception was interposed, at the trial of the case, against the action of the court in refusing the prayer.15

Special Exception Necessary to a “Granted” Prayer in Few Instances 

In the case of a granted prayer, the appellate court will seemingly review it for every material defect, whether it relates to the form or the substance of the prayer, if the record on appeal merely shows that a general exception was interposed, at the trial of the case, against the action of the court in granting the prayer;16 excepting, however, the three certain defects in granted prayers which are recognized in section 10 of article 5 of the Code, and which are described in sections 62 to 66 and in section 137 of this book. These three defects, when they appear in prayers, must first be pointed out, at the trial of the case, by way of a "special exception," otherwise they will not be reviewed on appeal in the case of a granted prayer.17

Exceptions of Appellee in Absence of Cross-Appeal On an appeal by plaintiff from a judgment for part of his claim, the refusal of a demurrer prayer asking for a directed verdict for defendant, offered at the close of all the testimony, will not be passed upon by the appellate court in the absence of any cross-appeal by defendant, and this is especially so where it appears that the defendant acquiesced in the judg ment.18

Origin of Term "Special Exception" 

The term "special exception," as used in the Maryland cases, seems to have arisen from the provision of this statute (Code, art. 5, sec. 10) which calls for a specific "objection" against a granted prayer that embodies either of the three defects which are described in the statute.21

When a Prayer Submitted a Question of Law

When a Prayer Submitted an Insufficiently Proven Fact 

See sections 64 and 71 for an understanding of when a prayer has submitted a fact to the finding of the jury that is without legally sufficient support in the evidence, as is indicated in the fourth and final clause of the said statute.

TITLE 13 § 138. Special Exception Not Necessary to a Jury Prayer Which 

Omitted a Fact-Nor to a Demurrer Prayer Which Assumed a Fact.

Prayer Which Omitted a Fact 

The case of Buckey v. White (137 Md. 124, 131) which seemed to rule that, in the absence of a special exception, the Court of Appeals could not review a granted prayer which had omitted a fact necessary and material to support the instruction sought by it—was expressly overruled by the case of Louis v. Johnson (146 Md. 115, 119-121).

Demurrer Prayer Which Assumed a Fact 

A special exception is seemingly never necessary in regard to a granted demurrer prayer which assumed a fact in dispute, as demurrer prayers often erroneously do.22 

As may be further observed from sections 62, 63, 80 and 136, a special exception is never necessary in regard to a rejected prayer which erroneously assumed a fact in dispute. 

§ 139. Seems Necessary to Note a General Exception to Refusal of Special Exception and Also to the Grant of the Prayer Itself. 

Where a special exception to a prayer is overruled, and where the prayer itself is granted, it seems necessary to note a general exception to the overruling of the special exception and, again, to the grant of the prayer itself; otherwise the appellate court may not review the granted prayer for any of the three defects or errors mentioned in section 10 of article 5 of the Code.23

When, however, a special exception is sustained, and the prayer to which it was addressed is, accordingly, rejected, the appellate court will review the rejected prayer for every discernible defect or error, including the three specified in the said statute, provided, of course, that a general exception was interposed by the appellant to the action of the trial court in refusing the prayer.24

§§ 140-141 TITLE 13 § 140. Must Note a General Exception to Modification of Prayer and Also to Refusal of Prayer as Offered-No Need of Special Exception Where Modification Does Not Fit Facts of Prayer. 

As is further explained in section 132, the appellate court may not review the action of the trial court in modifying a prayer of the appellant, unless the record of the case shows that he had noted, at the trial, a general exception to the refusal of his prayer as offered, and another general exception to the court's modification thereof.25

Where the trial court modified a prayer of the defendant in a negligence case, by the addition of the hypothesis involv ing, in effect, the doctrine of the last clear chance, although the doctrine was not applicable to the facts as were postulated in the prayer, even if the facts were sufficiently proved and true, it was held:26 (a) That the appellate court would review the modification of this prayer to determine if the doctrine of the last clear chance was applicable, as a matter of law, to the facts as were postulated in the prayer, even in the absence of a special exception to the prayer. (b) That the appellate court would not, however, in the absence of a special exception, review this modified prayer to determine if there was evidence in the case legally sufficient to sustain the hypothesis of the last clear chance. 

§ 141. Need of a Variance Special Exception in Regard to Prayer That Sought to Recover Upon Facts at Variance With the Pleadings 

Due to the Variance Prayer Act of 1914 (Code, article 5, section 11), as is further explained in sections 82 and 85 and sections 91 and 93, where a prayer seeks to recover or defend, as the case may be, upon a state of facts at variance with the allegations of the pleadings or the form of the declaration or the form of the pleas, the variance must be pointed out at the trial of the case by way of a variance special exception, in form as shown in section 93, unless the attention of the trial court was specifically directed to the same point of variance by a variance prayer of the case, in form as shown in section 92.27

TITLE 13 § 142. Need to Specify Objectionable Part of Remarks of Court in Bill of Exceptions-Need of Motion for Mistrial or Withdrawal of Juror.

It is the right of the party who desires to except to oral remarks of court, to have them reduced to writing, so that they may be reviewed on appeal. But in order to obtain their review by the appellate court, the objectionable part of the oral remarks of court must be distinctly indicated in the bill of exceptions.28 

As is told more fully in sections 5, 6, 11, 26, 27 and 172, an objection to a prejudicial remark of the trial judge or counsel may not be reviewed by the appellate court in the absence of a motion for a mistrial or the withdrawal of a juror, followed by a general exception to the refusal by the trial court of the motion; unless the remark can be regarded as an instruction upon the law of the case.29 

§ 143. Time and Manner of Interposing Objections and General and Special Exceptions to Prayers-Cannot Give Leave at Trial to File Special Exception After Trial. 

In order to take advantage of an error contained in a granted prayer on the ground that it (a) assumed the existence of a disputed fact, or (b) because it submitted a question of law to the determination of the jury, or (c) because it submitted to the finding of the jury an issue of fact that is without legally sufficient support in the evidence, special exceptions thereto must be taken at the trial of the case, when the prayer or instruction might be corrected; as was said to be the intent of the statute on this subject-section 10 (formerly 

9) of article 5 of the Code.30

Cannot Give Leave at Trial to File Special Exception After Trial

§ 144. Special Exception Must be Specific-May be in Oral Form -But Written Special Exceptions Are Preferred. 

It is not essential that a special exception to a prayer should be presented in writing; although written special exceptions seem to be preferred under the Maryland practice.33 

As is further explained in section 143, leave of court must be obtained for authority to reduce to writing after trial, an oral special exception which was interposed to the grant of a prayer during the progress of the trial.34 

A special exception, in relation to section 10 of article 5 of the Code, must specifically refer to the portion of the prayer which is claimed to have assumed a disputed fact; or which is claimed to have submitted a question of fact to the finding of the jury that was without legally sufficient support in the evidence; or which is claimed to have submitted a question of law to their determination.35

§ 145. Approved Forms of Special Exceptions. 

The following are approved forms of special exceptions: (See section 93 for approved forms of variance special exceptions).

Sufficient Evidence.) "The defendant specially excepts to the granting of plaintiff's prayer: "Because there is no legally sufficient evidence to sustain the theory of the said prayer, in that there is no legally sufficient evidence of the plaintiff's condition before the accident, or that the accident did disable him from performing his duties." Md. 78, 82-83.)

Sufficient Evidence.) (American Oil Company v. Wells, 164 Md. 422, 429.)

"Are in their nature permanent.' (May Company v. Drury, 160 

Md. 143, 150.)

complained of was calculated to disable the plaintiff from engaging in those employments for which she would have been qualified, and there is no evidence to show that the plaintiff's injuries are permanent or that she is permanently prevented from pursuing her usual avocation." (Montgomery Bus Lines v. Diehl, 158 Md. 233, 240.)

Illustration-E (Approved Form of Special Exception Based on Want of Sufficient Evidence-See Author's Note.) 

"The defendant specially excepts to the granting of the plaintiff's first and second prayers for the reason that the plaintiff has offered no evidence in this case legally sufficient to show consideration for the note or paper writing sued on and mentioned in plaintiff's said prayers." (Citizens Nat'l Bank v. Custis, 155 Md. 173, 177.)

Illustration-F (Approved Form of Special Exception Based on Want of 

Sufficient Evidence.) "The defendants except especially to the action of the Court in granting the plaintiffs' first prayer for the following reasons: "To Wit: First. There was no evidence offered in this case legally sufficient to establish the fact that the defendants undertook and promised to pay to the plaintiffs for the services in that behalf an amount equal to 1/3 (one-third) of the amount they might recover for the defendants less the sum of $3,000.00. "Second. There is no legally sufficient evidence in this case to show that the plaintiffs became entitled to receive from the defendants the sum of $34,186.18." (Smith v. Whitman, 159 Md. 478, 490.)

Illustration-G (Approved Form of Special Exception Based on Want of 

Sufficient Evidence.) “Defendant specially excepts to plaintiff's second prayer— "Because there is no evidence in the case legally sufficient to prove that Edward L. Held in his application did not make a misrepresentation or untrue statement. "Because there is no evidence in the case legally sufficient to prove that such misrepresentation or untrue statement is not material to the risk.

$ 269 

TITLE 13 

"Because the uncontradicted evidence in the case shows that said Edward L. Held did in his application make an untrue statement material to the risk. "Because there is no evidence in the case legally sufficient to sustain the hypothesis of said prayer." (Mutual L. Ins. Co. v. Held, 157 Md. 551, 557-558.)

Illustration-H (Approved Special Exception Based on the Assumption of a 

Fact, Etc.) "The defendant excepts specially to the granting of plaintiff's first prayer, and for cause of exception shows: (a) That there is no legally sufficient evidence in this case to support the hypothesis of said prayer. (b) Because there is no legally sufficient evidence tending to show that the plaintiff was prevented from performing each and every duty pertaining to his occupation for a period of fifty-two weeks or that he suffered any total disability, or that he was prevented from performing each and every duty of his occupation for one-half of his business time to trial, or that the plaintiff lost any time. (c) Because said prayer assumes as a matter of fact that he was prevented from performing each and every duty of his occupation for fifty-two consecutive weeks. Also that he was prevented from performing each and every duty for one-half his business time, not exceeding fifty-two weeks to date of trial, also that said prayer assumes that said plaintiff lost time. (d) Because said prayer assumes the same as a matter of law." (Indemnity Company v. Smith, 168 Md. 649, 654-655.)

Illustration-I (Approved Special Exception Based on the Submission of a 

Question of Law, Etc.) "The defendant objects to the granting of the plaintiff's first prayer and especially excepts and objects to the said prayer and to the granting thereof because there is no evidence in this case legally sufficient to show that the shares of stock mentioned therein were sold by the direction and consent of the defendant and because there is no evidence in the case legally sufficient to show that said shares when purchased were placed by the direction and consent of the defendant in the name of the plaintiff in a special account instead of a joint account as referred to in the contract and because said prayer submits a question of law to the Court sitting as a jury in that it requires the Court sitting as a jury to find a waiver of the provision of said contract relating to the sale of the said stock during 1929 and because there is no evidence in this case legally sufficient to show any such waiver." (Kahn v. Schleisner, 165 Md. 106, 116.)

§§ 146-147 TITLE 13 § 146. 

When a Special Exception in Effect Performs the Office of a Demurrer Prayer. 

A special exception to a prayer that points out that there is a want of evidence legally sufficient to sustain a certain element of fact which the prayer submitted to the finding of the jury may sometimes prove to be, for all practical purposes, as effective as a general demurrer prayer.37 

For example, in a will case (involving issues whether the plaintiff, in view of his settlement release, was entitled to caveat the will) where the trial court granted prayers of the plaintiff which instructed the jury that they should answer the issues of fact, upon which the trial proceeded, in favor of the plaintiff, if they should believe or find the essential hypothesis of facts which were enumerated in these prayers, and where there was a want of evidence in the case legally sufficient to support some of these hypotheses of fact, it was held, in substance and effect:38 (a) That the trial court had committed reversible error in overruling the defendant's (caveatee's) special exceptions to the said prayers of the plaintiff, which pointed out the said want of legally sufficient evidence. (b) That since the plaintiff was not entitled to defeat the contested will upon any other hypothesis of facts than those enumerated in the said prayers of the plaintiff, and since some of these facts were without legally sufficient support in the evidence, the case would be and was reversed without a new trial. 

§ 147. Bill of Exceptions-Latest Statutes on Subject-What Belongs in the Bill of Exceptions. 

Rulings on Prayers Single Act 

The action of the trial court on the prayers is regarded as a single act, and an exception to a ruling on special exceptions to prayers is therefore properly included in the bill of exceptions to the ruling on the prayers.3 39 

37 Johnston v. Schmidt, 158 Md. 555, 562, 570, 573-574 ("omission in the issues" as framed in the Orphans' Court was "sufficiently supplied by the granted prayer”-see page 562 of this opinion). 

38 Johnston v. Schmidt, 158 Md. 555, 562, 570, 573-574. 

39 Wathen v. Pearce, 175 Md. 651; Guth v. Elliott, 158 Md. 243, 250; 

Brown v. Patterson, 141 Md. 293, 297-298; Hall v. Albertie, 140 Md. 

673; Wash., B. & A. R. R. Co. v. Faulkner, 137 Md. 451, 467; Moses v. Allen, 91 Md. 42, 53.

$ 271 

TITLE 13 When Exception Embraces Rulings on Prayers and Other Rulings 

An exception which embraced rulings on motions to strike out testimony and on prayers and special exceptions, was considered by the appellate court only as to the rulings on the prayers and special exceptions, and not as to the motions to strike out testimony;40 and, moreover, such a confused bill of exceptions may be ignored entirely by the appellate court.41 

Separate Bill of Exception for Each Ruling on Evidence 

Each ruling of the court on the evidence should be made the subject of a separate exception, and when one bill of exception includes more than one exception the appellate court may refuse to consider them. So one bill of exception should not be made to embrace several exceptions to rulings on the evidence.42

Inadvertent Omission of Stenographer to Note Objection or Exception 

The inadvertent omission of the stenographer to note an objection or exception should not prevent the trial court from certifying to the facts in order that the case might be correctly presented on appeal.43

What Evidence, Etc. Belongs in the Bill of Exceptions— Opinion of Court 

How much of the testimony should be incorporated in the record of the case on appeal in order to enable the appellate court to pass upon the correctness of the prayers, obviously depends upon the nature of the prayers and the special exceptions thereto. Where the defendant presents a general demurrer prayer at the close of all the testimony, the record should contain a summary, at least, of all the evidence bearing upon the plaintiff's right of recovery. Except where an opinion of court may be construed as an instruction, it does not, as a rule, belong in the record on appeal.4 44

§ 273 

TITLE 13 [What Bills of Exceptions Should Contain] 

"Bills of exceptions shall be so prepared as only to present to the Court of Appeals the rulings of the court below upon some matter of law, and shall contain only such statement of facts as may be necessary to explain the bearing of the rulings upon the issues or questions involved; and if the facts are undisputed, they shall be stated as facts, and the evidence from which they are deduced shall not be set out; and, if disputed, it shall be sufficient to state that evidence was adduced tending to prove them, instead of setting out the evidence in detail; but if a defect of proof be the ground of the ruling or exception, then the particulars in which the proof is supposed to be defective shall be briefly stated, and all the evidence offered in anywise connected with such supposed defect, shall be set out in the bill of exception. 

[Heading and Numbering] 

"The bill or bills of exceptions shall be headed at the beginning, Plaintiff's (or Defendant's, as the case may be) Bill (or Bills) of Exceptions, and beneath that, if there should be more than one exception, shall appear the subheading Exception 1. Then shall follow the proper statement of the facts necessary to set forth the ruling excepted to, as otherwise herein provided, it being sufficient to set forth the interposing of the objection and the ruling made thereon without a further statement in the bill that exception was taken to such ruling. Should there be more than one exception, the next exception shall immediately thereafter follow, in a separate paragraph under the subheading Exception 2, in which shall in like manner be set forth the ruling objected to; and so on in the case of each bill of exceptions, which bills shall be arranged and numbered consecutively in the same order in which they occurred during the course of the case. 

[Judge to Sign But Once] 

"Only one signature by the court shall be necessary, which signature shall be affixed at the end of all the bills, and shall be construed as indicating the approval by the Court of all said bills, and which signature shall be immediately preceded by the words, 'the foregoing bill (or bills) approved this 19 ' day

And it shall be the duty of the judges of the courts below to require exception to be prepared in accordance with this rule."

§ 148. Exceptions and Questions Not Argued On Appeal May be Treated as Waived.

The first sentence of Section 4 of Rule 39 of the Rules of the Court of Appeals of Maryland reads as follows: 

"Questions and exceptions not argued may be treated by the Court as abandoned."

The Court of Appeals has, in obedience to this rule, repeatedly declined to review well reserved exceptions of which no point was made either in the appellant's brief or in the oral argument of his counsel in the Court of Appeals. In other words, exceptions in the record on appeal may be regarded as waived if argued neither in the brief nor orally.48

When the court gives an instruction in a civil case at law, whether framed by itself or the attorneys, it is the duty of the jury to heed and follow it in arriving at their verdict, and if the court errs the remedy is by a motion for a new trial or by appeal, or by both methods, successively.¹

§ 152. Right of Counsel in Civil Case to Read to Jury From Legal Works. 

While the trial court may, in its discretion, permit counsel in civil cases to read to the jury from law books or reported cases, such a practice is seldom followed, since it tends to lead to confusion, and the bearing of previous decisions is rather to be reflected in the instructions and rulings on testimony.14

As is explained more fully in section 165, the right of counsel to read from law books in Maryland criminal trials stands on a different and unique footing.15 

§ 153. Counsel Must Not Refer to the Rejected Prayers In Argu ment to Jury.

Since the jury have nothing to do with rejected prayers, counsel will not be allowed to refer to them for the purpose of influencing their conclusion either upon the facts or the law of the case.16

TITLE 14 § 154. Right of Counsel to Argue to Jury That Plaintiff Failed to Sustain Allegations of Declaration. 

Where the instructions given for the guidance of the jury make no adequate reference to the pleadings in the case, the jury are not required to look at the pleadings, to ascertain how they are to find; and so counsel, in such a situation, will not be permitted to read the declaration to the jury and argue that its allegations were or were not sustained by the evidence. - Doctrine of Harmless Error as Applied to Prayers-Burden is Upon Appellant to Show Error and Injury

Doctrine of Reversible Error as Applied to Prayers 

§ 155. Construction of the Prayers-"Cross Reference Table.” Jury's Intelligence is Well Recognized 

The Court of Appeals of Maryland recently declared that the law of a case is given to the jury in the light of the evidence which they have just heard, and so it is not incumbent on the draftsman of a legal instruction to incorporate therein every detail or circumstance brought out in the testimony upon a given point; and that the jury, presumptively composed of men of at least average intelligence, if not in greater degree, because of the modern method of their selection, should be credited with ability to apply the law, given them in plain terms, to the facts freshly received by them, with reason and common sense.¹ 

1 See footnote 6 to this sec.; see secs. 156 to 159; see "Cross Reference Table" within text of this sec. 

1A-Jones v. Wayman, 169 Md. 670, 676-677; Geiselman v. Schmidt, 106 Md. 580, 585; Northern Central Rwy. Co.v. State, 29 Md. 420, 440. 281

§ 155 

TITLE 15 Common Sense Construction-Free of Hypercritical Analysis 

The prayers or instructions of a case should be construed according to their essential and common sense meaning, relieved of refined distinctions or hypercritical analysis.2 

When Prayers Are Construed Regardless of Issues of Pleadings 

Except in cases involving the trial of specific issues of fact, as applies to Workmen's Compensation cases or issues of fact sent from an Orphans' court to a court of law for determination by jury, and except where the attention of the court is, in due form, directed to a variance between the pleadings and the proof, the prayers or instructions of a case will be viewed entirely in relation to the real issues of the case as developed by the evidence alone, irrespective of the state of the pleadings.5

Slight Verbal or Clerical Inaccuracies in Granted Prayers 

Since the jury must be credited with a reasonable degree of intelligence, it may be assumed, in construing the instructions of the case, that they were not misled by slight verbal or clerical inaccuracies in the granted prayers. 6

When Slight Fault in Prayer May be Cured by Other Prayers 

Though a granted prayer or instruction is not so explicit and free from fault as it might be, yet, if when taken in connection with the evidence on which it is based and the other instructions of the court, it is found to present the question at issue fairly to the jury, the judgment will not be reversed on account of such instruction.⁹ 

Prayer That Misstated Law Not Cured by Correct Prayer 

But a litigant will not ordinarily be heard to contend that a granted prayer of his submission, which misstated the law of the case, was corrected by certain of the granted prayers of his opponent which correctly stated the law of the case, if the prayers of his opponent did not supplement and aid his prayer, but were in direct conflict with it; since, under such circumstances, the jury could not without disregarding one or the other come to any correct conclusion.10

§ 157. Presumption in Favor of the Correctness of Rulings on Prayers-Estoppel and Concession by Own Mistakes or by Failure to 

Except.

Upon appeal from a judgment of the lower court, the appellate court will presume, unless the record of the case shows otherwise, that the trial court ruled correctly and did not err.12

Presumption in Favor of Correctness of Court's Ruling 

In other words, in the absence of a contrary showing, the appellate court will usually indulge in all reasonable presumptions in favor of the propriety and sufficiency of the granted prayers or instructions; and, if the record does not show otherwise, the appellate court will presume likewise in favor of the correctness of the rulings of the trial court in regard to the rejected prayers. 13 In the absence of any evidence in the record, or of a demurrer to the evidence, or of a special exception to a jury prayer based upon the ground of the want of evidence legally sufficient to sustain a certain fact or hypothesis which the prayer submitted to the finding of the jury, the presumption on appeal is that there was legally sufficient evidence to support the judgment of the court below.14

§ 287 

TITLE 15 Construction of the Prayers Where the Evidence is Incomplete 

Where evidence referred to in the prayers is not properly made a part of the record, the prayers must be considered without reference to such evidence, and entirely upon the soundness of the legal propositions which they state, except that, where a prayer predicated on a finding of fact is refused, and the evidence relating to that finding is not before the appellate court, the ruling will be presumed to be correct.15 

No Reversal of Directed Verdict Where Inadmissible 

Testimony Would be Excluded on Retrial

The Court of Appeals of Maryland refused to be so "astute”for the purpose of reversing the verdict, which the trial court had directed in favor of the defendant, and for awarding a retrial-as to hold that testimony introduced by plaintiff was legally sufficient to take his case to the jury, if this testimony would be excluded upon objection on a retrial.16 

Where Instruction Assumed Contracts Without Objection 

Where the court, sitting as a jury, assumed the existence of two oral contracts, in its ruling on the granted prayers, and the right of the plaintiff to recover was made to depend on their existence and effect, and where no special exception was interposed against this assumption of fact, the appellate court held that it would assume that there was legally sufficient evidence to establish the oral contracts.17 

Where Prayers of Both Sides Committed Similar Error

As is explained more fully in section 134, a party to the cause will not ordinarily be heard to complain of an error or defect in a prayer presented by his opponent, if a similar error was embodied in a prayer of his own production and submission.18

§ 158 TITLE 15 § 158. Doctrine of Harmless Error as Applied to Prayers-Burden is Upon Appellant to Show Error and Injury.

In the interest of the orderly administration of justice, and to avoid useless expense to the State and to litigants in its courts, it has long been the settled policy of the Court of Appeals of Maryland not to reverse for harmless error. 

And as a corollary of that policy, this high court has also held, especially in recent years, that in all cases the burden is upon the appellant to show injury as well as error.19 

Error, Without Prejudice, Not Sufficient

In other words, to justify a reversal of the judgment there should be found a concurrence of error on the part of the trial court, and of injury thereby resulting to the appellant. 

Error, without prejudice, is not sufficient for reversal in the Maryland courts, nor in most of the other enlightened courts of the nation.20 

"Judicial Ritualism" 

In recent years the Court of Appeals of Maryland declared that it would be a species of judicial ritualism, which it could not sanction, for it to hold that the check in suit was not in evidence, and that the case should be remanded that the plaintiff might prove what the defendant conceded. The check in question, in this case, was handed to a witness who held it in his hand while he was examined in regard to it, in the presence of the court and jury, and it was referred to again and again in the trial as if it had been formally offered and was before the jury, and, moreover, the defendant, in his testimony, admitted the execution of the check.21

“Trifling With Trial by Jury and With Justice Itself "

Where there was no good reason for supposing that the alleged inconsistency between certain of the prayers had the effect of misleading or confusing the minds of the jury, the appellate court declared that it would be trifling with trial by jury and with justice itself, to reverse the judgment and deprive the plaintiff of the benefit of the verdict.22 

Properly Directed Verdict But On Wrong Grounds

Where a general demurrer prayer of the defendant could properly have been granted, that the case was withdrawn from the jury on improper grounds, or that there was error in any other ruling, was not prejudicial to the plaintiff.23 

Rejection of Plaintiff's Recovery Prayers Where Verdict Went to Him

The Court of Appeals of Maryland ruled that if a plaintiff presents a number of prayers furnishing different grounds for recovery, and some are granted and others are rejected, but the jury finds for the plaintiff, it would be difficult to conceive any legal ground for complaint, if there be no difference in them affecting the amount of recovery, whether the jury found for the plaintiff on one theory or another.24 

Wrong Ruling on Damage Prayer Where Verdict Went to Plaintiff

Where the verdict of the jury was in favor of the plaintiff on the merits of the case, the defendant, who filed the plea of set-off, could not properly complain of an erroneous ruling by the trial court upon his damage prayer which made no reference to the merits of the case.25

§ 293 

TITLE 16 § 160. Jury "Judges of Law” in Criminal Cases under Md. Constitution-Demurrer Prayers and Motions to Strike Out Testimony to Same Effect Not Grantable. 

In a civil trial at law, the court is inherently empowered to pass upon the question of the legal sufficiency of the evidence to sustain the whole or any part of the claim or defense; and, moreover, the court must actually do so when called upon to make such a ruling by a demurrer prayer of either of the parties to the cause.¹

No Demurrers to the Evidence in Criminal Trials 

In consequence, however, of the repeated interpretation of section 5 of article 15 of the Maryland Constitution by the Court of Appeals of the State, both the trial courts and the appellate court are totally deprived of the power to pass upon the question of the legal sufficiency of the evidence to sustain the guilt or innocence of the defendant or to sustain any lesser or subordinate issue of fact in a criminal trial.2 In other words, since this section of the Constitution prescribes that "In the trial of all criminal cases, the jury shall be the 

Judges of Law, as well as of fact”—the Court of Appeals will not usurp this function of the jury by passing upon the legal sufficiency of the testimony to establish the crime charged, or permit the court at nisi prius to do so.³

Motions to Strike Out Testimony as Demurrers to the Evidence 

So demurrer prayers, being those which seek directed findings, can not be granted in criminal trials. Nor can the court grant a motion to strike out testimony in a criminal case, if the motion virtually amounts to a demurrer to the evidence.¹ 

Motions to Strike Out Evidence Obtained by Illegal Search, Etc. 

But the court can and in appropriate situations must grant motions such as those that move to strike out testimony upon

And this is so because the court alone can bind and conclude the jury as to what evidence shall be considered by them in a criminal case, as well as in a civil case. Moreover, the rulings and the instructions of the court regarding the admissibility of evidence cannot be questioned by counsel in their argument to the jury, in either a criminal or civil case.5 

When Motion to Strike Out Evidence is Too Broad 

In connection with the aforegoing, trial counsel should bear in mind that if they make at the trial table a motion to exclude the general testimony of a witness, which has been taken subject to exception, but fail to specify and designate the particular testimony which is sought to be excluded, no proper basis is afforded to grant the motion, and an exception thereupon taken may raise no question for determination by the appellate court.Ⓡ 

Sufficiency of the Corroboration of an Accomplice

While it is a recognized general rule that a person accused should not be convicted upon the uncorroborated evidence of an accomplice, the question as to the sufficiency of the corroboration must be left, in consequence of the Maryland Constitution (article 15, section 5), to the determination of the jury, as the judges of law and fact in criminal cases, or to the judgment of the court when it is substituted for a jury by the defendant's election of a court trial.?

Accordingly, it has been held that an objection that a conviction was induced by insufficiently corroborated evidence of an accomplice may be asserted by a motion for a new trial addressed to the trial court, or to the Supreme Bench of Baltimore City, as applies to motions for new trials in criminal cases tried in Baltimore City, but that it is not a ground of reversal on appeal.8 c. 31.

§ 295 

TITLE 16 Whether Slot Machines Were Gaming Devices 

The question whether the evidence was legally sufficient to show that the slot machines operated by the defendant were gaming devices, was adjudged to be a question solely for the court sitting as a jury when the court was substituted for the jury by the defendant's election; and so would not be reviewed by the Court of Appeals.⁹ 

Whether Movie House was Opera House under Sunday Laws The question whether the statutory offense of keeping open an opera house on Sunday was shown by the evidence that the defendant on that day was keeping open a moving picture parlor, was adjudged to be one exclusively for the determination of the jury; and so would not be reviewed by the 

Court of Appeals.10

Whether Corpus Delicti was Established In a prosecution for embezzlement by a town treasurer, it was held that the jury, and not the court, was empowered to determine whether the corpus delicti had been established.11 

But a defendant's own confession of the commission of a crime cannot convict him thereof unless there is independent evidence tending to prove the corpus delicti or that the crime was actually committed by some one.12 

Whether Guilty of Larceny Rather than Receiving Stolen Goods 

And, again, in view of the above quoted provision of the Maryland Constitution (section 5 of articles 15), it was adjudged, on a prosecution for receiving stolen goods or money, that it was for the jury to determine whether the evidence in the case showed the defendant to be guilty of larceny rather than of receiving stolen goods; since in criminal trials the court only determines the admissibility of testimony and the competency of witnesses; while the effect or weight of the evidence, once admitted, is exclusively for the jury.13

§§ 160-161 TITLE 16 Difference between Legal Effect and Legal Sufficiency of Evidence 

Since the court in a criminal trial can not give even an advisory instruction to the jury regarding the legal sufficiency of evidence,14 but may, in its sole discretion, give an advisory instruction to the jury regarding the legal effect of evidence,15 it becomes important to understand the difference between an instruction regarding the legal sufficiency of evidence as compared to an instruction regarding the legal effect of evidence. 

Telling Jury What Constitutes an "Agent" or "Disorderly House"

When the court gives an instruction to the jury regarding the legal sufficiency of evidence, as it may do in a civil case, it thereby peremptorily removes from the consideration of the jury the case or the issue of fact to which the prayer or instruction was addressed.¹ 16 On the other hand, a prayer or instruction regarding the legal effect of evidence, whether it be in a civil or criminal case, is generally addressed to an issue of fact that was left to the decision or finding of the jury; as applies, for example, to an advisory instruction in a criminal case that tells the jury that if they should believe the facts enumerated in it, then the defendant was an agent within the meaning of a certain criminal statute;¹7 or as applies to an advisory instruction in a criminal case that tells the jury that if they should believe the facts enumerated in it, then the establishment in question was a disorderly house within the meaning of the indictment.18

Code Provision for Court Trial 

The practice of waiving the usual trial by jury in criminal cases, is now expressly authorized by section 549 of article 27 of the Maryland Code of Public General Laws, which prescribes:21 "Any person presented or indicted may, instead of traversing the same before a jury, traverse the same before the court, who shall thereupon try the law and the facts." 

How Court Functions as Jury-When more than One Judge Sits 

When an election is made under this section of the Code, the court is substituted for the jury and has the same duties and functions to perform in passing upon the guilt or innocence of the accused.22 The only difference is that which results from the difference in the constitution and nature of the two tribunals. To make a legal verdict all the jurors must agree; but where the matter is traversed before the Court, if it is composed of two or more members, a majority of them must concur in rendering the judgment; and where there is an equal division among them and no judgment is rendered, the party is left in the same position as if no trial had taken place. It is in law a mistrial, and a retrial must of necessity be had.23

Prayers in Criminal Trial Where Court Sits as Jury 

While it does not appear, from any reported Maryland case, that an advisory prayer or instruction was ever employed in a criminal case in which the court sat as both court and jury, yet, an analysis of the language of the afore-quoted statutory provision regarding non-jury trials in criminal cases (section 549 of article 27 of the Code) and of the function of the court sitting as a jury in a criminal case, plus the established practice of prayers or instructions in non-jury civil trials, would seem to indicate that the trial court in a non-jury criminal

case could, in its sole discretion, grant an advisory prayer, if it embodied a correct rule of law, for the guidance of the court, sitting as the jury, in arriving at its verdict. In this connection, it should be borne in mind that no appeal lies from the fact-finding of the court sitting as a jury in either a civil or criminal trial at law.24

Opinion of Court Sitting as Jury Has No Place in Record 

A mere statement of opinion by the court when rendering its verdict in a criminal case tried without a jury, has no place in the record and is not a part thereof, since it does not constitute an instruction to itself, sitting as the jury, upon the law of the case. When a defendant in a criminal case elects to be tried before the court, in arriving at a conclusion on the facts, the judge simply exercises the same functions as twelve jurors; what he says or does means no more than if said or done by them. His opinion of the case is expressed by and confined by his verdict of "guilty" or "not guilty," and the mental operations by which he reaches a decision find their legal expression in no other way.25

Sufficiency of the Evidence When Court Sits as Jury 

The question of the legal sufficiency of the evidence to convict, is solely for the determination of the jury, as judges of law and fact, or for the judgment of the court when substituted for the jury by the defendant's election of a court trial.20 

§ 162. Right to "Advisory" Prayers or Instructions in Criminal Trials-Variance between Indictment and Proof. 

Since section 5 of article 15 of the Constitution of Maryland is very explicit in declaring that juries in criminal cases are the judges of both the law and the facts, the court cannot give them binding instructions in such cases.

§ 299 

TITLE 16 Practice of Advisory Instructions in Criminal Cases Long Sanctioned 

But the judges can give them advisory instructions and, though juries are not bound by them, the practice of giving such instructions at the request of either party has long been sanctioned in Maryland; and they may also be given by the court of its own motion without any request from either party.27

Court Not Bound to Grant Prayers or Initiate Instructions 

While a Maryland trial court has the right to advise the jury as to the law in a criminal case, it is not bound nor can it be required to do so, since the jury, by virtue of the aforementioned constitutional provision, are the judges of the law as well as of the facts.28 

Instructions Should be Given in Advisory Form Only

When, however, the trial judge has thought it proper to instruct, it has always been deemed necessary that he should be careful to put the instruction in an advisory form, so that the jury be left entirely free to find their verdict in accordance with their own judgment of the law, as well as the facts. And this is so because an instruction in a criminal case, when given, goes to the jury simply as a means of enlightenment, and not as a binding and positive rule for their government, as it does in civil cases.29

Court Cannot Bind Jury as to Definition of Crime or Legal Effect of Evidence 

Accordingly, the trial court in a criminal case cannot, by an instruction given to the jury, bind them as to the definition of the crime, or as to the legal effect of the evidence before them; although the court may, if it sees fit to do so, in

TITLE 16 Variance Not Cause for Quashing Indictment or Directing Verdict 

In the Maryland courts it was ruled that an indictment could not be quashed because of a variance in the proof offered in the trial of the offender; and that the rules of evidence and of practice afforded ample means to the traverser to prevent the jury from considering testimony inadmissible for variance or upon any other ground, but that a motion to quash the indictment is not an appropriate method. Nor can the legal sufficiency of the testimony to sustain the indictment be submitted to the trial court as a question of law, as under the Constitution of Maryland the jury, in criminal cases, is the judge of both the law and the legal effect and legal sufficiency of the evidence, whose admissibility alone is for the trial court.34 

Variance between Indictment and Confession

In order that a variance between a written confession by the defendant and the indictment, as regards the elements of the crime charged, may render the confession inadmissible, the variance must be material and such as to place the defendant in second jeopardy for the same offense.35

In the aforementioned Beard case (71 Md. 280), Chief 

Judge Alvey emphasized that the practice of giving advisory instructions to juries in criminal cases "is founded in the soundest practical reason and good sense." And this learned 

Judge added, in part:38 "For though the juries are made judges of the law, they are unlearned, and not infrequently composed, in part at least, of persons wholly uninstructed as to the laws under which they live. When sworn upon the panel it becomes their duty to decide the case according to the established rules of law of the State, and not according to any capricious rules of their own; and it must be supposed that they are always desirous of performing their duty, and making their verdicts conform to law. To enable them to accomplish that object, no proper light should be withheld from them”.

In the aforementioned Luery case (116 Md. 292-293), Chief 

Judge Boyd emphasized the need for advisory instructions in criminal prosecutions dependent upon the testimony of accomplices. And this learned Judge added, in part (our paragraphing):39 "But the undoubted fact is that the experience of the Courts, which is certainly much greater than that of juries, is that it is unsafe, at least in the great majority of cases, to rest a conviction upon the uncorroborated evidence of an accomplice "Under our system prayers are advisory and not binding on juries in criminal cases * * "It is true that a Court can not be required to instruct the jury in a criminal case in this State, but in view of the almost universally approved practice in other States of advising or cautioning them in the class of cases spoken of, we would recommend that trial Courts grant such prayers if properly framed, when requested, or when they deem it desirable, even if not requested".

§ 303 

TITLE 16 § 164. Argument to Jury Against Instructions of Court in Criminal Trials-Exceptions to This Right of Counsel. 

It is now well-settled that counsel are at liberty to argue the law of a criminal case to the jury in opposition to the express instructions of the court to the jury thereupon. 

Unique and Anomalous Prerogative of Counsel 

And, moreover, it is equally well settled that this unique and anomalous prerogative of counsel, born out of the interpretation of section 5 of article 15 of the Constitution of Maryland, which prescribes that the jury shall be the judge of the law as well as of the facts in all criminal trials, extends to the court's instruction to the jury upon the legal effect of the evidence before them, as well as to the court's instruction regarding the definition of the crime.40 

When Counsel Cannot Argue Against Instructions of Court 

There are, however some well defined exceptions to the right of counsel to argue to the jury in opposition to the court's rulings or instructions to the jury in a criminal case. For example, it was held: (a) That counsel in criminal trials can never argue to the jury in opposition to the court's rulings or instructions regarding the admissibility of evidence.41 (b) That the trial court could refuse to permit defendant's counsel in a criminal case "to argue in effect the question of the admissibility of evidence obtained by search and seizure without warrant." 42

§ 166. Propriety of Remarks of Court, State's Attorney and Defendant's Counsel-Prejudicial Cross-Examination. 

Remarks of Court 

In ruling upon the propriety of the remarks of the trial judge in a criminal case, the Court of Appeals recently reaffirmed the intrenched policy of the Maryland courts which declares that a trial judge, because of his high and authoritative position, should be exceedingly careful in any remarks made by him during the progress of a trial either in passing upon evidence or ruling upon prayers, and should carefully refrain, either directly or indirectly, from giving expression to an opinion upon the existence or not of any fact, which should be left to the finding of the jury.49

Ample Chance to Argue Case-To be Confined to Evidence 

Although the ends of justice require that counsel should be given every proper latitude in advocating his client's cause before the jury, he must confine his argument to the evidence in the case.50

§ 166 

TITLE 16 Court is Bound to Restrain Improper Argument 

While the trial court, in a criminal case, is not bound to initiate instructions to the jury upon the law of the case, nor to grant the prayers proposed by either of the parties, regardless of their correctness, and, moreover, while counsel are ordinarily at liberty to argue to the jury in opposition to the court's advisory instructions to them upon the law of the case, as is further explained in the previous sections of this title, a trial court is in duty bound to restrain, especially upon objection, improper and prejudicial argument of counsel, such as the making of statements that have no support in the evidence, either expressly or inferentially.51 

Comment on Defendant's Failure to Testify 

The State's Attorney cannot, as a rule, comment upon the failure of the defendant to testify and to deny the evidence of the prosecution.52

Improper Cross-Examination of Accused-Imputing Other 

Crimes The State's Attorney should not impute to the defendant, either during his cross-examination or at any other stage of the case, the commission of crimes which are inadmissible in the case on trial, or which the State's Attorney is unprepared to prove, even if admissible.53

Improper Argument-State's Attorney's Influence Over Jurors 

In the leading embezzlement case of Dick v. State (107 

Md. 11, 18-20), it was held that the State's Attorney had improperly, during the argument of the case to the jury, stated "that the construction of the statute, as to whether the defendant was an agent within the meaning of the (embezzlement) statute was something they had nothing to do with, in as much as the court had already determined that question in ruling upon the testimony." And the appellate court added:55

The statement of the State's Attorney "should have been disapproved by the Court and the jury directed to allow it no weight, as was expressly held in Hall v. U. S., 150 U. S. 81 *** A zealous and efficient State's Attorney naturally possesses a strong influence over jurors desirous of protecting society against such offences, and the declaration of the State's Attorney in this case was well calculated to impress the jury that they were at liberty to accept his view without regard to their own."

Prejudicial Cross-Examination 

In the leading robbery case of Duffy v. State (151 Md. 456, 467-470)-which case carefully reviews many of the other

Maryland cases that passed upon the question of the propriety of the cross-examination of defendants in criminal trials-it was held that the State's Attorney had improperly persisted in asking the defendant whether he had not once been charged with larceny and then ordered to leave the city, even after the prosecuting attorney was informed by the trial court that such questions were inadmissible unless there had been a conviction or an agreement by the defendant to leave the city in order to secure a dismissal of the charge, since this line of cross-examination amounted to an assertion that there had been such an agreement or a conviction, which might have prejudiced the jury.56

§ 167. When the Instructions and the Argument of Counsel to the Jury Must be Given in the Presence of the Accused.

The advisory instructions and the argument of counsel should be given to the jury in the presence of the accused. This practice must always be followed in felony trials; and applies to the advisory instructions regarding the form of the verdict.58 

§ 168. Time for the Giving of the Instructions to the Jury in Criminal Trials. 

In the leading criminal case of Vogel v. State (163 Md. 

276), a majority of the Judges of the Court of Appeals recommended, to the trial courts of the state, that when they see fit to give advisory instructions to the jury, their actual giving should be deferred until the argument to the jury by counsel is completed. If this practice is followed, the problem of protecting the jury's prerogative and the legitimate interest of the parties to the prosecution, and of insuring proper respect for the authority of the court, will be greatly simplified. 

And the majority of the appellate judges further reasoned that if the instructions are not given until the conclusion of the argument, the jury in the meantime has been informed as to the respective contentions of the state and defense in regard to the law, and the embarrassments which might result from a recognition of the right of counsel to dispute the court's pronouncement before the jury are effectually obviated.59

§ 169. Requisites of Prayers and Instructions in Criminal Trials -Form of the Verdict-Approved Forms of Instructions. 

Except that the prayers or instructions in Maryland criminal trials must clearly and definitely inform the jury that they are merely advisory, and that the jury is the judge of the law, as well as of fact, the propriety of the prayers or instructions in criminal trials, whether they be in oral or written form, will be measured by the same standards as those applicable to prayers or instructions in civil trials.61 

Instruction as to What Constitutes a Disorderly House 

In the criminal case of Beard v. State (71 Md. 275, 279), the Court of Appeals approved the following written instruction to the jury (upon the legal effect of evidence) :82 "If you find from the evidence that the traverser kept a bar-room and dance-hall with music, for the purpose and with the intent of bringing together and entertaining prostitutes and men desirous of their company, and that such persons habitually assembled there to drink and dance together, then you may find said establishment a disorderly house within the meaning of the indictment, even although you may also believe that the house was quietly kept, and no conspicuous improprieties were permitted inside. The jury being the judges of the law as well as fact, this charge is to be understood as advisory only of what the law is."

§§ 169-170 TITLE 16 Instruction Regarding Importance of Time of Crime 

In the criminal case of Wheeler v. State (42 Md. 563), the jury after 16 hours of deliberation, addressed to the court in writing a communication, requesting to be informed-"whether the charge contained in the third count of the indictment must be confined to the first day of January, 1874," being the time mentioned in that count. To this inquiry, the court correctly responded, in writing-"that it was sufficient, if the jury found the offense charged on the day mentioned or at any other time between that day and the day of finding the presentment;-that such was the opinion of the Court, by which however the jury was not bound.” 63 

"Instruction" Regarding Confession as Evidence 

In the criminal case of Toomer v. State (112 Md. 285, 293294), the foreman sent a note to the trial judge, from the jury room, asking if they should consider the prisoner's confession. 

The judge replied that the testimony concerning the confession was a part of the evidence which the jury was at liberty to consider; which was held to be a correct instruction, and one which did not suggest to the jury that they should consider the evidence of the State to the exclusion of the testimony of the defense or that it was entitled to more weight.64 

Instructions Regarding the Form of the Verdict 

Instructions to the jury regarding the form of the verdict must obviously be addressed to the nature of the indictment and to each count thereof, with due regard for the pleas and defenses such as insanity.65

Under the long-established practice in the Maryland courts, criminal cases in which fines or penalties are imposed can be submitted, by the mutual consent of the State and the defendant, to the judgment of the court upon an agreed statement of facts. 67

§ 171. Motions for New Trial and Arrest of Judgment in Criminal Cases Jurisdiction of Supreme Bench of Baltimore City. 

A judgment can be arrested only for substantial errors intrinsic in the pleadings or in the verdict apparent on the face of the record, and brought up for review by the motion. 

So it was held that neither the rulings on the evidence as offered in detail nor presented in its entirety, and so considered with reference to its legal sufficiency to support a verdict of guilty of the crime of false pretenses, can be considered on a motion in arrest of judgment.69 

Scope of Motion in Arrest of Judgment 

The scope of a motion in arrest of judgment in a criminal case has been narrowed by the terms of section 553 of article 27 of the Code of Public General Laws, by prescribing that questions raised on demurrer to the indictment and by plea of limitations cannot be considered on motion in arrest of judgment.70

No Appeal From Refusal of New Trial 

The Court of Appeals of Maryland can not review a ruling upon a motion for a new trial in a criminal case. That a motion is called a motion in arrest of judgment rather than one for a new trial does not determine its real character to the extent of enabling the Court of Appeals to review rulings

§ 172. Appeal to Court of Appeals in Criminal Cases-State's Limited Right of Appeal-Need of Exceptions and Motions for Mistrial. 

No Appeal by State From Acquittal 

After the acquittal of a defendant upon a regular trial on an indictment in a Maryland court for either a felony or misdemeanor, the verdict of acquittal can never be set aside or a new trial granted and it matters not whether such verdict be the result of a misdirection of the judge on a question of law or a misconception of facts on the part of the jury.76 

State's Limited Right of Appeal 

But the plaintiff in a criminal case-the State of Maryland -is entitled to appeal to the Court of Appeals from an order 75 See footnote 74 to this sec.; see Constitutional and Code provisions mentioned in text of this sec.

Defendant's Absolute Right to File Motion for New Trial and Appeal 

The right of a convicted defendant in a criminal case to file a motion for a new trial and to appeal to the Court of Appeals of Maryland, or to do both, successively, is unrestricted.78 However, no appeal can lie to the Court of Appeals from the refusal of the defendant's motion for a new trial,79 unless he was deprived of the opportunity to present his facts and law in support of the motion.80 

In this connection, it should be borne in mind that the Court of Appeals of Maryland is a law and not a fact reviewing tribunal on appeals to it from the criminal and civil courts at law.81

State Cannot Appeal From Bad Instruction to Jury 

Since the trial court in a criminal case is not bound to grant or give advisory prayers or instructions, the only kind that is permissible in such cases, no appeal lies from its refusal to grant or give a prayer or instruction, regardless of its soundness. In the event, however, that an erroneous instruction in a criminal case is prejudicial to the State rather than to the defendant, the error cannot be remedied on appeal.82

Error Regarding Not Guilty Counts 

The accused cannot ordinarily claim that there was prejudicial error with regard to counts on which there was a verdict of not guilty.83

Appeal Must be From Final Judgment 

Neither the defendant nor the State, in the limited instances in which the latter is permitted to prosecute an appeal in a criminal case, may prosecute an appeal except from a final judgment. In other words, the jurisdiction of the Court of 

Appeals in both criminal and civil cases at law is limited to the review of the final actions of the lower court.84 

So the Court of Appeals has ruled that it could not pass upon the selection of a trial court to which the case shall be removed until after the conclusion of the trial of the case and the rendition of the final judgment.85 And, again, it was ruled that the State could not appeal from an order overruling its demurrer to the defendant's special pleas, because this order was not final since it left the State free to traverse the special pleas, and also the general issue plea of not guilty.86 

Nor will the appellate court review an appeal immediately from an order sustaining a demurrer to but some of the counts in the indictment.87

No Appeal From Mere Opinion of Court 

No appeal lies from a statement of opinion by the court when rendering its verdict or sentence in a criminal case tried without a jury. Moreover, such an opinion of court has no place in the record on appeal, and is not properly a part thereof.89

Appeal From Refusal of Bill of Particulars 

In criminal cases the allowance of a bill of particulars is within the sound discretion of the court, and unless there be a gross abuse of this discretion, resulting in injury to the accused, the refusal of the demand for the particulars will not be reviewed by the appellate court.⁹º 

Appeal From Refusal to Strike Out Verdict for Want of Evidence

No appeal lies from the refusal of a motion to strike out the verdict and judgment for legal insufficiency of the evidence, since the jury is the judge of the law as well as of the facts in criminal trials, by virtue of section 5 of article 15 of the Constitution of Maryland. In other words, the appellate court has no jurisdiction to determine as to the legal sufficiency of the evidence upon which the verdict of guilty was rendered.91

Appeals From Sentences or Fines 

The unauthorized imposition of a fine or penalty in connection with a purported suspension of sentence is an imposition of a sentence and a judgment from which an appeal lies.92

Need of Exceptions to Rulings of Court

It is a general principle and a statutory provision that any ruling of the court which is not presented by a demurrer to the pleadings, an exception, a motion to quash, or in arrest of judgment or to strike out the judgment for fraud or irregularity, cannot be considered on appeal Neither the nature nor the size of the verdict, in a civil case, nor the gravity of the offense or the nature of the penalty, in a criminal case, can justify a departure from the precedent and statute upon which this rule firmly rests.9 94 

No Need of Exception When Court was Without Jurisdiction to 

Impose Sentence on Bad Form of Verdict But where the verdict of the jury was rendered in such form, in compliance with an instruction of the court in regard thereto, that the court had no jurisdiction to pronounce sentence thereon, the appellate court reviewed this instruction, verdict and sentence, regardless of the absence of an exception to this instruction, and even though it was approved by the defendant's counsel, along with instructions to the jury in regard to other possible forms of verdicts.95 

Need to Move for a Mistrial or Withdrawal of Juror

In order to reserve questions as to the alleged impropriety of remarks made by the court or state's attorney during the trial, the accused should move the court to withdraw a juror and declare a mistrial on account of the prejudicial effect of the remarks, and should reserve an exception in case of the court's refusal,96 except where the remarks under consideration amount to an instruction to the jury upon the law of the case, when the mere notation of an exception, against the remarks, will permit the appellate court to review the correctness of the remarks as a legal proposition.97
