TITLE 17 § 174. Rules for Taking Contract Cases From Jury-Consideration-Promise of Additional Compensation-Implied Obligations—Voluntary Services-Construction of Contracts-Parol Testimony. 

The general rules, discussed in sections 96 to 102, by which to determine when a case, claim or defense can be taken from the jury through the medium of a demurrer prayer, apply with equal force to actions ex contractu.¹

Right to Go to Jury Where No Damage is Shown 

The law presumes some injury or damage from every breach of contract, to the extent of nominal damages at least. And so an action for the breach of a contract cannot be taken from the jury even where no evidence was produced to show that the plaintiff sustained any injury in consequence of the breach. 

Moreover, it has been said that a plaintiff is entitled to a verdict for nominal damages for the defendant's breach of the contract even where it appears that the plaintiff profited thereby.2 

Need of Consideration for Simple Contract 

To state that every simple contract must be supported by a consideration is to state an elementary principle of the law of contract.3

§ 174 

TITLE 17 

Consideration Need Not Move to the Promissor

The consideration to support a promise need not move to the promissor, it being sufficient that the consideration is parted with to another as beneficiary." 

Failure of Consideration

Where the consideration of a contract entirely fails, the party in default cannot recover at law against the other party.8

Moral Obligation-Promise to Do What One is Bound to Do 

A merely moral obligation is not, in contemplation of law, a consideration to support a promise."

While the undertaking or doing of anything beyond what one is already bound to do, though of the same kind and in the same transaction, is a good consideration,10 a promise to do what one is required by law or contract to do is not, ordinarily, a valuable consideration.11

Additional Compensation for Work Due to Unforeseen Difficulties 

But in the leading case of Linz v. Schuck (106 Md. 220), where a contractor had agreed to build a house for $1,500, and was about to abandon his contract because he encountered unforeseen difficulties, namely, soft mud under a crust of earth, it was held that the contractor could recover from the owner on his promise to pay for extra work required to complete performance of the original contract. The effect of this promise of extra pay and its acceptance was to substitute a new and modified contract for the original agreement.¹ 12

§ 325 

TITLE 17 When Writing is Required for Extra Charges 

Where a building contract for the erection of a mill contained a provision reading "No extra charges to be made unless a written agreement be made and attached to the contract”—it was held that, in the absence of such a written and attached writing, the owner did not have to pay for extra work in and about the completion of the mill, even if ordered by him.13

But in an action for work and materials furnished under a "cost plus" building contract, it was held that a prayer of the defendant was also defective for having told the jury that a stipulation in the original contract, requiring additions and deductions to be agreed on in writing, referred to extra work on the building or elimination of parts of the work, as shown in the plans, and that for any such changes a written agreement was requisite, since it thus disregarded the issue whether defendant himself committed a breach of the contract preventing its complete performance, in which case the stipulation referred to would not be enforceable.14 

Implied Obligations-Voluntary Services 

If one merely accepts services from another which are val uable to him, in general, the presumption of fact arises that a compensation equivalent is to pass between the parties, and the burden of proof is upon the recipient of the services to rebut such presumption if he would escape from rendering such equivalent.15 But no one can legally collect compensation for voluntary services to another, however beneficial, in the absence of a contract of employment, express or implied.16

§ 174 

TITLE 17 Implied Promise to Pay Reasonable Value of Useful Services 

The rendition of useful services to a party furnishes prima facie evidence of their acceptance, and in the absence of proof to the contrary raises an obligation to pay therefor at their reasonable value, when no proof exists as to their special value.17

But since the presumption that one who performs services at the request of another is entitled to reasonable compensation is rebuttable, the defendant, in such a case, is entitled to show an express agreement that no charges would be made, or to show circumstances justifying the inference that such was the intention of the parties.¹ 18 

Personal Services Rendered to Member of Family, Etc. 

Generally speaking, it may be said that no presumption of payment arises in regard to personal services that are rendered by one member of a family to another. Moreover, in such a situation, it may be inferred that the services were intended to be gratuitous, and were rendered with a view to no compensation.19 And this rule has been extended to members of a household not related in blood or by marriage when the domestic associations of the parties involved the usual incidents of family relationship.20

But even where the parties are related in blood or by marriage, the circumstances under which the personal services

When Jury May Decide if Contractual Offer Was Accepted 

Where the defendant's alleged acceptance of an offer, for the purpose of the contract in suit, was indicated by debatable acts as well as by words, it was held that whether the defendant had accepted the offer contained in the plaintiff's letter, was a question that should have been left to the finding of the jury.22

But where the facts in evidence are in conflict or dispute, the question of whether or not they constitute a performance, or a breach, or a waiver of the breach, is generally one for the jury to determine, guided by the instructions of the court.25

Need to Prove Exact Language of Oral Agreement, Etc. 

Where the testimony is that the parties orally agreed to do a definite thing, it is not necessary that the language used in making the agreement shall be given. The general rule is that the substance and effect of the actual words spoken will suffice, the witness stating the substance as best he can from the impression left on his memory; and this rule is applicable to oral utterances in general, whether as forming contracts, or merely as admissions.26

Finding of Oral Contract for Jury Construction for Court 

The construction of an oral contract, whose terms are undisputed, like that of a written contract, is a matter for the Court to whom the law confides the interpretation of all contracts; but where the fact as to what were the terms or pròvisions of an oral contract is in dispute, and the testimony on the subject is conflicting, it should be left to the jury, not to construe the contract, but to find what it in fact was. That can ordinarily be done by instructions to the jury with hypothetical directions as to the law based upon the finding by them of the existence of specified terms in the contract.27

§ 329 

TITLE 17 

General Rules for Interpreting Written Contracts-Oral Testimony 

It is axiomatic that in the interpretation of a contract the intention of the parties must control. Where the intention is clearly and unmistakably manifested by the language used, considered in connection with the subject-matter of the contract, it will be gathered from the words used. But where the contract is open to construction in determining its meaning, the court may consider the circumstances as the parties viewed them, the subject-matter and the surrounding circumstances; and, for this purpose only, may admit parol evidence, 28 

Parol Evidence to Vary Terms of Written Contract— Usage or Custom 

But parol contemporaneous evidence is not admissible to contradict or vary the terms of a valid written instrument; except that proof of usage is admitted, either to interpret the meaning of the language of the contract, or to ascertain the nature and extent of the contract, in the absence of express stipulations and where the meaning is equivocal and obscure. 

In all cases of this sort, however, the rule for admitting the evidence of usage or custom must be taken with the qualification or proviso that the evidence be not repugnant to, or inconsistent with, the contract; for otherwise it would not go to interpret and explain but rather to contradict that which is written.29

§ 174 

TITLE 17 Parol Modification or Waiver of Written Agreement 

While parol contemporaneous evidence is inadmissible to contradict or vary the terms of a valid written instrument, it has been held, again and again, that it is competent to prove by parol a distinct subsequent agreement, waiving, abandoning or modifying the terms of the writing, or to prove an additional supplementary agreement by parol, by which something is supplied, that is not in the written contract.30 But it does not seem that this qualification of the parol rule can be extended to apply to a contract within the Statute of 

Frauds or to one under seal.31

Construction Put On Contract by the Parties 

While the practical construction put on a contract by the parties cannot control its express unambiguous provisions, the construction that the parties placed upon the contract by their conduct must be given weight in cases of doubtful meaning 32 

Construction Against Draftsman of Contract 

Moreover, it is a rule common to the construction of all written instruments that it is to be taken, in cases of doubtful meaning, against the draftsman.88

§ 331 

TITLE 17 Control of Specific Over General Provision of Contract 

Where two clauses or parts of a written agreement are apparently in conflict and one is general in character and the other is specific, the specific clause or part will take precedence over and control the general; although, where apparently conflicting provisions in a contract may be reconciled and accepted as binding on the parties, no one of them ought to be rejected.84

Control of Typewritten Over Printed Provision of Contract 

Where a part of a contract is printed, and a part is typewritten, the typewritten part controls in case of conflict.35

People's Bank v. Turner, 169 Md. 430 The entry of a savings deposit to the credit of plaintiff or her sister, or the survivor, did not give the bank a lien or right of setoff as regards a note of the sister held by the bank, in the absence of evidence showing that the latter had a separate interest in the deposit, it being for the bank to pay to whichever of the two presented the pass-book, rather than to select one of them as the payee, by asserting the set-off against her.

§ 355 

TITLE 17 § 176. Rules for Taking Negligence Cases From Jury-Plaintiff Must Prove at Least 4 Essential Elements-Contributory Negligence. 

The general rules, discussed in sections 96 to 102, by which to determine when a case, claim or defense can be taken from the jury, through the medium of a demurrer prayer, apply with equal force to negligence cases.

The 4 Indispensable Elements of Proof 

A plaintiff in a negligence case is not entitled to have his case submitted to the consideration of the jury unless some legally sufficient evidence is produced in support, at least, of each and all of the following four essential and indispensable elements of proof which the plaintiff must always affirmatively sustain : 

Primary Negligence (1) Proof of negligence on the part of the defendant or his agent or servant in the premises.¹

§ 359 

TITLE 17 Formula for Judging Contributory Negligence as a Matter of Law 

The law as repeatedly declared by the Court of Appeals of Maryland and supported by the great weight of authority elsewhere, is that, to justify the trial court in withdrawing the case from the consideration of the jury on the ground of contributory negligence by the plaintiff, the evidence must show some prominent and decisive negligent act on the part of the plaintiff which directly contributed to the accident, and was the proximate cause thereof, and that this negligent act must be of so prominent and decisive a character as to leave no room for difference of opinion thereon by reasonable minds.8

In other words, the act relied on to establish, as a matter of law, the existence of contributory negligence must be dis tinct, prominent and decisive, and one about which ordinary minds would not differ in declaring it to be negligent. And where the nature and attributes of an act relied on to show negligence contributing to an injury sustained can only be determined correctly by considering all the attending and surrounding circumstances of the transaction, it falls within the province of the jury to pass upon and characterize it, and it is not for the court to determine its quality as a matter of law.⁹

Slight Proof of Primary Negligence

§ 176 

TITLE 17 Mere Surmise of Primary Negligence-Scintilla of Evidence 

But whatever the facts or circumstances may be, unless there is some evidence of negligence, or evidence from which negligence may be legally inferred, the result of some act of omission or commission on the part of the defendant, there is nothing which calls for the submission of the case to the jury, and this requirement is not satisfied by mere conjecture and speculation as to how the injury complained of occurred. 

Nor will a scintilla of evidence or mere surmise that there may have been negligence justify the court in permitting the case to go to the jury.18

Speculation as to how or from what cause the accident occurred cannot be allowed to stand for proof, or be made the basis of a verdict in favor of the party upon whom the burden of proof lies. There must be evidence from which the jury can reasonably and properly conclude that the injury was produced by some negligent or wrongful act of the defendant.19

Moreover, the plaintiff must prove affirmatively the negligence alleged and that it caused the injury; and this burden is not met by testimony which tends to show that the negligence of the defendant may have caused, or even that it probably did cause, the injury, if it should further appear that the injury may have been produced by some other cause for which the defendant was not responsible.20

§ 363 

TITLE 17 Proof of Primary Negligence by Presumption or Circumstantial Evidence 

However, as may be better observed from sections under other titles of this book, a defendant's negligence may be established by circumstantial evidence, or by a presumption of negligence, as arises when the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur applies to the accident under consideration, or when it is shown that the accident was due to the defendant's violation of a penal statute or ordinance intended for public safety.21 

Proof of Proximate Cause 

It has been repeatedly declared that the question of proximate cause of the injury complained of is in very many cases difficult of determination; that it is not a question of science or legal knowledge, but one to be decided upon common sense principles in the light of the surrounding facts and circumstances of the case under consideration; and that the courts do not indulge in refinements and subtleties, as to causation, that would defeat the claims of natural justice.22 

When, however, the controlling facts bearing upon the question of proximate cause are uncontroverted, and are susceptible of but one legitimate inference, the question of proximate cause becomes one of law for the court to decide, rather than one of fact for the jury to determine.23 

Ordinarily, however, the question of proximate cause is one that should be left to the determination of the jury.24

Injury to the person complaining is an essential element of actionable negligence. The negligence alleged and the injury

§ 365 

TITLE 17 Duty Regarding Highways-May Assume Their Safety 

There is also a duty imposed by operation of law upon everyone to use the public highways with ordinary care and prudence, so as to avoid injury to others thereupon. In this connection, it should be observed that all persons having occasion to travel over public highways are entitled to assume that the highways are in reasonable repair and free from dangerous traps or obstructions of any kind.29

Few Relations Are Free of Duty 

Finally, it has been said, again and again, that there are few relations or situations in life in which the law does not impose the duty on everyone not to injure another by his acts or omissions wanting in due, reasonable or ordinary care, when harm is observable and preventable.30 

Invitees, Licensees and Trespassers

Whether the owner or occupant of private property owed to the person injured thereupon any legal duty of protection, against the injury complained of, will most generally depend upon the question whether the injured party was, in contemplation of law, an invitee,31 licensee,32 or a trespasser33 at the time of the injury.

Clark, 128 Md. 245 by defendant's dog In order to render the owner of a dog liable in damages to one bitten by the dog, it is necessary to show that the dog had a vicious propensity and that such vicious propensity was known to the owner But the owner's knowledge need only be such as to put him on his guard, and to anticipate, as an ordinarily prudent person would do, the conduct of the dog which resulted in the injury complained of. 

Ewing v. Rider, 125 Md. 149 Suit to recover damages for injury to plaintiff's growing and harvested crops by defendant's chickens over a period of years

Limitations - Measure of Damages - It is a fundamental principle of the law of damages that a person injured in his personal or property right shall be compensated therefor. 

N. C. Railway Co. v. Green, 112 Md. 487 Code, art. 

23, sec. 244, prescribes: "Railroad companies shall be responsible for injuries resulting in death or otherwise inflicted upon any stock, as cattle, horses, sheep, hogs, and so forth, or by fire occasioned by their engines or carriages, upon any of their roads and branches thereof, unless the said companies can prove to the satisfaction of the justice or other tribunal before which the suit may be tried that the injury complained of was committed without any negligence on the part of the company or its agents; provided, however, that no such presumption of negligence on the part of Railroad Companies shall arise in any case of fire occurring in or about water front or other railroad terminals used for receiving, delivering or transhipping freight, in the handling of which and the ordinary conduct of business therein, persons not in the employ or under the control of such Railroad Companies, their servants and agents, are engaged in and about such premises, and where *Taken from Jury.

Brady, 110 Md. 568 Plaintiff was bitten by defendant's dog- Need of caution where owner suspects that his dog is "mad" due to possible hydrophobia Evidence is admissible to show that defendant's servant in charge of the dog noticed its strange behavior, suspected that it was mad, and communicated his fears to the defendant Under the circumstances 

of this case, knowledge by the servant, the custodian of the suspected dog, of its diseased condition is to be imputed to the master When the owner of a dog has reason to suspect that it may be mad it is his duty to use every precaution to prevent the animal from inflicting injury upon others. - Twigg v. Annapolis and Elkridge R. R. Co. v. Baldwin, 60 Md. 88

Suit by R. R. Co. against owner of trespassing ox for damage caused by its upsetting of plaintiff's cars and engine The defendant was clearly liable In other States where the question has arisen, the Courts have uniformly held the owner liable for damages resulting from a collision with stock trespassing on a railroad track through the negligence of the owner. 

Balto. & Ohio R. R. Co. v. Lamborn, 12 Md. 257 – Suit to recover the value of a horse killed by defendant's locomotive At common law a plaintiff could not recover for injuries to which his own fault or negligence directly contributed, and this principle is not changed by the acts of 1838, ch. 244, and 1846, ch. 346 (now 

Code, art. 23, sec. 244) which makes a railroad liable for injury to cattle and stock on their roads, unless it can disprove its negligence — The owner of cattle is bound to keep them in an enclosure or in custody at his peril, for every entry by them on another's possession is a trespass and this principle applies as well to the intrusion of cattle and horses, upon the land over which a railroad company is entitled to its franchise as to the property of a private owner. *Taken from Jury.

Myers, 127 Md. 527 Suit against firm of attorneys for alleged negligence by one partner in regard to investment of client's funds - - A law partner not engaged in the business of investigating moneys for clients, is not responsible for the acts of a co-partner in making an investment, which does not appear on the firm books and of which he has no knowledge Taken from jury as to some of the partners. Cochrane v. Little, 71 Md. 323Suit against attorney for negligently advising client "as to his legal responsibility and liabiity as surety upon a certian bond”- It was held that the Court erred in refusing to instruct the jury that if they believed from the testimony that the plaintiffs' testator paid the money mentioned, and executed the release given in evidence, for the purpose of relieving his son-in-law from prosecution, and himself from worry and trouble, and not by reason of any advice given him by the defendant, then the plaintiffs were not entitled to recover; there being testimony tending to support the hypothesis of the prayer. *Taken from Jury.

*Peoples Service Drug Stores, Inc., v. Sommerville, 161 

Md. 662 Action for injuries to patient caused by failure of defendant druggist to properly label box containing drugs as required by statute Filling of prescription The neglect of a druggist to label a box of strychnine capsules "Strychnine" and "Poison", as required by statute, did not give a right of action on account of injury caused by taking the capsules, if the absence of labels was not the proximate cause of the injury. 

Decided on 

*State v. Consol. Gas, Etc., Co., 146 Md. 390 

demurrer to the declaration It being essential for the maintenance of an action under Code, art. 67, for wrongful death, that the deceased might have maintained an action had be survived, there can be no recovery for a child's death as a result of a defect in an article purchased by the child's parents, the child not being in privity of contract with the vendor as regards the warranty on the sale, and so not being capable, had he survived, of suing on such warranty - The vendor of an article manufactured by another, and not inherently dangerous, which it sold in the same condition as when it was received, without any knowledge that the article was not perfectly safe, or that the manufacturer was irresponsible or incompetent, is not liable to a person, with whom it had no contractual relation, for injuries caused by defects therein. *Taken from Jury.

§§ 177(10)-177 (11) TITLE 17 

391 Case 5Case 6 

Bottling Co. v. Sindell, 140 Md. 488 - Plaintiff was injured when he imbibed broken glass in a sealed beverage bottle which defendant sold to storekeeper, who in turn sold it to plaintiff, who drank from it at the store. - Flaccomio v. Eysink, 129 Md. 367 Plaintiff sued a retail whiskey dealer, who sold him whiskey adulterated with wood alcohol, although labeled as "Pure Sherwood", and also the wholesale dealer from whom the retailer procured the whiskey - Plaintiff went blind after consuming a part of this whiskey at his home In the absence of any evidence to show that the wholesale dealer or his agents knew, or by the exercise of reasonable care could have known, that the whiskey contained wood alcohol, or that his agents were guilty of negligence in the purchase or sale of the whiskey, such wholesale dealer could not be held liable For such a suit against an immediate vendor to be maintainable, there must be some allegation and evidence of guilty knowledge, fraud, deceit or negligence of the defendant or his agents, or some statute imposing absolute liability upon the manufacturer or vendor in question Since there was in this case no allegation of a warranty of the article sold in any of the counts of the declaration, the Court of Appeals did not pass upon the sufficiency of evidence to support such an averment.

Sub-section 177(14)

Case 1 Case Case 3 FEDERAL EMPLOYERS' LIABILITY ACT Recent and Leading Cases Thereupon. 

Towing Co. v. Dean, 174 Md. 498 Plaintiff, a seaman, was injured due to defective flooring of boat Suit under the Jones Federal Act Approved prayers in such cases The alternative common law remedy of an action to recover compensatory damages, as distinguished from the allowance covered by the old maritime rules, may be enforced by a seaman through appropriate proceedings in personam on the common law side of both federal and state courts, upon the ground of negligence, the seaman, in such a suit, not only assuming the burden of proving negligence, but also, under the Federal Employer's Liability Act, sec. 3 (45 U. S. Code Ann, sec. 53), subjecting himself to a reduction of damages in proportion to any contributory negligence on his part. 

*Rudo v. Steamship Co., 168 Md. 281 Suit for injuries sustained by seaman on land, or on dock which was an extension of land Not within the purview of sec 33 

of the Jones or Merchant Marine Act of 1920.

Roueche v. Hotel Braddock, 164 Md. 620 Suit for loss of guest's baggage and money by fire in defendant's hotel 

Code, art. 71, secs. 5, 6, exempting an innkeeper, who furnishes a safe for the keeping of guests' money and other articles, from liability for the loss of money and articles not placed in the safe, does not apply in the case of money and effects which are necessary for the traveler's personal needs.

Coquelet v. Union Hotel Co., 139 Md. 544 Action against hotel proprietor for refusing to assign a room to plaintiff and her husband Malice - Punitive

Damages In the absence of malice or wantonness, or circumstances of aggravation, one can recover, on account of refusal of hotel accommodations, only such damages as were the immediate and necessary consequences of the wrongful act A rule of a hotel that persons without baggage shall not be given a room, in the absence of proper identification, is entirely reasonable.

*Gillet v. Shaw, 117 Md. 508 Infants and persons of unsound mind are liable for injuries caused by their tortious negligence, and so far as their responsibility is concerned they are held to the same degree of care and diligence as persons of sound mind and full age. This is necessary because otherwise there would be no redress for injuries committed by such persons But to hold an infant liable for a tort, the tortious act must be committed by him, himself, or under his immediate view or by his direction or authority - Where the guardian of an adjudged lunatic had purchased an automobile and engaged a chauffeur for him, for injuries caused by the automobile and the chauffeur out of the immediate view of the lunatic, and not by his direction or authority, neither the lunatic nor his property is liable.

Measure of damages in the case of an action for wrongful death, under Code, art. 67, as amended by Acts of 1929, of a class of dependents added by the Workmen's Compensation Act (This decision, insofar as it applies to funeral expenses, has since been altered by Statute). 

Dunnigan (State, use) v. Coburn, 171 Md. 23 The statute (Code, art. 67, sec. 1, as enlarged by Act of 1929) which gives a right to sue the personal representative of one responsible for the wrongful death of another, is in derogation of the common law, since it gives a right which did not exist at common law, and so must be construed strictly · Code, art. 67, sec. 1, as amended in 

1929, gives a right of action for wrongful death against the wrongdoer's executor or administrator, "provided" the action is brought within six calendar months after the wrongdoer's death - This provision, as to the time of bringing the action, is to be regarded as a condition precedent to the right to sue, and not as a limitation of the remedy, and consequently a declaration which fails to aver that the action was brought within six months after the wrongdoer's death is demurrable.

Limitations of doc- - Deford v. State, 30 Md. 179 In this leading case upon the law of "independent contractor" and "nuisance", the suit was brought to recover for the death of a pedestrian upon a sidewalk who was killed by the fall of a portion of the front wall of the defendant's building then under construction by defendant's contractors 

It was held that while the defendant was not liable for the acts of these contractors, yet, if it could be shown that the wall which was in course of erection on his premises, by his sanction, under his contract and for his use and benefit, was constructed in so defective and dangerous a manner as to constitute a nuisance, he would be responsible for the consequences resulting from the defective work allowed to be done by them.

Western Union Tel. Co. v. Fish, 148 Md. 210 - An action against defendant (telegraph company) on account of a mistake in transmission of message to plaintiff's agent

Obscurity of language - In order to charge a telegraph company with a loss resulting from its negligence in transmitting a message, it is necessary only that it be informed that it relates to a business transaction, and that loss will probably occur if it is altered or delayed, and it is unnecessary to apprise it of the details of the message If a telegraph message itself is clear enough to indicate that it relates to a business contract of importance, and that loss will probably result through negligence in its transmission, damages for such loss will *Taken from Jury.

Preston, 174 Md. 302 spiracy to ruin plaintiff financially by forcing into receivership corporations in which he was a large stockholder The test of a conspiracy, for the purpose of a civil suit, is whether the acts complained of are unlawful, and the plaintiff, as a result thereof, has been damaged - An act, which, if done by one alone, constitutes no ground of action on the case, cannot be made the ground of such action because done by and through a conspiracy of several, the fact of conspiracy being merely a matter of aggravation. - Suit by

Klingel's Pharmacy v. Sharpe & Dohme, 104 Md. 218

Sult to recover damages resulting from an illegal conspiracy - Combination to enhance prices to boycott and blacklist bination is a conspiracy in law whenever the act to be done has a necessary tendency to prejudice the public, or oppress individuals, by unjustly subjecting them to the power of the confederates, and giving effect to the purposes of the latter, whether of extortion or mischief; and the same proposition in one form of expression or another, is laid down in all the criminal law But an act which does not constitute a cause of action when done by one person does not become actionable merely because it has been done by conspirators; that an unlawful combination to do an act, which, if done, would injure another, does not of itself and without more, furnish a ground for a civil suit; and finally, as a corollary to the previous proposition, that though a conspiracy to do an injury exists a plaintiff cannot recover against the conspirators unless some act has been done in furtherance of the conspiracy which has resulted in damage to him.

Evening News Co. v. Bowie, 154 Md. 604; second appeal in 151 Md. 285; first appeal in 148 Md. 569 Libel suit by sheriff of county against newspaper owner for publication reflecting on his official conduct The presumption that words are defamatory arises much more readily in cases of libel than in cases of slander- Any unprivileged, false and malicious publication which, by printing, writing, signs or pictures, tends to expose a person to public scorn, hatred, contempt or ridicule, constitutes an actionable libel- Defendant, by pleading justification, assumed the burden of proving that plaintiff was guilty of such official delinquency.

Fertitta V. Herndon, 175 Md. 560 Suit to recover against partners for malicious prosecution through an alleged agent One who does not swear out the warrant cannot be held liable for "malicious prosecution" unless he instigated a criminal action against plaintiff or caused one to be maintained or voluntarily aided or assisted in its prosecution. 

Angelozzi v. Cossentino, 160 Md. 678 Suit by discharged employee for malicious prosecution and false imprisonment The fact that persons, summoned as witnesses on a criminal prosecution, testify falsely against the defendant therein, would not of itself support a verdict against them in an action for malicious prosecution.

Bugg, 156 Md. 36 Suit against a non-resident corporation for malicious prosecution of a civil attachment suit, which its local resident manager had instituted in order to collect a bill It was for the jury to determine whether the position of resident manager included within its scope, as a natural and appropriate means of accomplishing the purposes entrusted to him by the principal, the resort to attachment suits to compel the payment of bills.

§ 179 

TITLE 17 § 179. Recent and Leading Will Cases Addressed to Approved 

Issues.

The general rules, discussed in sections 96 to 102, by which to determine when a case, claim or defense can be taken from the jury, through the medium of a demurrer prayer, have been frequently applied to the trial of issues of fact sent from an Orphans' court to a court of law for determination by jury. 

Section 20 is devoted to a discussion of the trial of Orphans' 

court issues in courts of law.

Cases Relating to the Formation of Orphans' Court Issues 

In this section 179 we submit a list of recent and leading Will cases addressed, as may be observed, to the formation of issues in the Orphans' courts of Maryland.

Cases Relating to the Trial of Issues in Will Cases 

In this section 179 we also submit a list of recent and leading cases addressed, as may be observed, to the trial in courts of law of specific issues in Will cases.

Caveat to Will and 

Tatem v. Wright, 139 Md. 20, 21-28 to Codicils This is a leading case upon the propriety of the form of issues in Will cases- Many approved forms of such issues, and some disapproved forms, are set out in this case- - Issues should be framed concerning the matters set forth in the petition and answer, and should be so framed as to enable the jury to give a single answer one way or the other to the questions to be submitted- A caveat to a Will is a proceeding in rem, and all parties in interest need not be made parties to the proceeding. 

Berry v. Safe Deposit Co., 96 Md. 45; second appeal in 93 

Md. 560; first appeal in 93 Md. 240These three appeals in this leading Berry Will Case passed upon many phases of the law relating to issues in Will cases, including questions of evidence and the question of the legal sufficiency of the proof to sustain the issues, and especially the issue of mental capacity. 

Gross v. Burneston, 91 Md. 383 Upon a caveat to a will the issues sent from the Orphans' Court to a Court of Law for trial should be framed concerning the matter set forth in the petition and answer Where the averments of a petition attacked the will as a whole and alleged that it was not the will of the testatrix, that she lacked testamentary capacity, and that the will was procured by fraud and undue influence, the Orphans' Court properly refused to grant issues asked for by the executor, directing the jury to find what part or parts of the will, if any, were procured by undue influence or by fraud, since there had been so allegation that only a part of the will was void on account of fraud or undue influence. 

Munnikhuysen v. Magraw, 35 Md. 280, 282, 288-289 

This is a leading case upon the propriety of the form of issues in will cases The issues approved in this case, as well as those disapproved, are set out with the opinion The effect of a caveat to a will, and the sending of issues for trial to a court of law, is not to revoke the probate or suspend the powers of the executor These remain to await the final action of the Orphans' Court after the trial and verdict upon the issues.

Commission's "Decision" and Not Its Finding or Opinion is Reviewable

The statutory right of appeal is from the "decision" of the State Industrial Accident Commission, and not from its findings or opinion; and so if an order of the Commission is right and proper, it should be affirmed even where the Commission's findings are erroneous. The same rule was ap plied where the trial court affirmed, by way of a directed finding, a correct decision of the Commission upon an ⠀erroneous theory.4 "Prima Facie Correct" and "Burden of Proof" Provision

The last clause of section 56 of article 101 of the Code, as amended in 1935, relating to an appeal to a court of law from the "decision" of the State Industrial Accident Commission, 

"In all Court proceedings under or pursuant to the Article, the decision of the commission shall be prima facie correct and the burden of proof shall be upon the party attacking the same." 

Meaning of "Prima Facie Correct” and “Burden of Proof" Provision

While the meaning and effect of this "burden of proof" and "prima facie correct" provision is perfectly clear when applied to burden of proof prayers in Workmen's Compensation trials on appeal from the State Industrial Accident Commission, its influence upon demurrers to the evidence in such trials is not so clearly settled.5

TITLE 17 

7 "Burden of Proof" Prayers

In view of the language of the last clause of section 56 of article 101 of the Code, as amended in 1935, the party who prevailed before the State Industrial Accident Commission is ordinarily entitled to the grant of a prayer which informs the jury that the decision of the Commission is prima facie correct, and that the burden of proof is upon the party attacking the same, or, in other words, upon the party who appealed from the adverse decision of the Commission. 6 

Effect of "Prima Facie Correct" and "Burden of Proof"

Provision Upon Demurrers to the Evidence It has been said, again and again, that the provision of statute (Code, 1935 Supp. art. 101, sec. 56) which prescribes that the "decision" of the State Industrial Accident Commission "shall be prima facie correct and the burden of proof shall be upon the party attacking the same," does not mean that if no facts are established before the Commission sufficient to support its decision, that there is any burden of factual proof on the person attacking it, for the decision of the Commission cannot itself be accepted as the equivalent of facts which do not exist, and, in all cases, whether there is evidence legally sufficient to support the decision of the Commission is necessarily a matter of law to be decided by the court as any other question of law would be." 

On the other hand, where the decision of the Commission involves the consideration of conflicting evidence as to essential facts, or the deduction of permissible but diverse inferences therefrom, its solution of such conflict is presumed to be correct, and the burden of proof is upon the party attacking it to show that it was erroneous. But even there the burden may be one of persuasion rather than proof, for the appellant to overcome it need not produce additional evidence, but may rely upon the identical evidence before the

Commission. It is enough if he can convince the court or jury that the Commission erred in interpreting the facts or the inferences deducible therefrom, or in construing the law applicable thereto.8

Right to Directed Finding Upon Undisputed Facts 

It has been repeatedly said that where the facts are undisputed, and permit no inference consistent with the existence of a supposed or asserted right, the existence of such right, whether it arises before the Commission, the trial court, or the Court of Appeals itself, is an unmixed question of law; for if it were otherwise, the rights of the parties to proceedings under the statute would depend not upon the law but upon the unguided and unrestrained discretion of men.⁹ 

But the mere failure to offer testimony in denial of a fact given in evidence before the jury by the party who carried the burden of proving the fact in a Workmen's Compensation case on appeal, will not ordinarily entitle that party to an instructed verdict in his favor on the theory that it is an undisputed fact. In this connection, it should be observed, as is further stated in section 96, that a verdict cannot ordinarily be directed in favor of a litigant who carries the burden of proving the fact.10

Jury Question Where Any Legally Sufficient Evidence was Produced 

Finally, it seems correct to say, as a general rule, that if any legally sufficient evidence was produced before the jury in a Workmen's Compensation appeal in support of the issue of fact which the demurrer prayer under consideration asked

Proper Taking of Case From Jury Upon Improper Ground 

The appellate court may affirm the action of the trial court in taking a Workmen's Compensation case from the jury even where the trial court did so upon an inadequate legal ground, if the record of the case shows that the directed finding could have properly been made upon another and adequate legal ground.12

§ 181 

TITLE 17 § 181. Recent and Leading Workmen's Compensation Cases -Ad dressed to Approved Issues.

Section 21 is addressed to the practice of prayers and in structions in the trial of Workmen's Compensation Cases in courts of law, on appeal from the State Industrial Accident Commission. Section 180 is addressed to the question of when such cases can be taken from the jury through the medium of demurrer prayers. 

32 Separate Issues Nearly All Approved 

The great majority of the following 32 issues, all of which were employed in the trial of Workmen's Compensation Cases in courts of law, were seemingly approved as to form, either expressly or impliedly. On the other hand, several of those issues seem to be defective for having submitted, in effect, pure questions of law to the finding of the jury, or are no longer applicable, due to a subsequent change in the Workmen's Compensation Law.

The few issues which embody mere questions of law, or which are no longer appropriate because of a change in the 

Workmen's Compensation Law, are so indicated. The rea son for including such defective or inappropriate issues, as the case may be, was to enable the citation of the case or cases which discussed the branch of the Workmen's Compensation Law to which the issue under consideration was addressed.

Some "Approved" Issues Impliedly Submit a Question of Law 

However, it should be observed that, from a practical standpoint, some of the following "approved" issues of fact submit, impliedly at least, questions of law to the determination of the jury. For example, the following approved "Issue 

No. 2," namely, whether the claimant was an "Independent

Contractor," really requires the jury to determine whether the claimant was an independent contractor within the pur view or meaning of the Workmen's Compensation Law. But such issues have been approved, nevertheless, because there seems to be no better method for submitting them to the jury as supposed issues of fact.

Note To Above Issue No. 6 

Upon the above "Issue No. 6", as may be observed from the opinion in Tobacco Co. v. Goslin, 163 Md. 74, 78, it was decided that the claimant, a salesman, was not entitled to compensation under Code, article 101, section 32, sub-section 43, since his contract of employment was not made in the State of Maryland. 

However, the form of this issue was not passed upon in this case, since it appears that both sides employed this issue as the means for raising the aforesaid question of law. But this issue obviously presents no issue of fact whatsoever to the finding of the jury, as such issues should do as a matter of form. On the contrary, this issue presents a mere question of law that may apply, according to the wording of the issue, to any portion of the Workmen's Compensation Law.
